text:
THE BIGGEST SELLER OF A NEW SPINOFF IS OFTEN A FUND THAT NEVER LOOKED AT IT:

When a company splits one of its divisions off into a separate listed company, the new shares are not sold to anybody. They are handed out. Existing shareholders wake up owning two stocks where they owned one, and not one of them asked for the second.

That is the setup for the most useful idea in this corner of the market. For a short window after the split, a large share of the selling comes from holders who are required to sell and are not expressing any view about the business at all. Price and opinion come apart, on a schedule published in advance.

And here is the part most versions of this story leave out: a discount produced by mechanics is not the same thing as a bargain.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING

A spinoff is a distribution, not a sale. The parent hands its own shareholders shares in a subsidiary at a fixed ratio - one new share for every five held, say. No money changes hands, nothing is raised, and there is no offering price, because nothing is being offered.

That is where it differs from a company going public for the first time. In an IPO a company sells shares and takes in cash. In a spinoff the shares already belong to the parent's owners the moment the board says so.

THE ARITHMETIC, IN ROUND INVENTED NUMBERS

Nothing in this section is a real company.

100 shares at $50 is $5,000. The board spins off a division at one new share for every five held, so 20 new shares arrive. The new company opens at $10, worth $200. The parent, having handed a piece of itself away, is now worth about $48 a share, or $4,800.

$4,800 plus $200 is $5,000. Nothing was created and nothing was destroyed. One holding became two.

The cost basis - what the tax authorities treat as the price paid - splits the same way, by relative value. $48 of parent against $2 of spinoff per original share is 96% and 4%. So $48 of the original $50 stays with the parent shares and $2 moves to the new ones. Nothing is taxed on the day it happens; the tax arrives whenever either one is sold.

Nobody has to work that out alone. A company doing this files IRS Form 8937, the Report of Organizational Actions Affecting Basis of Securities, and posts it publicly. It is due within 45 days of the action or by January 15 of the following year, whichever comes first, and it states the split. A common convention for the values is the first day of ordinary trading, using the average of that day's high and low price for each company.

THE TAX RULE THAT MAKES IT FREE, AND WHAT IT QUIETLY GUARANTEES

Section 355 of the US tax code is what lets this happen without a tax bill for either side. Its conditions are worth knowing, because they describe what a spinoff is allowed to be.

- The parent must have control before it distributes: at least 80% of the voting power, and 80% of each class of shares that do not vote.
- Both companies must be actively running a business immediately afterward, and each of those businesses must have been running for at least five years.
- The split cannot be a disguised way of handing out accumulated profits, and it needs a real business reason beyond saving tax.

Read the second one again. A company spun off under that section is not a startup. By rule it is a business with at least five years of operating history behind it, which is more than a newly listed company usually offers.

THE TWO-YEAR HANDCUFF

There is a companion rule, Section 355(e). If 50% or more of either company - measured by votes or by value - is acquired as part of a plan that includes the split, the parent owes tax on the whole distribution. Any acquisition inside two years of the split is presumed to be part of such a plan. That presumption can be argued against, but it is the starting position.

The practical effect: a freshly spun-off company generally cannot be taken over for about two years without wrecking the tax treatment the entire exercise was built around. So the "somebody will just buy it" story has a date attached, and the date is roughly two years out.

WHO THE FORCED SELLERS ARE

Now the part that explains the price.

On September 14, 2015, S&P Dow Jones Indices - the firm behind the best-known US stock market benchmarks - announced one standard for how spinoffs enter its US indexes, effective for splits dated on or after October 1, 2015. The spun-off company is added at a price of zero after the close on the day before it begins trading separately. If it does not qualify for that index in its own right, it is removed on the first day of ordinary trading.

That is not a market opinion. It is a timetable.

An index fund's whole job is to hold what the index holds. It receives the new shares because the parent holding entitled it to them, the new company leaves the index almost immediately, and the fund sells. The decision was made by a rulebook, on a date published beforehand, by people who are not permitted to care whether the business is any good.

A second group has the same problem and no rulebook to point at. A fund that owns only large companies has just been handed a small one. A fund that owns one industry has been handed a company from another. A fund that requires a dividend has been handed something that pays nothing yet. None of them are selling because they looked.

And here is the honest half. That selling is real and it is documented, and it is also entirely public - the eligibility rules are published, the dates are published, and anyone can read both. Mechanical selling explains why a price might be set by people with no view. It is not evidence that the price is wrong.

THE DOCUMENT THAT ARRIVES BEFORE THE PRICE DOES

Because no shares are being sold, a US spinoff registers with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 10 rather than the Form S-1 an IPO uses. Form 10 registers a class of shares; S-1 registers shares being sold. The SEC reviews and comments on it either way, and the information statement that goes with it usually reads like a prospectus - it simply has no price on the cover, because nothing is priced.

So on day one there is a full description of the business, several years of numbers, the management team and the risks, all filed weeks earlier. What there is not is a price history, an analyst following it, or a bank that spent a month telling people the story.

Four things in that document do most of the work:

- WHICH SIDE GOT THE DEBT. The parent decides how much borrowing leaves with the spinoff, and often takes a cash payment from the new company on the way out. Set the debt the new company carries against the cash the business generates - what is left after running it and paying for equipment.
- HOW REAL THE HISTORY IS. Those years of financials are carve-out accounts: what the division would have earned alone, including an assigned share of head-office costs. Assigned is not the same as incurred, and standalone costs afterward are usually higher rather than lower.
- WHAT STILL TIES IT TO THE PARENT. Transition services agreements, where the parent keeps running payroll or computer systems for a fee for a year or two. Supply agreements. Who covers whom for old liabilities. A company earning a large slice of its revenue from its former parent is not independent yet.
- WHO RUNS IT AND HOW THEY ARE PAID. A division head is now a chief executive with a share price attached.

THE TWO PRICES THAT EXIST BEFORE THE SHARES DO

Briefly, because this trips people up every time. Between the record date - the cutoff for who is entitled to the new shares - and the day they are actually handed over, the new company can trade on a "when-issued" basis: a conditional market in something not yet issued. It typically opens the trading day before the record date and closes on distribution day. Through that stretch the parent trades in two markets at once, one carrying the entitlement to the new shares and one without it. Anyone owed a fraction of a share is paid in cash instead.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE

It runs both ways, and the honest version has to say so. Sometimes a parent spins off the half it wanted rid of - the shrinking business, the one carrying the borrowings - and the sellers, mechanical or not, turn out to have been right. A smaller company with one line of business and no larger balance sheet behind it is genuinely more fragile than the thing it left. And the discount, if there is one, is measured against a value nobody has published, because these shares have no past.

What a split reliably produces is a stretch of time in which the price is being set for reasons that have nothing to do with the business. It produces a reason to look. It does not produce an answer.

WHERE THIS SITS IN THE LEN5ES

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 hunts a business priced under what it looks worth, or one carrying a dated event that has not played out - and a spinoff is close to the definition of that second half. The event comes with a calendar: the day it starts trading separately, the index removal, the two-year window in which it effectively cannot be sold to anyone. What that Len5 asks is not whether the shares fell, but whether anything about the business explains why.

The Quality-Value Len5 wants a durable business at a fair price, and a split hands it a gift and a trap in the same envelope. The gift is that five-year rule: a real operating record to judge durability against. The trap is that the record was kept inside somebody else's accounts, with head-office costs assigned rather than paid.

The Growth Len5 wants expansion you are not overpaying for, and the question a split raises is whether the growth was ever the division's own. A business that grew because a large parent funded it may not grow the same way once it pays its own bills. The reverse happens too: a division starved of money for years because it was never the parent's priority now decides for itself.

The Income Len5 watches cash genuinely reaching owners and genuinely funded by the business. New spinoffs frequently pay nothing at all. And the parent's own payment can move, because the earnings behind part of it just walked out the door.

The Momentum Len5 watches a name already breaking out on news of its own, and this is the one style a brand-new spinoff cannot speak to: a chart with two weeks on it is not a trend, and a rulebook wrote most of those two weeks. Hypergrowth watches early, fast-growing disruptors, and the five-year test rules out early by construction.

Every other holding in an account is there because somebody chose it. A spinoff is there because a board mailed it out. That difference has a short shelf life - a few weeks, while the mechanical selling works through - and then the shares are just another company, priced by people who did look.

Not investment advice.

The U.S. Air Force is preparing to keep the RQ-4 Global Hawk flying well into the 2030s, with a 17 August contracting notice outlining modernisation and sustainment potentially through June 2033, according to Army Recognition.

The service intends to award Northrop Grumman a sole-source contract covering development, retrofit and sustainment from January 2028 to June 2033 — a one-year base, four one-year options and a six-month option.

Global Hawk offers more than 34 hours of endurance, a ceiling of about 18,300 m (60,000 ft) and long-range radar surveillance for persistent ISR across Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

The work goes beyond maintenance to hardware and software upgrades, integration, logistics and training. The Air Force said it lacks the technical data to compete the work to another contractor.
Current law bars retiring the RQ-4 or cutting sustainment ahead of divestment through 30 September 2030. 

The planned support would run almost three years beyond that. No successor aircraft is named in the notice.

text:
Jellyfish took three of the six reactors at France’s Gravelines nuclear plant offline this summer and cut a fourth to half power, as they shut Scotland’s Torness for a week in 2011, because a plant that swallows a canal of seawater to stay cool has no defense against a bloom except to stop | Brendan Brown, ScienceBlog

Just before midnight on August 10, the largest nuclear power station in Western Europe began switching itself off. At Gravelines, on the French coast between Dunkirk and Calais, three of the six 900-megawatt reactors tripped offline in succession as the filter drums of their seawater pumping stations clogged solid, and by morning a fourth unit had been cut to half power. With a fifth already down for maintenance, a plant capable of powering millions of homes was reduced, for days, to a single reactor running flat out.

The attacker was not a storm, a strike or a cyberweapon. It was barrel jellyfish, Rhizostoma octopus, a creature that is 95 percent water, has no brain, and cannot swim against a current, arriving in a swarm so dense that local fishermen eventually hauled 26 tonnes of them out of the intake channels.

The soft spot in a hard machine

A nuclear plant is armored against almost everything, but its one non-negotiable appetite is cooling water. Gravelines drinks from a canal connected to the North Sea, swallowing enormous volumes continuously to condense steam and cool equipment, and that water arrives through intakes guarded by rotating drum screens designed to strain out debris. The screens are the soft spot. A jellyfish bloom is, from the filter’s point of view, the sea turning to wet gelatin: thousands of tonnes of soft bodies that pull apart, pack into mesh, and renew themselves endlessly from the water column. When the screens can no longer pass enough water, the reactors do the only safe thing available and shut themselves down automatically, exactly as designed. EDF’s statements each time stress that safety was never at issue, and that is true; the jellyfish cannot break a nuclear plant. They can only make it stop, which, for a machine whose product is measured by the hour, is expensive enough.

What makes Gravelines the case study is the sequel structure. The same thing happened at the same plant, on nearly the same date, the year before: in August 2025 a swarm jammed the pumping stations, all four operating reactors tripped, and with the other two already in maintenance the entire station went dark, taking some ten days to fully reconnect. EDF responded with money and hardware, hundreds of thousands of euros’ worth of cameras, thermal imagers and three fishing boats trawling preventively around the intakes day and night. This August 11 the bloom came anyway, and by the operator’s own admission the swarm grew faster than the patrol boats could work. A unit restarted on August 18 was knocked out again within days by a fresh influx. Against a bloom, the state of the art is a net and a hope.

An old enemy, thriving

None of this is new, which is rather the point. In the summer of 2011, moon jellyfish swamped the intakes at Torness on Scotland’s east coast and shut both of its reactors for about a week while crews scooped the screens clear. Sweden’s Oskarshamn plant, then the site of one of the world’s largest boiling-water reactors, was stopped for days by a bloom in 2013. Japan’s coastal plants have battled giant Nomura’s jellyfish; plants in Israel, Florida and California have throttled or tripped on gelatin; and France’s Paluel station, up the Channel coast from Gravelines, lost reactors to a swarm barely a month after the 2025 Gravelines blackout. The industry has a folder for these events, and the folder is getting thicker.

The thickening is the story’s second layer. Jellyfish are among the few marine animals for whom the modern ocean keeps improving: warming water extends their breeding seasons and speeds reproduction, overfishing removes both their predators and their competitors for plankton, and coastal construction offers endless hard surfaces for their polyp stage to colonize. Marine scientists argue about whether jellyfish are rising globally or oscillating locally, but the operators of seawater-cooled plants are not waiting on the literature; EDF’s patrol boats, and the bloom-forecasting systems being trialled around the North Sea, are bets that the problem is structural. It is a neat irony that the low-carbon power source most often promoted as an answer to warming seas keeps being interrupted by one of warming’s clearest beneficiaries.

The moral of the gelatin

There is a temptation to file the jellyfish shutdowns under nature’s revenge, and the marketing writes itself: the brainless blob versus the atom. The engineering reality is less poetic and more instructive. Every thermal power station, nuclear, coal or gas, is a heat engine that must reject heat, and the ones parked on coastlines solved that problem by assuming the sea would always be available as an infinite, well-behaved coolant. The assumption held for decades because the sea’s contents were an afterthought. A bloom inverts it: the coolant arrives pre-mixed with more biology than any screen can process, and the mightiest machine on the coast discovers that its output depends on plankton dynamics it neither controls nor predicts.

The reactors at Gravelines came back, as they always do, once the screens were cleared and the sea thinned out. The jellyfish will also come back, on something close to an annual schedule, and the plant’s defense next August will be what it was this August: boats, cameras, and the willingness to stop. Against an enemy that is mostly water, arriving by the tonne through the one pipe you cannot close, stopping is not a failure of the design. It is the design, and the jellyfish have learned nothing, planned nothing, and won anyway, twice.

🚨 #BREAKING: Qatar Charity @qcharity to build first seawater desalination plant in #Somaliland, in co-operation with Somailand's Ministry of Water.

In co-operation with Somaliland’s Ministry of Water development, Qatar Charity (QC) has launched the first seawater desalination plant in Somaliland.

The project aims to provide a sustainable source of drinking water and enhance water security as the city continues to face persistent challenges in accessing clean water.

Valued at approximately $500,000, the project offers a practical model for innovative responses to water scarcity.

It is expected to improve regular access to safe drinking water, reduce reliance on unsafe or remote water sources, and strengthen water security, with positive implications for public health, living conditions, and economic activity in the coastal city.

Somaliland’s Minister of Water Development Mohamed Abdulmalik Ahmed described the project as a major milestone for Zeila, saying that it would help mitigate the impact of water shortages and improve residents’ access to safe drinking water. He noted that the plant will produce around 150 cubic metres of desalinated water per day, supported by storage tanks with a total capacity of 250 cubic metres.

The facility is also equipped with an integrated solar-powered system to ensure sustainable operation and reduce operating costs.

#Qatar #QatarCharity

text:
I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.

The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.

Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.

Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.

The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.

Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.

The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.

Lady Antebellum became Lady A.

Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”

Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.

Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.

Then there were the military bases.

Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.

Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.

Fort Benning became Fort Moore.

Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.

Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.

Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.

Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.

Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.

Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.

We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.

Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. 😎

Attention XRP Holders: Shift Your Focus Beyond Price! 🚨

As your XRP holdings grow, it's crucial to consider aspects beyond just the asset's market value. Ownership, custody, protection, and succession planning become increasingly important.

Purchasing XRP is just the beginning. Depending on your unique situation, it may be beneficial to consult with qualified legal and tax professionals about establishing an LLC or a trust.

Here are some essential planning considerations:

• Ownership Structure: Understand how your digital assets are held.
• Access and Control: Determine who can access your assets in case of unforeseen circumstances.
• Estate and Inheritance Planning: Ensure your assets are passed on according to your wishes.
• Long-Term Asset Management: Plan for the administration of your digital assets over time.
• Separation of Business and Personal Activities: Keep your investments organized and distinct.
• Documenting Your Strategy: Create a clear plan for managing your digital assets.

Don't overlook the importance of custody. Keeping your XRP on a centralized exchange means you're dependent on that platform for access and withdrawals. Self-custody offers greater control but comes with the responsibility of securely managing your private keys and recovery information.

There is no universal solution; the best approach depends on your individual needs. 

Educate yourself about your options before they're needed. I've compiled a comprehensive guide covering LLCs, trusts, XRP custody, and long-term digital asset planning.

text:
Paul Ronzheimer just gave us the most unintentionally perfect political display in years. He rolls into the office of Hans-Thomas Tillischneider, the AfD heavyweight in Saxony-Anhalt. He’s positioned to become education minister if the party keeps polling at 40 percent ahead of those regional elections. Friendly chat about German problems. Peace marches outside screaming that Ukraine is sucking the country dry. The usual isolationist script. Then the camera catches the black mug on the shelf. Bold red star. Cyrillic lettering: ARMY OF RUSSIA. Souvenir, sure. Tillischneider immediately starts sweating bullets. Claims he cannot remember who gave it to him. Pivots to the matryoshka dolls and the samovar like some confused tourist who accidentally collected Kremlin merch. He tries to hide the mug in a cupboard that refuses to cooperate. The journalist politely asks if there is perhaps a Bundeswehr mug somewhere in the collection. Of course not. not a gotcha about bad taste in office decor. The live demonstration shows how deeply the pro-Russian current runs inside the AfD leadership. The man is a senior figure in the movement.m. He is the ideological brain behind a party that could soon control education policy in one of Germany's key eastern states. And his reflexive instinct when caught is to lie, deflect, and treat the Russian army mug like radioactive evidence. He will not own whatever twisted nostalgia it represents. The German expression writes itself: Nicht alle Tassen im Schrank. Not all cups in the cupboard. The voters will not miss the joke.

Look at the broader picture. AfD has spent years laundering Kremlin talking points about NATO expansion, Ukrainian corruption, and the need to end this tiresome war so Germans can have cheaper gas. Their competitors on the left are recycled communists with identical reflexes toward Moscow. Sarah Wagenknecht's outfit offers the same anti-Ukraine poison with a different ideological wrapper. Meanwhile the Christian Democrats under Merz understand they are bleeding support to people who sound like the CDU of the 1990s but carry Russian army crockery. The entire German political class is trapped in a loop. Confronting reality means admitting that years of energy dependence, cheap Russian narratives, and deliberate blindness to hybrid threats have produced a political force that keeps genuine Russian army memorabilia as lifestyle accessories.

Ukraine cannot afford European politicians who treat the war as a distant inconvenience to be negotiated away the moment domestic polls tighten. Every AfD office that looks like a Moscow gift shop is proof that the Kremlin still maintains political infrastructure inside NATO countries. They do not need tanks in Berlin when useful idiots will carry water for them in state parliaments. The mug is not the problem. The worldview that proudly displays it while pretending neutrality is the problem. And that worldview is gaining ground because too many mainstream actors spent years downplaying the threat. They never dismantled the networks that feed it.

The irony is brutal. AfD spent a decade preparing for its breakthrough. It positioned itself as the only party that truly speaks for ordinary Germans tired of migration, green policies, and endless foreign entanglements. Then a Russian army mug surfaces at the worst possible moment and reminds everyone that part of their DNA still answers to the old imperial power in the east. Moscow cannot win on the battlefield in Ukraine, so it wins by exporting its rot into European domestic politics. Tillischneider fumbling that mug on camera is a small but perfect illustration of how that strategy works in practice: cultivate fellow travelers, let them rise, watch them normalize what should be radioactive.

Germany under Merz was supposed to mark a turning point after Scholz's strategic sleepwalking. Pistorius has been solid on defense spending. But the eastern states are sliding toward parties that treat Russian imperialism as a legitimate conservative position. If AfD takes real power anywhere with attitudes like this on display, expect immediate pressure to loosen sanctions. Expect pressure to question NATO commitments. Expect pressure to frame Ukrainian resistance as the real obstacle to peace. That cannot be allowed to become German policy. Not while Ukrainian forces are still absorbing the bulk of the Kremlin's military machine to keep the nightmare from reaching the Rhine.

The cupboard is missing more than one cup in Saxony-Anhalt. It is missing strategic clarity across much of the European political spectrum. Until that changes, every exposed Russian mug, every leaked conversation, every Wagenknecht-Tillischneider flirtation is another data point proving that the information war is concrete. It sits on shelves in politicians' offices and waits for the next election cycle to do its damage. Ukraine's job remains the same: survive, strike back with drones and sanctions pressure, and force the West to confront the fact that tolerating this fifth column is not neutrality. It is slow-motion strategic suicide.

text:
OTD in 1778, the Stockbridge militia was devastated at the Battle of Kingsbridge, near present-day Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx.

The unit, made up largely of Mohican, Wappinger, and Munsee men from Stockbridge, Massachusetts, had served with the Continental Army since early in the Revolution. Among those killed was Wappinger leader Daniel Nimham, a prominent advocate for his people’s land rights.

The battle had little effect on the course of the war, but its consequences for the Stockbridge community were profound. The unit was shattered as a fighting force, and Nimham’s death weakened Native efforts to resist dispossession in the Hudson Valley.

The Stockbridge had allied with the American cause partly to protect their lands and autonomy. American victory would offer them little protection from settler expansion.

text:
The Three Pillars (Force, Fraud, or Coercion): To prosecute a crime like trafficking or severe exploitation, the law requires proof that the defendant used one of three concrete things. "Force" is physical violence; "fraud" is active deception (such as lying about a job offer, marriage, or financial security to trap someone); and legal "coercion" requires a specific scheme, plan, or pattern intended to make a person believe they will suffer serious harm, legal ruin, or physical restraint if they try to leave.
​Systemic Isolation vs. Bad Choices: Courts look closely at power dynamics. A toxic relationship or a manipulative partner involves bad choices between two free adults. Criminal exploitation, however, involves systematic deprivation of liberty—such as confiscating passports, controlling all access to money, threatening family members, or constant psychological intimidation designed to destroy a person's independent agency.
​The Burden of Proof: The legal system completely rejects the idea that an adult's vulnerability excuses a predator, but it also rejects convicting someone based solely on "feeling manipulated." Prosecutors must present hard evidence—such as financial records, digital communications showing systematic threats, or witness testimony documenting a pattern of control—to prove that a victim's free will was systematically overridden by design.

Hyderabad to become India’s global knowledge hub    

Highlights

•University of London campus in Hyderabad soon  
•Northeastern University to explore establishing offshore campus at Bharat Future City
•Harvard University expressed intent to begin short-term courses for government, corporate professionals in Hyderabad
•Virginia Tech to bring industry-aligned, future-ready learning frameworks in Telangana 
•London School of Economics (LSE), School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) to explore course offerings, offshore classrooms in Hyderabad
•Oxford University to explore setting up of shared research centres, centres of excellence (CoE) in state
•World-class faculty from major universities to come to Hyderabad to offer specialized higher education courses
•$3 trillion Telangana Rising vision rises with partnership with world's best educational institutions 

The Telangana Rising delegation led by Hon'ble Chief Minister Shri A. Revanth Reddy, along with IT and Industries Minister Shri D. Sridhar Babu, and comprising officials Mrs Santha Kumari, Vice Chairperson of Dr MCR HRD Institute, Mr K Ramakrishna Rao, Advisor to CM and Ex-officio Special Chief Secretary and Mr N. Sridhar, Principal Secretary, CMO, during their visit to the United Kingdom, and the officers’ tour to United States from August 19 to 29, scored major wins towards the goal of transforming Hyderabad into India's first and biggest global knowledge hub. 

Hyderabad, a powerhouse in software, pharma, life sciences, manufacturing, and a rising power in defence and aerospace, will soon be transformed into India's first global knowledge hub with the presence of America's Ivy League and the best educational institutions from Europe and Asia. 

Northeastern University (Boston) and the University of London, a federation of 17 independent schools in England, will be setting up their first offshore campus in India, in Hyderabad. 

London School of Economics (LSE) and School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), during their very fruitful discussions with the delegation agreed to send teams to explore setting up offshore schools, supporting industry interaction, improving pedagogical methods, classroom interaction models, and bringing their faculty to be stationed here. 

Harvard University has expressed intent to start their short-term executive education programmes for senior government and corporate officials at Dr MCR HRD Institute in Hyderabad. 

The TelanganaRising team had fruitful discussions with representatives, top leadership, senior faculty members and administrators from Oxford University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, London Business School, Cambridge University and Imperial College London. 

Hon'ble Chief Minister held a meeting with officials to review the trip and the progress made, and gave directions on the way forward. He asked officials to lead, manage and oversee the realization of the vision to create the global knowledge hub and to bring the world's best academic institutions – universities, colleges and schools – to Hyderabad through collaborations or offshore campuses so they may offer their certification programmes and courses here with utmost focus and dedication. 

"I am happy and proud to share with my four crore people of Telangana that our vision to transform Telangana into a $3 trillion economy by 2047, with an intermediary goal of $1 tn by 2034, has received a big boost with the successful conclusion of agreements, memorandums of agreement and letters of intent with some of the best institutions of the world. We will bring the best educational offerings to the youth and children of not only Telangana but entire India," said Chief Minister Revanth Reddy, summarising the highly successful tour to the UK.  

Chief Minister Reddy encouraged youth and children to use these institutions to become best professionals globally and contribute to the vision of Telangana Rising. 

Officials who went to the USA and met teams from Northeastern University, Virginia Tech University and concluded agreements successfully briefed the Chief Minister about the details of the discussions and explained that more agreements will follow soon. 

The Chief Minister, who holds the education portfolio, has made education, skills and sports for youth and children one of his flagship drives and is rejuvenating and revitalising the entire education system from nursery, KG, primary, middle and high school, skilling and sports education, and has made massive investments into the infrastructure in Telangana public schools, Young India Integrated Residential Schoos, Young India Physical Education and Sports University, polytechnics and the transformation of ITI into Advanced Technology Centres (ATCs). 
IT and Industries Minister Shri D. Sridhar Babu, who led the meeting with the London Business School, said, "Historically, Hyderabad has grown in the knowledge economy, be it software, pharma, life sciences, research and GCCs, because of our excellent manpower trained by our wonderful tech and engineering colleges, business schools, medical colleges and universities. With the creation of a global knowledge hub in Hyderabad, there will be an exponential growth in the state with the entry of even more GCCs and companies in Telangana. Our skills university, ATC and polytechnics will also ensure skilled blue-collar workers, which will give a massive leg up in developing manufacturing activity in our state."

Speaking about the successful tour, Mrs Santhi Kumari said, "We will begin classes, especially short-term classes and executive programmes at our Dr MCR HRD Institute campus. Classrooms are being redeveloped and redesigned for the purpose of world class education dissemination. People of Hyderabad and India, be it government officers and PSU employees and private employees, can participate in educational programmes from these great institutions from Hyderabad soon." 

Speaking about the programmes, Mr Ramakrishna Rao said, “We will develop the global knowledge hub in Hyderabad, with different facilities coming up at the MCR-HRD campus, and in the future, at the Bharat Future City." 

Chief Minister Revanth Reddy also instructed officials to ensure that the Invest Telangana Global Summit on December 7, 8 and 9, also had a separate track on global educational institutions and sports facilities and their impact on the state.

I'll paste it for you again:

The chart in that post is drawn from a March 2025 survey of 1,005 Jewish Israelis. It was commissioned by Penn State historian Tamir Sorek, fielded by the Israeli firm Geocartography Knowledge Group, and first reported in Haaretz.

The questions measured support for:
Forced expulsion (“transfer”) of Gaza residents
Forced expulsion of Arab citizens of Israel
The idea that the IDF, when taking an enemy city, should act as the Israelites did at Jericho under Joshua — i.e., kill all inhabitants

Overall results reported in the articles:
82% supported expulsion of Gaza residents
56% supported expulsion of Israeli Arabs
47% agreed with the Jericho/killing-all-inhabitants framing

The religious-observance breakdowns on the graphic match the figures circulated from that survey:
Gaza expulsion: Secular 70%, Traditional 91%, Orthodox 90%, Haredi 97%
Israeli Arabs: Secular 38%, Traditional 65%, Orthodox 68%, Haredi 91%
Kill all residents of a conquered city: Secular 31%, Traditional 60%, Orthodox 59%, Haredi 63%

Sorek later published a fuller academic write-up of the same survey (Ethnic and Racial Studies, Dec 2025). Other Israeli polls from the same period found high but not identical support for “evacuation” or “transfer” of Gazans (often in the 60–75% range among Jews, depending on wording and whether “don’t know” was offered). Some analysts argued the Sorek/Geocartography wording and response options produced higher “support” numbers than other instruments.

That is the dataset behind the image.

text:
Calling this a “BIG MESSAGE TO AMERICA” makes for a powerful headline, but foreign policy deserves a little more context.

Before portraying India’s latest engagement with Iran as some dramatic response to Washington, it is worth going back to the India US trade framework announced in February 2026 and looking at what India itself was prepared to offer.

India agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and a wide range of American agricultural and food products, including tree nuts such as almonds and walnuts, fresh and processed fruits, soybean oil, animal feed products, wine and spirits.

India also agreed to address long standing barriers affecting US medical devices, remove restrictive import licensing procedures affecting American ICT products, and work towards accepting US developed or international standards in identified sectors.

On digital trade, both countries agreed to work towards rules addressing barriers considered discriminatory or burdensome.

And perhaps the biggest commercial commitment of all:

India stated its intention to purchase $500 billion worth of US energy products, aircraft and aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products and coking coal over the next five years.

The framework specifically envisages increased trade in technology products, including GPUs and equipment used in data centres.

Of course, America is not giving India nothing in return.

The US agreed to an 18% reciprocal tariff rate on originating Indian goods and, subject to successful conclusion of the agreement, proposed removal of reciprocal tariffs on categories including generic pharmaceuticals, gems and diamonds and aircraft parts. Certain aircraft related tariffs would also be removed, while India would receive preferential treatment for specified automotive parts.

So this is clearly a negotiation involving give and take on both sides, not a simple story of one country surrendering to another. The official framework itself describes these as reciprocal and mutually beneficial commitments. 

Now come to Iran.

PM Modi today reiterated India's long standing relationship with Tehran and explicitly said India wants to expand and diversify its trade basket with Iran. 

That is certainly significant, particularly when new American sanctions are creating additional difficulties for trade with Iran. Indian exporters are already dealing with payment, shipping, insurance and logistics complications arising from the sanctions environment. 

But why must this automatically become a “BIG MESSAGE TO AMERICA”?

Iran has its own strategic importance for India through Chabahar, connectivity with Central Asia, regional security, energy considerations and trade. Maintaining that relationship serves India's independent interests.

That is what strategic autonomy should actually look like.

India can negotiate a massive commercial relationship with Washington, offer tariff and market access concessions, commit to substantially higher purchases of American products and seek concessions for Indian exports in return.

At the same time, India can expand its relationship with Tehran wherever Indian interests require it.

These two things do not have to contradict each other.

Every diplomatic development need not be converted into “India versus America”, “Modi versus Trump”, “surrender” or “strong reply.”

Foreign policy is not a social media contest.

That is not surrender to America. But neither is engagement with Iran automatically defiance of America.

It is diplomacy and strategic balancing.

The questions we should really be asking are much more substantive:

What did India offer? What did America offer? What commitments are actually binding? What does India gain economically and strategically? What are the costs? And does final outcomes match India's National Interest.

That is a far more meaningful way to evaluate India's foreign policy than turning every diplomatic engagement into a **“BIG MESSAGE TO AMERICA.”**

text:
Top 10 Foreign Companies for 2026 Revealed

An old friend who had worked at Microsoft for eight years posted a photo of his workstation. The caption consisted of just two words: "Goodbye."
But I understand that feeling; after eight years at a company—where every sticker and trinket on the desk holds a story—simply walking away is significant.
It reminds me of five years ago when we were pulling all-nighters at a foreign tech firm in Wangjing; he used to say, "This 'iron rice bowl' at a foreign company is something to cherish."
Let’s start with the tech sector.
Everyone in the industry knows about the restructuring of Microsoft’s Azure R&D teams this year. Employees in Beijing and Shanghai received email notifications, but the real story was the severance package: a base of "N+4" months' salary, up to a maximum of "N+7."
They call this "paid graduation." Just think about that term—in foreign companies, even saying goodbye is done with dignity.
Of course, Microsoft’s benefits remain top-tier. Full-time employees get 15 days of fully paid annual leave and 15 days of fully paid sick leave per year; there’s no time-clock punching, work hours are flexible, and remote work is supported. The cafeteria offers a choice of Chinese and Western cuisine, snacks and drinks are unlimited, and there are even nap pods for your midday rest.
Then there’s Google, which has claimed the number one spot globally. I won't even list the standard perks—social insurance and housing funds, stock options, paid leave, and regular health checkups. The key is that they truly practice flexible work: as long as the job gets done, nobody cares what time you arrive.

text:
Doug Gilchrist is Kelowna’s city manager. He is the unelected boss of city staff. His job is to protect the public interest and explain big spending in plain English. The problem is he helped the city swallow a failed private hotel and then talked like you were stupid for noticing.

Here is what happened. For years an Edmonton developer, Westcorp (Philip Milroy’s company, Gail Temple the public face) promised a huge hotel on the old Willow Inn site at 289 Queensway. Permits were issued. Permits died. The lot stayed a parking lot. In October 2025 the City of Kelowna paid 27.8 million dollars for that lot, an office on Pandosy, and the downtown marina. Taxpayers were told after the fact. No referendum. Staff said the loan from the Municipal Finance Authority was under the legal borrowing cap so you did not get a vote. Mayor Tom Dyas sold it as vision. Gilchrist sold it as the city taking the driver’s seat. Westcorp still got to manage the marina, the office, and the parking after they cashed out.

That is the accountability hole. A private project that could not get financed became public debt. The seller kept the keys. The highest paid man in city hall, Gilchrist, about 374,000 dollars, went on camera excited, offered his phone number, and treated criticism like a misunderstanding. Sharron Simpson called it a bailout. Ron Cannan asked what it had to do with water and roads. The Taxpayers Federation said stop playing developer. Gilchrist’s answer was marketing. If he wants the title, he puts the purchase contract, the Westcorp management deal, the MFA terms, and the three to five year flip risk in public with his name on it. Until he does that, he is not accountable. He is just the guy who made a stalled hotel sound like a win.

text:
$INTC The Motley Fool: CEO Lip-Bu Tan Just Gave 12 Million Reasons to Buy Intel Stock

 -- Excellent article by Billy Duberstein below on Intel -- 

In early August, Intel raised $23 billion in equity at $95 per share, up from an initial target of $15 billion. In conjunction, CEO Lip-Bu Tan personally bought $12 million worth of stock as part of the offering.

Just one month before, on Intel's July earnings call, CFO David Zinsner said Intel wouldn't raise more money unless it did "extremely well" in attracting demand for its foundry. After the capital raise at the recent Deutsche Bank Technology Conference on Aug. 26, Zinsner shed more light on how the new billions will be used.

The answers were tremendously bullish, making Intel's current stock price, which sits even below the recent offering price, look like a bargain.

Intel is filling its fabs as fast as it can

While there is a possibility that Intel will use $15 billion of the offering to buy out Brookfield Infrastructure Partners, which owns 49% of Intel's existing Arizona fabs, Zinsner hinted that the new funds will probably go toward new fabs. Zinsner pointed out that Intel must commit to buying a large amount of chipmaking equipment over the next few years, which will require a stronger financial backstop.

The details point to a massive amount of new capacity coming online. Intel will be expanding capacity at its existing Fab 34 in Ireland, which produces the Intel 3 node, along with Fab 52 in Arizona, which produces Intel's new 18A node. Intel is also finishing tooling up Fab 62, another massive Arizona fab next to 52 that will produce 18A variants and possibly 14A, Intel's next node.

But that's not all. At the conference, Zinsner also described how Intel will convert some of its Oregon facilities, which are typically research "pilot" lines, into higher-volume manufacturing lines to support 14A as soon as possible. In addition, Zinsner said Intel was moving as "fast as it could" to build out its Ohio fabs:

"There is the ability to have eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio. Mod one is the one obviously we are working on right now. If we could make it go faster, we would. We are going as fast as we can to get that one ready."

It should be noted that before the agentic AI revolution took off, Intel had slowed the build-out of the Ohio fab system. In early 2025, Intel said it was delaying the opening of that fab until at least 2030, pushed back from an initial target of 2026. Well, today Intel is looking to bring that on "as fast as possible," probably in 2028 or 2029. That's quite a change in the span of a year.

Mods one and two will cost a reported $28 billion, which is roughly the same amount invested in Fabs 52 and 62 in Arizona. In other words, this is a massive amount of capacity in addition to Intel's near-term build.

Finally, Zinsner didn't mention Intel's Fab 38 in Israel, where construction was suspended in mid-2025. However, that Fab "shell" is already complete, and would probably be the fastest to market for producing chips outside of Fab 62. Some commentators have recently pointed to increased activity at the Israel fab and to a new site facility operator position that has been posted. That suggests Intel is also likely looking to equip Fab 38 with tools.

Keep in mind that Fab 34 in Ireland, where Intel makes Intel 3, and Fab 52, where 18A production is ongoing, aren't even at full capacity yet. So when you factor in Fab 62, the first two Ohio fabs, Israel Fab 38, and an expansion of its Oregon facility, Intel's internal capacity should increase severalfold over the next few years.

Given that last quarter's revenue was already over $16 billion, indicating a $65 billion annualized run rate, Intel's revenue could theoretically approach $200 billion over a few years if it fills all these fabs it is now accelerating.

Why is Intel so confident? 14A looks massive

It should be noted that when he took on the role of CEO in early 2025, Lip-Bu Tan said he would slow down prior CEO Pat Gelsinger's aggressive capacity build-out and would only build capacity against committed demand. Intel even said in its Q2 2025 quarterly report that development of the upcoming 14A node wasn't guaranteed unless there was significant external demand.

While Intel hasn't officially announced it has landed external customer commitments for 14A, and likely won't due to customer confidentiality concerns, Zinsner basically admitted as much, noting:

"Lip-Bu and the team are now meeting on a weekly basis with customers. They are moving away from just looking at data to thinking about, "Well, how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?" We are now at a point where we have conviction around customers on 14A externally..."

Later on, Zinsner discussed Intel's innovative EMIB-T packaging, which may offer cost and performance advantages over $TSM Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's CoWoS technology. Zinser noted Intel's packaging technology is leading to new opportunities to cross-sell customers to Intel's front-end foundry capabilities:

"[Packaging] is a great on-ramp vehicle to show how we can perform not only from an innovation perspective, but also just the blocking and tackling of operationally, how we provide the parts, when we provide them, what our yields look like in high volume. All of those things get tested in advanced packaging, and we win customers there, and I think there is a great opportunity to cross-sell them on the front end as well. Quite honestly, we've already seen that show up even now."

Not only is Intel apparently winning significant external customer volume for its foundry, but its product team is also apparently bullish on 14A. Zinsner noted that under Tan, management let Intel's internal product team choose its foundry, whether Intel's processes or TSMC's. Zinsner said that even though Intel's internal team is "probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody," it has also committed to designing high-volume products on 14A.

text:
WTA US Open 

Sinja Kraus vs Karolina Muchova

🧠 Form & Context

Sinja Kraus

📈 Strong headline form: Kraus is 7-3 over her last ten and 56-29 across the last 52 weeks.
🟤 Lower-level and clay concentration: Much of her winning volume came outside WTA main-tour hard-court fields.
❌ Severe tour-level surface weakness: Kraus is 1-9 on hard at WTA level across her career.
🔁 Return resistance: She wins 59.0% of second-serve return points and 38.9% of return games.
⚠️ Serve protection: Kraus holds 64.5% of service games and saves only 49.3% of break points.
📉 Cooling trend: She has lost two of her last three matches.

Karolina Muchova

🔥 Outstanding established form: Muchova is 9-1 over her last ten and 45-14 during the last 52 weeks.
🏆 Elite hard-court résumé: Her career WTA hard record is 125-56, with a 28-9 record during the last 52 weeks.
💪 Dominant service profile: She holds 78.1% of service games and wins 69.1% of first-serve points.
🧗 Proven against strong opposition: Muchova is 39-13 against Top 100 opponents over the last year.
🕒 Seven-week absence: She has not played competitively since the Wimbledon final.
🚩 Stale hard-court flag: Her last hard match was a 6-1, 6-1 defeat against Gauff in Miami, although that result is five months old and was followed by excellent form on other surfaces.

🔍 Match Breakdown

The talent and proven-level difference is substantial. Muchova’s hold rate is almost fourteen percentage points higher, and her career success on hard is supported by repeated results against Top 100 opposition. Kraus’s 7-3 recent record cannot be assessed at the same level because her WTA hard record remains 1-9.

Kraus’s second-serve return numbers offer a potential route. If Muchova is rusty and misses first serves, Kraus can extend return games and make the favorite work physically. What Kraus has not demonstrated is the ability to sustain that pressure against an opponent of Muchova’s level over an entire WTA hard-court match.

The inactivity is the main reason not to use the straight-sets or deeper game handicaps. Muchova may require several games to find timing, and her last recorded hard-court performance technically triggers the model’s collapse protocol despite its age.

🔮 Prediction

The quality gap is too large to oppose Muchova, but the seven-week layoff makes Muchova moneyline the only sensible pre-match position.

Optimum Communications has announced an expanded, multi-year agreement with T-Mobile, giving Optimum access to T-Mobile's 5G Standalone network, a broader device portfolio, and enhanced domestic and international roaming. Optimum has now surpassed 700,000 mobile lines.

The agreement enables faster response times, improved reliability, and next-generation mobile services. It also extends coverage to rural and hard-to-reach areas and expands the range of smartphones, wearables, and connected devices Optimum can offer customers.

Cable operators have been building mobile businesses on MVNO agreements for years, and the strategy is working. Customers who buy both broadband and mobile churn at significantly lower rates than single-product subscribers. Deeper access to T-Mobile's 5G SA network makes Optimum's mobile product more competitive on performance, which makes the bundle stickier, which matters more as broadband competition intensifies. The upgrade is a customer retention play as much as a network improvement.

🇩🇪🇺🇸 SYNTHESIS: Why global capital doesn't flow into the German tech ecosystem (hint: it's not the notaries)

I'd like to expand on an argument I've been making these past few days about Germany, notaries, and tech company-building. The starting point was @patrickc originating the ritual quarterly complaint about German notaries and the friction they add to company formation. I argued that the notaries are a distraction and that the real explanation is macro. Let's try and trace the full mechanism.

1️⃣ Where do the savings go?

Germany exports like crazy. This brings in revenue, but not revenue that necessarily flows into a pool of risk capital that could fund startups. Specifically, about half of Germany's trade is intra-eurozone and settles in EUR; much of the rest is denominated in USD or other currencies. And regardless of the currency denomination, what matters is where the revenue lands once it enters the German economy.

Now, wages and consumption have been repressed in Germany, particularly since the Hartz reforms of the early 2000s. The result is that savings accumulate on corporate balance sheets and on the government balance sheet (which is less indebted than most peers, thanks to the _Schuldenbremse_). In other words, savings do NOT accumulate on household balance sheets—or rather, German households do save, but in the most conservative manner, in bank deposits, insurance products, and _Bausparverträge_. None of these insulated and essentially risk-free channels route capital toward venture-style risk.

Strong corporate balance sheets are often cited as one of Europe's strengths. That sounds like a good thing, but it's precisely the feature that starves the tech ecosystem. As the late Clay Christensen taught us, if corporations hold the keys to the national savings, then they will invest in becoming ever more competitive—which, in Germany, means to double down on exporting. They will spend on capex, on R&D for existing product lines, and on supply chain optimization. They will simply not invest in startups. CVC exists in Germany, but is negligible relative to the savings pool it sits next to.

This is the same pattern you see in China. Chinese SOEs and large corporates behave identically: they reinvest in manufacturing competitiveness, triggering involution, not in building a tech ecosystem. The savings are there, but there's no willingness to deploy them toward risk and innovation. China compensates with two things: pre-existing large tech companies (Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu) who take care of funding startups within their walled gardens and the CCP, which operates the entire nation like a venture capital fund ("Middle Kingdom Ventures"), in a very sharp contrast to whatever the German federal government does (which is not much).

2️⃣ The missing overflow mechanism

In the US, venture capital runs on what I call the "overflow mechanism." In effect, the US trade deficit floods the country with foreign capital. This capital likes to pile into safe assets—Treasuries, agency debt, blue-chip equities. As a result, domestic capital, such as endowments and pension funds, gets crowded out and has to move up the risk curve to find proper returns... which means that some of that displaced capital ends up in VC funds. In truth, a fully functioning venture capital industry exists at scale ONLY in the US, as a by-product of the country acting as a magnet for foreign capital (that, plus a few tax incentives and favorable regulations, ERISA etc.).

Now compare this to Germany. There is certainly no equivalent overflow mechanism from Germany's capital markets toward venture capital. After all, Germany runs a trade surplus, not a deficit. Capital flows out, not in. And as for the savings that stay, they are locked up in corporate and government balance sheets, controlled by actors whose incentive is to reinvest in manufacturing competitiveness. There is no crowding-out dynamic that would push domestic capital up the risk curve and into startups.

3️⃣ The eurozone amplifier

As always, the eurozone's architecture makes this worse. In a world where Germany still had the Deutsche Mark, persistent trade surpluses would push the currency up, making German exports more expensive and naturally rebalancing trade over time. That adjustment mechanism would also, over time, shift the composition of the domestic economy—less export-dependent, more domestic-demand-driven, and therefore more hospitable to the kind of capital allocation that feeds a tech ecosystem.

Inside the eurozone, however, this adjustment mechanism is gone. The euro is weaker than a hypothetical Deutsche Mark would be (because it also reflects the fundamentals of weaker eurozone economies, such as Italy and France), so German exports stay artificially competitive. The surpluses persist. The corporate savings pile up indefinitely. Every step of the chain that starves the tech ecosystem is reinforced.

4️⃣ What a German reversal would look like

Now imagine a German reversal: higher wages, unleashed consumption. Suddenly you need to invest at home to serve the domestic market, which rebalances trade and brings the surplus down. Down the line, Germany becomes red hot as a destination for foreign capital—because foreign investors see a large, wealthy consumer market opening up after decades of repression.

So much capital comes in, in fact, that some of it finds its way to startups. This can happen through two channels: a domestic overflow mechanism, analogous to the US one, where abundant capital in safe assets pushes some domestic investors such as German pension funds up the risk curve; and a foreign channel, where institutional, stateless LPs seeking returns start allocating to European venture funds because Germany now offers a large addressable market where all the lights are turning from red to green.

Each step follows from the previous one. But the probability of getting there is very low. Germany's entire postwar economic identity is built around export discipline and fiscal restraint. The reversal requires abandoning both.

5️⃣ What a US reversal would look like

Now let's have a look at the mirror image. Suppose the US is determined to bring down its trade deficit. Because demand is sustained but Chinese goods don't come in anymore because of tariffs, it creates a supply shortage, which must be compensated by local players. That requires investment—in manufacturing capacity, in supply chains, in physical infrastructure.

In turn, if what you're doing is making manufactured goods to serve the domestic market, the returns are much lower than whatever exists in tech or financial services. This matters for two reasons. First, less imports means less dollar outflows, which means less recycling of those dollars back into US assets. Second, the US economy becomes less attractive to foreign investors because capital is being allocated to lower-return activities. Less recycling AND lower returns: both work in the same direction and contribute to reversing capital flows.

In the end, American households buy less at a higher price (expensive domestic goods rather than cheap Chinese ones). At the same time, foreigners don't want to invest as much in the US because of a rebalanced economy (they hold less dollars, and don't see attractive returns anymore). It all comes down to this: a larger share of a smaller pie of capital is allocated to substituting for suppressed Chinese imports. That is how you cool down the US economy and free up capital for the rest of the world.

Do you assume Silicon Valley will perform as well then?

6️⃣ The impossible tradeoff

This is the dilemma Trump's America has to confront: you can't have rebalancing and sustained capital inflows at the same time. This follows directly from balance-of-payments accounting: if you reduce the current account deficit, you mechanically reduce the capital account surplus. There is no way around this. If the US wants to bring manufacturing back and shrink the trade deficit, it will lose some of the capital inflows that feed its financial ecosystem—including its cherished venture capital industry.

I wonder if this realization is why Trump has been touring the world trying to secure commitments to invest in the US from South Korea, Japan, Gulf countries, and the EU. Of course it is now clear that those commitments will never be implemented. But was there some understanding of the impossible tradeoff and some clumsy attempt to beat the odds? The behavior is consistent with someone trying to replace the structural mechanism—trade deficit leading to dollar recycling—with ad hoc bilateral commitments. Whether this reflects conscious understanding or instinctive dealmaking dressed up as strategy is unknowable, but the pattern fits.

7️⃣ Conclusion

The argument I've been making comes down to this. Germany's tech ecosystem is starved of capital because every feature of the German economic model—export orientation, wage repression, fiscal restraint, corporate control of savings—channels the national surplus away from risk capital and toward manufacturing competitiveness. The eurozone's architecture removes the exchange-rate adjustment that would naturally rebalance this over time, locking the pattern in place.

Meanwhile, the US tech ecosystem thrives because every feature of the American economic model—trade deficits, capital inflows, domestic crowding-out— channels abundant global capital toward risk-taking. Venture capital is a by-product of that structure.

If you reverse either model, you reverse the capital flows. Germany with higher wages and unleashed consumption starts attracting the kind of capital that funds startups. America with a shrinking trade deficit starts losing the capital that (indirectly) funds Silicon Valley. Macro, not notaries, is the problem.

text:
🇩🇪🇺🇸 I just realized as I reread my reply to @SaladBarFan and @fitzr1189 below that Germany is the polar opposite of the US in almost every respect:

• Fiscal restraint as opposed to ballooning deficits
• Export powerhouse as opposed to deindustrialized wasteland
• Repressed wages and consumption (= Hartz reforms) as opposed to the US middle class’s high living standards, the envy of the world!

And we wonder why one country manages to build tech companies while the other cannot? It’s definitely not because Germany has notaries reading company bylaws aloud.

The truth is that all of the above work against global capital flowing into the German tech ecosystem. If you have (i) relatively low domestic demand, (ii) low wages, (iii) limited fiscal stimulus, and (iv) an economy geared toward exports and industrial production, you create a very different environment for startups and tech companies than you do in the US.

In other words, the broader problem with Germany’s economic model is that all of its policy choices and economic specialization make it harder to attract the global capital needed to build and scale tech companies. Definitely no "overflow mechanism" from Germany’s capital markets toward venture capital!

@patrickc: food for thought for the Rhine Group.

Blockchain technology has matured considerably, but there is still a major difference between having powerful infrastructure and making that infrastructure easy for millions of people to use. Mainstream adoption requires both sides of that equation to work together.

BitTorrent Speed reaching more than 585 million wallet accounts offers an interesting perspective on this challenge. A product can introduce users to blockchain functionality through an experience that feels straightforward instead of requiring them to understand the technical architecture before they can participate.

That approach matters because most people do not wake up looking for a blockchain.

They wake up looking for a product that solves a problem.

If blockchain happens to make that product faster, more transparent, more accessible, or more useful, then the technology becomes valuable because of the experience it enables.

This is one of the most important lessons for builders across Web3.

Do not make users carry the complexity of the infrastructure.

Build the infrastructure to handle the complexity for them.

As decentralized technology expands into more areas, products will increasingly compete on simplicity, reliability, and usefulness. The projects that understand this will have a better opportunity to bring blockchain beyond its existing audience.

The milestone reached by BitTorrent Speed is therefore interesting not only because of its scale, but because it reinforces the importance of designing blockchain products around people.

The future should feel easier than the present.

Every improvement that removes unnecessary steps brings Web3 closer to becoming normal digital infrastructure rather than something users have to consciously think about.

That is where meaningful adoption begins.

text:
Dear Young People.
Read this before you waste another day playing small:
​1. Nobody is watching you.
When you stumble, they aren’t paying attention. When you succeed, they’re still thinking about themselves. Stop paralyzing yourself over the opinions of people who haven't spent ten seconds thinking about you today. You are free. Go act like it.
​2. Delivery kills potential.
The world is full of brilliant people who never delivered. Money and respect are just byproducts of problems solved. Become the person who swallows the hard tasks, asks the right questions, and simply figures it out. Reliability is rare—be irreplaceable.
​3. You are spending your most finite asset.
If your parents are in their 60s and you visit once a year, you don’t have decades left—you have roughly 15 to 20 visits. Let that sink in. Call them. Protect your health. Wake up with energy that shifts the atmosphere of every room you enter.
​4. Cut the anchors.
Most people are only along for the ride while it is easy, fun, or useful. True friends stand beside you when you have nothing left to offer. Trade comfort for people who challenge your thinking and force you to rise.
​5. The cure to overthinking is motion.
The world is not run by geniuses; it is built by ordinary people who possessed an abnormal willingness to start. Make decisions your 10-year-old self would find brave, and your 80-year-old self would thank you for. None of us make it out alive anyway.
​You do not need every step mapped out. Anchor your compass, keep your standards high, stay grateful for the breath in your lungs, and move.
​Now go do the thing.

Be ready for:
▫️ Caste, caste, caste
▫️ Kashmir

1 Sept - 🇵🇰 Pakistan, Muzaffarabad

1 Sept - 🇮🇳 India, Srinagar
Yes, this one is in India - not abroad - but it has been deliberately timed to mirror the Muzaffarabad conference across the LoC on the same day. Hurriyat has called on people to gather at Syed Ali Gilani's grave in Hyderpora and on imams to offer special prayers.

An American church congregation is hosting a programme on Indian identity and religious majoritarianism, co-sponsored by Hindus for Human Rights.

Five weeks in Geneva where Pakistan raises Kashmir and India spends its time exercising right of reply. It has happened at every recent session — and the side-event list still isn't public.

Harvard's South Asia institute opens its year. Its most recent India-politics seminar was on citizen reactions to religious nationalist rhetoric.

Three days at SOAS, the largest annual gathering of UK scholars who study India. Days out, they still haven't published what the panels are about.

Christophe Jaffrelot launches "Shared Sacred Sites in South Asia". Jaffrelot is one of the most famous Western academics writing on Hindu nationalism. Cornell platforms a talk on Pakistan's transgender law and Muslim transmasculine religiosity. Ivy League South Asia programmes set the vocabulary that reaches Western policy.

A Swedish state university is teaching anti-caste thought as political theory. Caste is now a European academic subject with its own funded seminar circuit.

15 Sept - 🇺🇸 USA, Yale University
Yale hosts a talk on populism in Pakistan. Please note which South Asian populism gets studied and which gets condemned.

18 Sept - 🇨🇦 Canada, Justice For All Canada
Three years since Ottawa accused Indian agents on the floor of Parliament. A Commons intervention should be scheduled on that day.

Michigan opens its year with a lecture on Rummana Hussain — the artist whose work turned openly political after the Babri Masjid demolition.

18-28 Sept - 🇺🇳 United Nations, New York
Pakistan gets a UN General Assembly platform on Kashmir again. Note what's missing: the OIC Contact Group met on the margins in 2024 and 2025, has no 2026 meeting announced, and Kashmiri groups are openly lobbying the new OIC chief to convene one.

Japan runs a national South Asian studies society with a 39-year-old annual conference. Almost nobody in India is watching what it says about us.

CSIS holds the only dated South Asia event across eleven major Western think tanks this month. Carnegie, Brookings, Chatham House and eight others have nothing on India at all.

22 Sept - 🇳🇱 Netherlands, Leiden
A Dutch institute convenes "Asia in the World: Knowledge on the Move" — European academia decides what counts as knowledge about India, and India isn't at the table.

23 Sept - 🇨🇦 Canada, York University Toronto
Canada's most active Asia research centre opens another full year of programming, in the centre of Khalistan diaspora politics.

23 Sept - 🇺🇸 USA, University of Pennsylvania
Penn hosts a talk on Gandhi and leprosy.

24 Sept - 🇳🇱 Netherlands, Leiden
IIAS fellow seminar. Europe funds resident fellowships to study our region year-round; we fund almost none to study theirs.

India's colonial military history is being taught at the Munk School this month — the seminar is on sepoys and the French East India Company.

A US conference opens with a panel titled "Hindutva in America: Capturing Political Power and Controlling Cultural Narratives".

A Canadian university session on how geopolitics shapes journalism in Asia. Remember that India's image abroad is built in rooms like this one.

text:
What is the process to obtain an absentee ballot?

The process to obtain an absentee ballot generally involves **confirming voter registration**, **requesting a ballot** through your local election office, and **returning** the completed ballot by mail or in person before the deadline. Specific steps and deadlines vary significantly by state.

**General Steps**
*   **Check Eligibility and Registration**: Ensure you are registered to vote and verify if your state offers no-excuse absentee voting or requires a specific reason.
*   **Request the Ballot**: Submit an application via your state’s online portal, by mail, email, fax, or in person. Some states, like **Ohio** and **South Dakota**, allow you to fill out an online form and mail it, while others like **Georgia** require a printed, hand-signed application with ID.
*   **Receive and Mark**: Once the application is processed, the ballot is mailed to you. You must mark it according to instructions, often requiring a **witness or notary signature** (e.g., in **Alaska**, **North Carolina**, and **Rhode Island**).
*   **Return the Ballot**: Send the ballot back by mail (ensuring it arrives by Election Day) or drop it off at a designated location.

**Key State-Specific Requirements**
*   **Deadlines**: Applications must often be received days before the election. For example, **Alabama** requires mail applications **7 days** prior, while **Virginia** requires them by the **11th day** before the election. **Minnesota** recommends applying at least **two weeks** in advance.
*   **Identification**: Many states require a copy of a photo ID or driver’s license number with the application (**South Dakota**, **Georgia**), or the last four digits of your Social Security number (**Virginia**, **North Carolina**).
*   **Automatic Mailing**: Some states, like **Hawaii** and **Vermont** (for general elections), automatically mail ballots to all registered voters without a separate request.
*   **Military/Overseas**: U.S. citizens abroad or in the military can use the **Federal Post Card Application (FCPA)** to register and request a ballot in one step.

For the most accurate instructions, visit your state’s Secretary of State website or the **U.S. Vote Foundation** portal.

text:
France actively pitched the Rafale to Uzbekistan when French President Macron went to Tashkent in November 2023. He took Dassault officials with him. Yet Tashkent rejected the Rafale and ultimately chose China's J-10CE.

Why: France offered the advanced multirole Rafale, but the deal faced major hurdles. Production backlogs + cost. At over $200 million per jet fully equipped, the Rafale was too expensive for Uzbekistan's modest defence budget. Despite using old Soviet era jets like Fulcrums & Flankers, the Uzbek Air Force is strongest in the region.

China then offered its J-10CE at roughly $40-50 million each. This means that at one Rafale's cost, Uzbekistan could buy 3-4 J-10CEs with best of upgrades. Uzbekistan was worried about J-10’s credibility but then an encounter between India-Pakistan change the game for Chinese aircraft. As IAF kept its aircraft away from Pakistan’s sky after initial face off and went ahead with standoff weapons, the J-10 earned some inquiries in the third world.

The other reason: Uzbekistan had already built an entire air defence network around Chinese systems like FD-2000B & FM-90. The J-10CE would make the integration easier for Uzbek Air Force. So Uzbekistan chose an affordable fighter that cannot be ignored with long range BVR missiles.
