text:
She was allowed to see her jailed nine year old exactly one time in three months, and she had to share the hour with a stranger. The stranger was a London reporter carrying a camera hidden under a basket of fruit, because a photograph on a foreign front page was the only thing anybody believed might get the boy out. So the one visit a mother got with her child, she spent partly watching a basket on the floor, and she could not warn him it was there. Ask yourself what it costs to sit still for something like that and let it happen.

Has a bad reputation.

Four words, handed to the newspapers of North Carolina in the winter of 1959, weeks after that visit, attached to the name of the woman who had sat there watching the basket.

Her name was Evelyn Thompson, and she cleaned houses in Monroe for fifteen dollars a week. By the time that sentence reached print she had lost the job, lost the house, and lost her nine year old son to a reformatory ninety miles down the road.

The words were not careless. They were the plan.

What they were sent out to cover had started on a Tuesday afternoon three months earlier.

October 28, 1958. Two boys were playing in a yard on the white side of the railroad tracks that cut Monroe in half.

James Hanover Thompson was nine. His friend David Simpson, who everybody called Fuzzy, was seven or eight depending on which record you trust.

The schools were segregated down to the brick. But children still found each other after the last bell, because the mothers of the Black children cleaned the houses of the mothers of the white children, and the children came along.

James had been in that yard before, holding his mother's hand while she worked.

Late in the day a kissing game started. A seven year old white girl named Sissy kissed Fuzzy on the cheek, kissed James on the cheek, and went home to her supper.

She mentioned it at the table. Her mother called the police.

By dark a group of men had crossed the tracks with a shotgun, hunting the Thompson house. The house was dark and the police reached the boys first, which is the only reason this is a story about a reformatory and not a story about a rope.

James and David were walking their wagons toward town when the cruiser came alongside.

Officers got out with the guns already up. They shouted slurs at two grade schoolers and called them rapists, which is a word neither boy could have defined for you.

They took them down to a cell underneath the police station. Grown men worked them over in there, hitting the body and not the face, which is a decision somebody made on purpose.

When the boys screamed, the answer that came back through the door was to shut up back there.

Then nothing. Nobody came.

The first day passed, then the second, and no mother was allowed through that door, and no lawyer. Nobody sat down to explain to a nine year old what he was accused of.

Two children sat in a basement in the dark, in the same clothes they had worn in the yard, with no adult in the world on their side. Above them the building went about its business.

On Halloween the door opened, and men came in with sheets pulled over their heads.

They stood over two small boys and told them they were going to be hanged. They said it slowly enough that the boys understood it.

James was crying.

The men left and the door shut behind them. The boys were still in there.

Fifty years on, the words James still reaches for about that night are that he was scared to death.

They stayed six days. Then a juvenile judge named J. Hampton Price telephoned the Morrison Training School at Hoffman and reserved two beds, and only after the beds were held did he sit down to determine whether the boys belonged in them.

He met with Sissy and her parents alone, in a closed room, so James and David never once stood in front of the child who kissed them.

Then he held what he himself called a separate but equal hearing, with no lawyers for the boys. Their mothers were kept outside the door.

He found them guilty and explained his reasoning. The boys had gone quiet when the charge was read to them, and he counted the quiet as a confession.

On November 3 he sentenced them to stay at Morrison until they turned twenty one. Twelve more years for the nine year old.

Back across the tracks, Evelyn Thompson was told the state would be keeping her son until 1970.

Within days her white landlord sent an eviction notice.

She and David's mother, a widow named Jennie Simpson, were both fired from the fifteen dollar a week jobs that fed their families. In Monroe in 1958 there was no second kind of work for a Black woman to go get.

Then the nights started.

Men drove past the house in the dark and fired at it. Not once, not as a warning, but as a routine the family learned to expect after supper.

Evelyn Thompson stopped sleeping. Her daughter, Brenda Lee Graham, remembered her mother walking the floors of that house in the dark and praying out loud.

When she stopped walking, she sat at the window and watched the road.

She had a household of children in there and one of them was already gone. So she stayed up and she watched, and when the shooting came she got the small ones down and she kept watching, because there was nothing else a person could do.

Then in the morning she went out on the porch with a broom.

Before the little ones were awake, the women of that house swept the bullets off the boards.

You sweep so the children do not see them, and you sweep so the porch looks like a porch again. You do it every morning, knowing that tonight there will be more.

Brenda Lee Graham remembered the crosses too, burning in the front yard, close enough to see plainly from the window her mother sat at.

Somebody killed James's dog, and the boy all of this was supposedly about was ninety miles away at Hoffman and knew none of it.

In three months, Evelyn Thompson was permitted one visit. One.

The woman who walked in beside her was Joyce Egginton, a reporter who had travelled from London for the story, because there was no legitimate way into a North Carolina reformatory for a foreign journalist. Egginton went in as a social worker escorting the family, and the fruit basket went in with her.

So Evelyn Thompson was driven ninety miles toward the one hour she had waited three months for. Beside her sat Robert Williams from the Monroe NAACP, and Conrad Lynn, the New York attorney who had offered to take the case for nothing, and a white woman she had met that same day.

The boy could not be told. A nine year old cannot be asked to act natural in front of a camera he does not know about, so James sat and talked to his mother while a stranger a few feet away photographed him.

There is no record of what she said to him. Nobody wrote it down, because nobody in that building thought a conversation between that woman and that boy was worth recording.

The visit ended on schedule. She stood up and left her son at Hoffman and got back in the car, and the next time she was allowed to see him would be after he came home.

On December 18, the photograph ran on the front page in London.

It went everywhere. Papers across Europe picked it up, clergy on both sides of the Atlantic protested, and schoolchildren in the Netherlands mailed letters to the governor of North Carolina by the thousand.

The basket of fruit worked.

Within weeks Governor Luther Hodges, Judge Price and other officials went to the state's white press with a correction to issue. The foreign and national coverage, they explained, was full of inaccuracies and misinformation that needed setting straight.

Then they opened the juvenile files that the law required them to keep sealed.

Reporters were handed material said to come from social workers, from teachers, from the police. To protect the men who had jailed two children, the state broke the confidentiality rule that exists specifically to protect children.

The boys were printed as incorrigible. They were printed as wayward delinquents.

It was explained to the public that Morrison had been for their own good.

Then they went at the mothers, because the boys alone were not enough. Jennie Simpson's children, the papers were told, were forever in trouble with the police.

And Evelyn Thompson has a bad reputation in her community.

North Carolina's newspapers ran it. There is no sign that a single one of them picked up a telephone to check.

Look at what those four words were built to carry.

A mob with a shotgun, and six days in a basement. Sheets over heads on Halloween, and beds reserved before the hearing.

Silence entered into the record as a confession. A twelve year sentence for a kiss on the cheek.

All of it answered with a line about a housekeeper's reputation, in a state where almost nobody was left arguing the other side.

Robert Williams was the one man in Monroe who had refused to let the case stay buried, and it cost him from a direction nobody would guess. The historian Timothy Tyson, working on Williams's life, found an FBI report in which Thurgood Marshall is said to have told agents that Williams ought to be investigated over his defense of the two boys.

Those words are an allegation inside a government file and cannot now be put to the man who supposedly said them. What is not in dispute is that Williams was suspended by his own organization while the boys were still at Hoffman.

On January 12, 1959, a superior court judge named Walter Johnston heard their appeal. Both mothers were in the room this time.

Judge Price took the stand, and according to the Winston-Salem Journal he used the n word about the boys twice while testifying.

The hearing ran two hours. Somewhere in it David, who was seven, fell asleep in his chair with his head on James's shoulder.

He woke up to hear that they were both going back to Hoffman. Both boys cried.

A Black paper called The Carolinian ran the photograph of the two mothers coming down the courthouse steps afterward, in tears, a Confederate soldier standing in stone over the entrance behind them.

The caption was two words. In Despair.

What finally worked happened where nobody could see it. Eleanor Roosevelt got word to Eisenhower, Eisenhower leaned privately on Hodges, and on February 13, 1959, the boys came home.

Read the accounts and you will find that release called a pardon, called clemency, called amnesty, depending on who is writing.

Not one source calls it an exoneration, because it was not one. Clemency lifts a punishment and leaves the finding underneath it exactly where it sat.

No court ever said the boys had done nothing. The state simply stopped holding them.

And the four words about their mother were never withdrawn, never corrected, never followed by anything at all.

Two days after the boys came home, an AP reporter found the family in Charlotte public housing, where the NAACP had moved them for their safety, and sat down with Evelyn Thompson.

It was the first time anybody with a notebook had asked her.

She did not make a speech. She told him what the boys had actually been doing that afternoon, which was raking leaves for a white lady and playing cowboys and Indians, and that the kisses were playful-like.

Then she said the one line she left behind that reads like a wound. They had not had much peace since it happened.

She was right, and it did not stop.

James came home so changed his own sister said it was like meeting somebody she had never known. The state made him report weekly to a psychologist in Charlotte.

James carried what that man said to him for the rest of his life. He was asked whether he was some kind of maniac, and he was told he ought to be sterilized.

That was not a figure of speech. North Carolina sterilized more than seven thousand people between the 1920s and the 1970s, and researchers have since named the Morrison Training School as one of the institutions that fed children into the program.

David said a sergeant back in Monroe told the Charlotte police to come looking for him whenever a crime happened nearby. He told Oprah Winfrey in 1993 that he was never able to get out of the system.

Both men were arrested over and over as they grew.

Neither one of them, then or since, has ever put a word of blame on the little girl. Sixty-eight years on, no official of that city or that state has apologized to either of them, and not one dollar has ever been paid.

Which leaves the record of North Carolina on the woman who raised one of them.

It is four words, given to reporters by the men who took her son, printed without a phone call, and left standing ever since.

Her children hold a different record and they will recite it for you.

Church seven days a week, and a plate for anybody who turned up hungry. Always a dollar for a friend who needed one.

Jelly roll cakes for birthdays, killer fried chicken and pecan pies on a Sunday.

Her youngest son Dwight went and read the old coverage himself as a grown man, working through his own family's history. He could not find his mother anywhere in it.

He says she is his hero, and that he cannot imagine what she carried.

Dwight Thompson was born in 1961.

Two years after the state of North Carolina put it in the newspapers that this woman was not fit to raise the children she already had, she went ahead and had one more.

Her son puts it better than anybody else ever has. After everything that happened, his mother had the audacity to have another child.

NOTE: This post is shared for historical and educational awareness about the 1958 Kissing Case and the treatment of Black children in the Jim Crow justice system, not to glorify violence, hate, or harm.

Post 4. 

The buyer who can wait

Into that unfinished map walks a state that can wait.

Canadian intelligence has treated Beijing’s interest in Indigenous leadership as more than folklore. A 2019 NSICOP draft, later reported, recorded a late-2011 invitation of Aboriginal leaders advertised as tourism. A PRC embassy official described the pitch as beipian, to be fooled, and said the true intention was Aboriginal-controlled natural resources. CSIS has assessed that subnational governments, including Indigenous governments, are soft targets. The United Front system is built to cultivate counterparties. A fragmented title system multiplies them.

The Canada China Business Council has run dedicated Indigenous business missions to China to connect First Nations economic development corporations with Chinese offtake, equity and tourism capital. In June 2026 Eby led a provincial trade mission to Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. He said British Columbia had been “too dependent on the United States.” On the list: timber, as American softwood duties bite, and LNG Canada Phase 2. PetroChina already sits inside the LNG Canada consortium. First Nations in the northwest have been offered an option to invest up to a billion dollars in a storage tank if the expansion proceeds. That is legitimate participation when title is clear. It is a second set of counterparties for a Chinese state firm when title is not.

CSIS has separately warned that Canada’s critical minerals and agricultural exports are strategic targets. China dominates midstream processing of many of the metals that sit under British Columbia’s disputed hills. A Canadian or allied developer faces years of assessment, overlapping claims, injunction risk and political reversal. A state-directed buyer faces a different clock. It can offer equity, offtake and cultural diplomacy to the rights-holder while Ottawa and Victoria argue. Cheap extraction is not always a fire-sale price on day one. It is the price you get when the Canadian seller cannot finish a map and the Chinese buyer can wait ten years.

Carney’s federal reset and Eby’s provincial sales trip are the same file in two offices. Beijing’s state media, during the prime minister’s visit, urged Canada toward “strategic autonomy,” meaning autonomy from Washington. That is not a partnership of equals. It is a wedge, applied to a Five Eyes member whose exports still run overwhelmingly south and whose intelligence community still names China as the foremost interferer. Diversification from a volatile American administration is a rational Canadian instinct. Treating the foremost foreign interferer as the alternative customer, while the land register is in court and the foreign-agent registry is not yet a working machine, is not strategy. It is improvisation with a smile.

Sovereignty is the ability to build

The temptation, in London as in Ottawa, is to reach for the spy novel: the premier as agent, the holding company as cut-out, the banquet as a drop. That verdict is the one that lets the actual problem off. Public intelligence has not produced a finding that Canadian first ministers take orders from Zhongnanhai. Control, in the intelligence sense, means tasking and clandestine direction. What the record supports is colder.

Canada has a durable private network that opened China in 1978 and never left the table. It has a public inquiry that named the threat and a political calendar that reset the commercial relationship before the remedies were built. It has campuses that are both engines of allied innovation and permissive environments for talent-harvesting. It has a diaspora that includes both citizens entitled to protection and organisations that function as United Front infrastructure. It has a province whose land law now operates as dual sovereignty in practice, multiplying the number of people a foreign state must cultivate in order to sit on the rock, the gas and the trees.

text:
Data centers don’t just go anywhere. They go where they can exploit land, energy, and tax incentives.

Virginia had the internet backbone. Texas has cheap acreage, gas-fired power, a faster grid hookup, and a sales-tax holiday on servers and electricity. That is why Texas has roughly 480 data centers and Colorado has about 57.

Colorado has talent. It does not have cheap spare megawatts, and it never offered the standard equipment tax break. So the campuses go to Texas, Georgia, and Utah where the incentives are great instead.

This is not an accident. State officials courted the companies with tax holidays and easy siting while locals fought the power bills, water use, and land grab. 

Residents are saying no, but the deals keep getting signed anyway.

This tweet about Escape to the Country is especially for one of my followers as she knows the househunters.   Hopefully I'm not too unkind. 😬

Series 27 episode 17. 
Aberdeenshire. That, apparently, has more castles than supermarkets.  

Aussies Sonya and eldest student son William, who's a stranger to a barbershop, are renting a property in Aberdeenshire but the tenancy is due to expire shortly.  Their new house will be for them, Sonya's husband and other two adult children.  And dogs, cats, horses, ponies, budgies, hens, roosters, a partridge.  And a pear tree.  Good grief. 😜🤣 
Sonya wants 3 - 10 acres for the menagerie and her student son wants to be near public transport. Sonya also wants a pony window - a window in the property from where she can always see her ponies.  Well, there's a first for ETTC!! 😳😧

1. Pitcaple.
A beautiful 5 bed stone single storey L shaped cottage that's been recently renovated.  It's open plan and contemporary inside.  Mum Sonya loves the big kitchen that she says will suit them as they're all very messy.  Yikes. 😬 But it's a 15 minute walk to a bus stop for the student son - however, he's ok about that, especially when he sees the cinema room.  It's set in 2.5 acres leading to a river.  Mum Sonya says it's perfect except there's not enough land for her zoo.  Well its perfect now, Sonya.  Until your messy family get there, Sonya!  Offers over £610,000.

2. Rothienorman.
This is a huge palatial type mansion.  With turrets!  A baronial hall and a double staircase!  The master bedroom has 2 ensuites! 😳 There's another 3 bedroom house in the grounds, which stretch to 24 acres!  Mum Sonya loves the land but student son says it's too far from public transport. It's £715,000.

3. The mystery house is 7 miles from Hatton.
It's a 21 bedroom mega mansion. The living room used to be a ballroom.  There's an annexe.  There's stables and woodland.  There's even a pony window. 🐴🐎 It has 9 acres.  It's madness.  Total lunacy. You'd need an army of staff.  Offers over £675,000.

Alastair Appleton has lost the plot.  I'm not surprised Mum Sonya isn't buying any of these, although property 1 was her favourite.  

But luckily the family aren't out on the streets.  They've found another property to rent while continuing their search which I'm sure will be more successful than the ridiculous houses Alastair showed them.  Phew. Do better, Alastair! You've been warned.🤣

text:
The Moral Relativism of Islamic Apologetics
A strange paradox has taken root in modern religious discourse. When critics, historians, or internal seekers cite foundational data from classical Islamic sources, a predictable reflex follows. Point to the most authoritative volumes, or to the Qur’an itself, on the age of a marriage, Banu Qurayza, temporary wartime unions, or the gradual prohibition of alcohol, and the citation is treated as a smear.
The irony of the “Islamophobia” label in these settings is glaring. If reading a text aloud, from its own undisputed archive, is experienced as an attack, the problem is not external. The worldview is treating its native history as a hostile exhibit. When a system experiences its own sources as an insult, it has already suffered an internal crash.
These items are not the argument. They are the recognized points of contention. Anyone who has engaged the subject knows the list. The question is not whether one episode can be contextualized in isolation. The question is what happens to a theology of eternal moral exemplarity once the defenses required by the whole list are examined together.
Once the smear-label fails and the data must be faced, the replies collapse into three options.
First: it was acceptable then because it was the norm, and it is no longer acceptable now. That is historical relativism. Second: it was not acceptable then and is not acceptable now. That is an ethical condemnation of Muhammad and of the tradition that treats his conduct as binding. Third: it was acceptable then and remains acceptable now. That is doubling down, and it collides at once with modern legal and moral rejection.
There is no fourth move that preserves both a transcendent, unchanging moral exemplar and a public posture acceptable to the contemporary West. The rest of the repertoire is a rotation among these three. Watch how the rotation runs: relativism covers the history, tolerance covers the present, and when both run out, the fallback is voluntarism.
Historical relativism says an act is right or wrong according to the time or the group that performs it. Faced with the list, the apologist asks for an exemption. Foundational figures cannot be judged by modern standards; they were operating inside the legal and tribal norms of seventh-century Arabia. The supporting move is whataboutism: young royal marriages in Europe, crusading violence, Christian slave systems. The history, we are told, was no worse than anyone else’s.
Two replies recur for each item, and neither is a fourth option. One disputes the record: a hadith is called unreliable, a term redefined, a betrayal denied. Where that succeeds, it removes an item; it does not touch the theology, since a discredited report was never binding. It succeeds rarely: the core reports on the marriage, the judgment against Banu Qurayza, and the legal standing of captive women are affirmed, not disputed, by mainstream classical and contemporary Sunni scholarship. What that scholarship offers instead is the other reply: girls matured earlier then, the tribe broke a pact, the practice regulated something worse. That is the first move restated with footnotes.
That is the first move restated with footnotes. Another move is usually, look the people in history of Europe or in the bible did similar things. That defense is a category error. Christianity and Judaism have never claimed that medieval kings, or even prophets, were flawless exemplars whose personal acts established eternal law. The biblical archive is honest about human depravity. If Solomon turns to foreign gods, the act can be named evil without the system collapsing, because the human actor is not the unrevisable blueprint. The Islamic system cannot name anything Muhammad did as evil, even when the act is widely recognized as such. That is not a debating tactic. It is a structural feature of the theology.
The point holds against the hardest case too: God’s own commands, not a prophet’s conduct. The conquest of Canaan and the binding of Isaac are in the text. They are not denied, and they are not pretty. They are also not treated as a standing pattern for believers in every age. The commands name a people, a land, and a moment. From the start they were read as history directed at an executioner for a particular sentence, not as a universal licence. No mainstream church is hunting the seven nations. That reading is not a modern rescue. It is how the texts themselves are bounded.
A fringe church or a crusading king can be called evil without the system collapsing. That option is open because no medieval army, and no companion of Jesus, carries unqualified moral immunity. The Islamic structure does not grant the same option. Muhammad is uswa ḥasana. The generation around him cannot be charged with evil without tearing the chain that carries the religion. To call the act evil is to call the exemplar, or the generation that carried him, evil. That is the door the other traditions leave open and this one closes.
The traditional Sunni canopy has no such room. Its claim is a universal moral exemplar whose conduct is an unchanging pattern. The Qur’an states it directly: “There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example (uswa ḥasana) for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day” (33:21).
The moment the apologist excuses the exemplar by saying everyone else was doing it, the damage is done. If an action is not wrong when the surrounding culture accepts it, morality is set by the herd. The representative of a divine system did not keep a compass pointing north regardless of weather. The compass pointed wherever the seventh-century crowd was walking.
Reformers are defined by refusal of their era’s status quo. Wilberforce, King, and Gandhi did not join the herd; they corrected it. The same contrast is carried in the Gospel line, “You have heard it said of old… but I say unto you.” To argue that a divine system’s ultimate representative merely mirrored the metrics of his geography is to place him on the herd’s side of that line. If the defense requires showing that the exemplar was no worse than a medieval warlord, the transcendent claim has already sunk into relativism.
The double game appears when the same voice turns from the seventh century to the modern West. Historical relativism is dropped. In its place comes the secular demand that plural societies tolerate moral frameworks they do not share.
Western institutions are told they must accommodate traditional ethical and legal claims under the banner of diversity and conscience. The demand runs one way. The modern world must practice tolerance toward an absolute ethic, while historical relativism is used to excuse that ethic’s past. The same apologist who defends dhimmi status and jizya as legitimate for non-Muslims under Islamic rule will not accept the mirror arrangement for Muslims living under non-Muslim rule. The principle runs one direction: for me, but not for you. It also does not treat rival religious law, personal moral autonomy, or internal dissent as equal options. It claims an unchanging right to govern behavior by divine authority.
The contradiction is structural. Relativism is borrowed to protect history. Tolerance is borrowed to protect present standing. The system being protected rejects both as first principles.
When the two lines collide, doubling-down is baptized as theological voluntarism. The reasonable face is dropped. The claim is no longer “it was the norm then.” It is: yes, it happened; yes, it remains valid; yes, it looks horrific to a modern mind; God decreed it; God knows best; the required response is submission.
Acts are then good solely because they are commanded in that moment, not because they reflect a stable good or a non-contradictory character. If a practice commodifies the body or licenses what would otherwise be named predation, God may sanction it for a season. Law becomes an instrument that bends to circumstance.
The tradition recorded the pattern from inside the household. After a revelation that expanded the Prophet’s marital discretion (Qur’an 33:51), Aisha said, “It seems to me that your Lord hastens to satisfy your desire” (Sahih al-Bukhari 4788; Sahih Muslim 1464a). That is not an outsider’s smear. It is an observation that the timing of revelation tracked personal wish. Voluntarism turns the observation into a principle: the command is the good, and the good need not be intelligible.
That this is not the opening move in public debate is itself evidence. Raw voluntarism is reserved for insiders because the seventh-century ethic is already rejected in practice, even while the text still requires its defense.
A coherent worldview cannot run on a shifting foundation. If the ultimate moral exemplar needs a historical footnote to avoid an ethical disaster, and a secular Western framework to secure his followers’ modern rights, the canopy has not leaked. It has imploded.
The point is not that every contested episode must be litigated in turn. It is that the defenses are few, and each spends a different part of the capital the theology claims to own. Relativism spends transcendence. Condemnation spends the exemplar. Doubling down spends any claim to inhabit a liberal public square. Voluntarism spends reason.
The apologists may continue to demand blind submission from their followers, enforcing a medieval code through institutional power, but the internal logic has already shattered. The system has saved its history by sacrificing its theology, proving that its ultimate authority is not a transcendent, unchangeable truth, but a shifting mirror of human convenience.

text:
The combined deaths in Nepal and China surpassed 900, with more than 4,700 people missing, and a private-sector association representing power companies said at least 900 workers have been unaccounted for from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal, or IPPAN, said there’s an estimation of at least 500 of the 900 missing workers trapped in the tunnels, although authorities have provided varying numbers and said several foreign teams were assisting Nepali rescuers.

At least one expert said the tunnels offered enough space for people to take refuge and that some workers could have access to oxygen. But others warned that the chances of finding survivors were diminishing.

Dangi said some workers had managed to make contact and call for help when the disaster struck last Wednesday, and some others who managed to flee reported to authorities and relatives that many of their colleagues were still in the tunnels. But he said that, six days after the disaster, fears grew that some might have suffocated.

“We are working in search and rescue of the stranded people from hills, settlements and river areas,” said Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal’s army spokesman.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Monday that 903 deaths had been counted in that country, with 4,247 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, and Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over a hundred Nepalis. | via @AP

text:
People who say America has no culture are just jealous.

Change my mind.

American culture is the greatest, and it is at its best when it remembers the moral foundations that made its freedom possible. Our culture was shaped by generations who believed that liberty came with responsibility, that rights ultimately came from God rather than government, and that strong families, honest work, faith, courage, and self-discipline were essential to a healthy nation. Those ideas helped create a country where ordinary people could worship freely, raise their families according to their convictions, build businesses, own property, serve their communities, and pursue a better life.

That culture has spread across the world because it offers more than entertainment or material success. At its heart is a belief in human dignity, individual worth, redemption, and the possibility of renewal. American music, movies, technology, entrepreneurship, charity, churches, missions, and traditions have reached nearly every corner of the globe.

A country that protects religious liberty, honors the family, rewards hard work, defends the innocent, encourages generosity, and recognizes that freedom requires virtue possesses something worth preserving.

The strongest America is not one that abandons its inheritance, but one that remembers it. Faith in God, love of country, devotion to family, service to neighbor, and gratitude for the freedom entrusted to us.

text:
"US expected to hold 55% of partnership to produce 17 oilfields
Full development to take more than 25 years, analysts say
Experts, lawyers worried over legality, contract opacity
US could gain access to a base of exportable crude output.

 A massive long-term oil deal expected to grant the U.S. access to a fifth of Venezuela's crude ​reserves has energy experts and lawyers questioning its legality and eventual execution, while calling on both governments for contract transparency.
The unprecedented pact, announced by U.S. ‌President Donald Trump on Friday and confirmed by Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez, will put a whopping 65 billion barrels of recoverable oil under Washington's control, a volume that surpasses total U.S. proved oil reserves of 46 billion barrels.
The agreement did not pass through a competitive process, and its negotiation remained a secret until last week, even amid a sweeping reform of Venezuela's primary hydrocarbons law and the migration of ​dozens of joint ventures and contracts to new terms, which authorities and operators have not completed.

North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company led by controversial Venezuelan investor Alejandro Betancourt that has been acting as a bridge between Caracas and Washington, told the New York Times ​that it is looking forward to working with the U.S. amid media reports that the company is set to be involved in the deal.

According to Venezuelan interim President Rodriguez, the pact will last at least 25 years, in line with the OPEC country's Hydrocarbons Law, securing $100 billion in investment and $209.3 billion in royalties ​and taxes, which would leave some $19 in Venezuela's hands from each barrel produced.
Experts have expressed doubts over the deal's legality, especially since the U.S., not Venezuela, is set to ​select the model and companies to operate the fields.
"Despite being formally recognized by the U.S., the agreement can be brought to court in the future," said Juan Carlos Apitz, head of Central University of ‌Venezuela's law ⁠faculty.
The South American country's expected tax revenue, meanwhile, also seems below what the law mandates.
"Taxes to be collected, announced by the interim government, are incredibly low," Francisco Monaldi from Rice University's Baker Institute said in a social media post on Saturday. He criticized what he called a lack of transparency surrounding Venezuelan oil policy, which has been under ​U.S. oversight since it captured President Nicolas ​Maduro in January.

WHAT IS TECHNICALLY ACHIEVABLE?
The 65 ⁠billion barrels will come from 17 oilfields, with most reserves deposited in eight large blocks in the vast Orinoco Belt, Venezuela's main output region, and the remaining areas across Lake Maracaibo, the country's legacy and investment-thirsty hub, according to a list seen by Reuters.
An analysis by Caracas-based ​consultancy Gas Energy Latin America found the fields contain 63.7 billion barrels of proved reserves calculated using a technically feasible, though ​as yet unachieved 20% ⁠recovery factor. Exhausting their recoverable reserves is expected to take more than 25 years, some experts have said.
However, the areas offer the U.S. a mix of green and brown field assets, allowing the operator to begin with a base of exportable output that can grow as infrastructure repairs in Lake Maracaibo are completed and development plans for the Orinoco Belt's virgin areas, which contain extra-heavy ⁠oil, are ​put in place.
The U.S.'s intended 55% participation in the partnership would continue expanding the volume of Venezuelan oil ​shipped to the United States, currently at about 60% of total exports.
Facing political pressure over gasoline prices that have ticked up amid the ongoing conflict with Iran, Trump said on Sunday that the fresh Venezuelan barrels will ​help replenish the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which this month fell to 290 million barrels, near a 44-year low." https://t.co/PzllEz2e5S

text:
☠️🩸HITLER- THE SKULL WAS NEVER HIS
April 30, 1945 is the official ending.
Bunker. Pistol. Fire. Case closed.
Then the paperwork started leaking.
The FBI kept feeding files on Hitler sightings for years after the war. Not a podcast rumor. Tips, photographs, South American leads. Washington spent time and money chasing a man the world was told was already ash.
The ratlines were real. That part is not theory. Networks moved Nazi officers out of Europe with new papers, new names, and a straight shot to Argentina, Chile, Paraguay. Eichmann made it. Mengele made it. The question the official story never likes is simple: if the pipeline worked for the lieutenants, why is it unthinkable for the boss?
Then the bone.
Moscow displayed a skull fragment as Hitler’s. Later testing said the piece belonged to a woman, roughly thirty-five. The jaw evidence is what historians still lean on. The skull the public was shown is the one that cracked the legend open.
Tim Kennedy went on Rogan with the investigator’s version: declassified files, escaped Nazis, German-speaking pockets in South America that never fully dissolved. History Channel turned it into television. The files turned it into a problem.
The theory writes itself from there.
The bunker death was theater. A double burned. A body swapped. A myth sealed so the Allies could declare the war spiritually over while the real target slipped down the same ratline his doctors and officers used. Hidden in the south. Guarded by communities that still fly old flags behind ranch gates.
Reality check, because the file deserves one: most serious historians still say he died in Berlin. Suicide, burning, Soviet recovery. The leap from “FBI collected tips” to “he lived in the Andes” is a leap.
But the eerie part is not the leap.
The eerie part is how many official pieces refuse to sit still.
The hunt continued after the funeral. The escape routes worked. The skull they waved at the cameras was not the man.
History needed an ending. South America offered a door.

text:
Illegal Monday

INTERVENTION FOR PRESIDENT TRUMP

First, thank you all for agreeing to participate.

We know interventions are uncomfortable, but sometimes you have to sit down with someone you genuinely support and tell them something they may not want to hear.

So, Mr. President, have a seat.

Before anybody says anything negative, we need to start here:

You have followed through on an extraordinary number of the promises you made to the American people.

You have taken on illegal immigration.

You have challenged unfair trade.

You have confronted countries that spent decades taking advantage of American markets.

You have forced conversations about foreign labor and visa abuse that Washington didn't even want Americans discussing.

You have made protecting the American worker part of the national conversation again.

You deserve credit for that.

You're doing a great job.

Now comes the intervention.

Mr. President, if you really believe Americans should come first for American jobs, we need you to set the example. 

Hire Americans at your own businesses.

And then ask the billionaires, CEOs, hotel owners, restaurant groups, technology companies, manufacturers and financial institutions standing beside you to do the same.

Because there is something fundamentally wrong with America's wealthiest people telling working-class Americans that foreign labor is necessary because they simply cannot find anyone willing to work.

We have more than 100 million working-age Americans outside the labor force.

Obviously, not every one of them can or should be working. They include retirees, students, caregivers, disabled Americans and others.

But with a population that large sitting outside the labor force, the first question shouldn't be:

"Where can we find more foreign workers?"

It should be:

"What would it take to get more Americans back into the workforce?"

And sometimes the answer is uncomfortable.

Pay them more.

Improve the job.

Train somebody.

Offer predictable hours.

Create an entry-level position again.

Stop demanding five years of experience for work somebody could learn in six months.

Give a 50-year-old displaced worker another chance.

Hire the kid coming out of high school and teach him something.

If an employer says, "Americans won't do this job," ask the next question:

At what wage?

Because we don't actually discover a labor shortage until employers compete for labor and the price of labor rises.

That's how markets work.

When the price of copper rises, nobody says America has a copper participation problem.

When the price of oil rises, nobody says oil has a poor work ethic.

Supply becomes scarce.

The price rises.

Yet somehow when American labor becomes scarce, enormous corporations have convinced Washington that the solution is to import more supply so the price doesn't rise.

Think about that.

For decades, some of America's richest businesses have accumulated enormous wealth while employing foreign workers at wages the market apparently could not attract enough Americans to accept.

Those workers then spend or remit some portion of their earnings abroad.

Meanwhile, the American worker who might have taken the job at a higher wage never sees the wage rise enough to bring him back.

That's not an American labor shortage.

That's a business model.

And Mr. President, this is where you have an opportunity that goes beyond immigration enforcement.

You can change the expectation.

Imagine the President of the United States saying:

"My companies are going American-first."

Then challenging every CEO who visits the White House:

How many Americans did you hire this year?

How many entry-level Americans did you train?

How much did your median American worker's wage increase?

How many foreign-worker positions did you first genuinely attempt to fill with Americans at a market-clearing wage?

Put those numbers on the scoreboard.

Celebrate the companies doing it.

Make hiring Americans prestigious again.

You have spent years telling American workers:

I haven't forgotten you.

This is the opportunity to prove it in the most tangible way possible.

Not with another program.

Not with another government check.

Not with another promise.

A paycheck.

A skill.

A career.

A chance to support a family.

You wanted to be the president who finally put American workers first.

Here's the intervention:

Finish the job.

Set the example yourself.

Hire Americans.

Ask America's billionaires to hire Americans.

Ask America's corporations to train Americans.

And before anyone in Washington says America needs another million foreign workers, make them prove that American wages were allowed to rise high enough to find out.

There may be no greater thing this administration could do for working Americans.

Mr. President, you have the opportunity.

Make American labor valuable again.

text:
A British backpacker got lost on a mountain trail near my hometown last autumn, ran out of daylight, and knocked on the door of the nearest house he could find.

The elderly couple who lived there didn't speak a word of English. He didn't speak a word of Japanese.

They fed him dinner anyway, using hand gestures and a lot of laughing at their own confusion. Then they gave him their guest futon and wouldn't let him leave until morning, even though he tried to insist he'd be fine walking back to the trailhead in the dark.

The next morning, the husband walked him all the way back to the main road himself, nearly forty minutes on foot, just to make sure he found it.

The backpacker tried to pay them. They refused, visibly a little offended he'd even offered.

He told my dad, who ran into him at a train station days later still talking about it, that it was the first time in his life a stranger had taken care of him without wanting anything back, not even his name.

He said he never even learned what the couple was called. He just remembers the shape of the mountain outside their window, and how warm the rice was.

text:
Azel is a human genealogical figure, while Azazel is a complex supernatural entity tied to sin removal rituals and later demonology.

Azel is a biblical name appearing in 1 Chronicles, while Azazel is a figure in Leviticus often interpreted as a wilderness demon or fallen angel associated with the scapegoat ritual.
Clarifying the Terms
Your query “god Azel” appears to blend two distinct figures:
Azel – a human figure in biblical genealogies.
Azazel – a supernatural being or concept in ancient Hebrew tradition.
Below are the distinctions.
1. Azel (אָצֵל) – Biblical Person
Azel is not a god, but an Israelite listed in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin.

text:
The Joyful Mysteries of the Rosary: The Fiat of Mary: A Model of Obedience and Faith

In the quiet village of Nazareth, a young woman's simple yet profound words changed the course of human history: "Let it be done to me according to your word." With this "fiat," Mary, the Mother of God, demonstrated an unparalleled example of obedience and faith that continues to inspire Catholics worldwide. Her response to the Angel Gabriel, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke, serves as a beacon of hope and a model for all believers seeking to align their lives with God's will.

Mary's "fiat" is not merely a historical event but a timeless invitation to surrender our own lives to God's plan. As we delve into the significance of her words, we will explore how this moment of divine encounter can guide us in our own spiritual journeys. Through the teachings of Scripture, the wisdom of the Church Fathers, and the insights of saints and popes, we will uncover the profound depths of Mary's obedience and faith, and discover how her example can inspire us to live more fully as disciples of Christ in today's world.

The Annunciation, as described in Luke 1:26-38, marks the moment when Mary, a virgin betrothed to Joseph, receives the news from the Angel Gabriel that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, the Son of God. When faced with this extraordinary revelation, Mary's response is one of complete trust and submission: "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38). This simple affirmation, known as the "fiat," encapsulates the essence of Mary's faith and obedience.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church affirms the significance of Mary's fiat, stating, "By her 'fiat,' Mary became the Mother of God. At the message of the angel, she did not hesitate to give her consent: 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord, be it done unto me according to thy word'" (CCC 494). This act of obedience is not a passive acceptance but an active participation in God's plan of salvation.

St. Augustine, one of the greatest Doctors of the Church, reflects on the profound nature of Mary's obedience: "She who believed that 'nothing will be impossible with God' believed, too, that what was happening in her womb was the work of the Holy Spirit" (Sermon 293, 3). Mary's faith allowed her to embrace the mystery of the Incarnation, trusting that God's power and love would guide her through the challenges and joys of motherhood.

The Second Vatican Council, in its document Lumen Gentium, further illuminates the significance of Mary's fiat: "The Father of mercies willed that the Incarnation should be preceded by assent on the part of the predestined mother, so that just as a woman had a share in bringing about death, so also should a woman contribute to life" (LG 56). Mary's "yes" to God's plan not only brought forth the Savior but also opened the way for all humanity to be reconciled with God.

Throughout history, saints have drawn inspiration from Mary's example of obedience and faith. St. Bernard of Clairvaux, in his homily on the Annunciation, beautifully captures the transformative power of Mary's fiat: "You have heard, O Virgin, that you will conceive and bear a son; you have heard that it will not be by man but by the Holy Spirit. The angel awaits an answer; it is time for him to return to God who sent him. We too are waiting, O Lady, for your word of compassion; the sentence of condemnation weighs heavily upon us" (Homily 4, 8). Mary's response not only changed her own life but also became a source of hope and redemption for all people.

In our modern world, where individualism and self-reliance often take precedence, Mary's fiat challenges us to surrender our own plans and desires to God's will. Pope Francis, in his apostolic exhortation Evangelii Gaudium, reminds us of the importance of this surrender: "I invite all Christians, everywhere, at this very moment, to a renewed personal encounter with Jesus Christ, or at least an openness to letting him encounter them; I ask all of you to do this unfailingly each day" (EG 3). Mary's example encourages us to approach each moment with a spirit of openness and trust, ready to say "yes" to God's call in our lives.

The obedience and faith demonstrated by Mary's fiat also have implications for the Church's mission in the world today. In his encyclical Redemptoris Mater, St. John Paul II reflects on the role of Mary in the life of the Church: "Mary's faith can also become the light of our faith and the support of our hope" (RM 28). As we face the challenges of a secularized society, Mary's example can inspire us to remain steadfast in our commitment to the Gospel and to trust in God's providence, even when the path ahead seems uncertain.

Furthermore, Mary's fiat calls us to a deeper appreciation of the dignity of every human life. In his encyclical Evangelium Vitae, St. John Paul II connects Mary's obedience to the Church's pro-life mission: "In the very first pages of the Bible, we read that God created man 'in his own image and likeness' (Gen 1:27). This reveals the incomparable value of every human person and the inviolability of human life" (EV 34). Mary's "yes" to life, even in the face of potential hardship and societal judgment, serves as a powerful witness to the sanctity of every human being from the moment of conception.

As we reflect on Mary's fiat, we are invited to examine our own lives and consider how we can respond to God's call with greater obedience and faith. In a world that often values power and control, Mary's example challenges us to embrace humility and trust. As St. Teresa of Calcutta, known for her devotion to Mary, once said, "Mary, Mother of Jesus, give me your heart so beautiful, so pure, so immaculate, so full of love and humility, that I may be able to receive Jesus in the Bread of Life, love Him as you loved Him, and serve Him in the distressing disguise of the poor" (Personal Prayer).

In conclusion, Mary's fiat stands as a timeless model of obedience and faith for all Catholics. Her simple yet profound words, "Let it be done to me according to your word," encapsulate the essence of a life surrendered to God's will. Through her example, we are reminded of the power of trust and the transformative potential of saying "yes" to God's plan for our lives.

As we navigate the challenges and opportunities of our own spiritual journeys, may we draw inspiration from Mary's fiat and strive to imitate her unwavering faith and obedience. Let us turn to her as our guide and intercessor, seeking her maternal care and guidance as we seek to follow her Son more closely.

In the words of Pope Francis, "Whenever we look to Mary, we come to believe once again in the revolutionary nature of love and tenderness. In her, we see that humility and tenderness are not virtues of the weak but of the strong, who need not treat others poorly in order to feel important themselves" (EG 288). May Mary's example inspire us to embrace the revolutionary power of love and tenderness in our own lives, trusting that God's grace will guide us on the path to holiness.

As you reflect on Mary's fiat, consider how her example of obedience and faith can impact your own spiritual life. In what areas do you feel called to surrender more fully to God's will? How can Mary's trust and humility inspire you to live more authentically as a disciple of Christ in today's world?

On this Monday, August 31, 2026, we turn to the Joyful Mysteries. These mysteries invite us to ponder God's tender entry into human history. They speak directly to practicing Catholics today.

The First Joyful Mystery is the Annunciation. The angel Gabriel announces to Mary that she will bear the Son of God. Mary responds with perfect trust. She says, "Let it be done to me according to your word." In our world of uncertainty, this mystery calls us to surrender plans to God's will. It inspires us to embrace unexpected vocations amid career pressures and family demands.

The Second Joyful Mystery is the Visitation. Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth. She carries Jesus to one in need. Joy fills the house as John leaps in Elizabeth's womb. Today, this urges us to bring Christ to others. We visit the lonely, the sick, or the stressed neighbor. In a digital age of isolation, personal encounters foster community and evangelization.

The Third Joyful Mystery is the Nativity. Jesus is born in a stable. Mary and Joseph welcome him in poverty. Shepherds adore the newborn King. This mystery reveals God's humility. For modern Catholics, it challenges consumerism. We simplify lives. We find God in small, ordinary moments like family meals or quiet prayer.

The Fourth Joyful Mystery is the Presentation in the Temple. Mary and Joseph offer Jesus according to the law. Simeon and Anna recognize the Messiah. Obedience marks this event. Today, it reminds us to fulfill Church practices. We attend Mass weekly. We raise children in faith. Fidelity strengthens us against secular drifts.

The Fifth Joyful Mystery is the Finding of Jesus in the Temple. Mary and Joseph search for the boy Jesus. They find him teaching among the doctors. He says, "I must be about my Father's business." This teaches persistence in seeking God. In distractions of work and screens, we prioritize prayer. We return to Jesus when we stray.

Together, these mysteries form a path of joyful discipleship. They show Mary's role in salvation. God works through ordinary lives. For us, they counter anxiety with hope. They inspire service over self. They affirm obedience brings peace. Practicing Catholics gain strength to live faith amid trials. The Joyful Mysteries renew our commitment daily.

Today, contemplate the First Joyful Mystery, the Annunciation. Reflect on areas needing surrender. Ask Mary to help say 'fiat' to God's call in your life. Let trust replace fear.

Pray the Rosary. Mary, Queen of the Holy Rosary, pray for us.

text:
UNC Sports Weekly: Defense Delivers in Dublin; Fens’ Eligibility Put on Hold
 
North Carolina opened football season with a 15–10 victory over TCU in  Dublin, riding decisive defensive stops to a 1–0 start. Basketball  produced a significant eligibility setback involving center Cameron  Fens, while baseball announced two player-development promotions ahead  of fall practice.
 
Football: UNC 15, TCU 10 — Aug. 29
 
 The Tar Heels held TCU scoreless over the final 49 minutes at Aviva  Stadium, winning the program’s first international game. After a 10–10  first quarter, a second-quarter safety and third-quarter field goal  provided the winning margin. [UNC game report](https://t.co/Y21lCXfbXl)
 
Standout performances
 
 - Xavier Lewis: Seven tackles, 4.5 tackles for loss and two sacks.
 - Billy Edwards Jr.: Completed 16 of 28 passes for 232 yards in his UNC debut.
 - Jelani Thurman: Career highs of four receptions and 94 receiving yards.
 - Jordan Shipp: Five catches for 71 yards.
 - Jaylen McGill: Scored Carolina’s only touchdown on a nine-yard run.
 
 Edwards credited the defense while acknowledging room for improvement:  “We've got a lot of stuff to clean up, but at least we can do it in the  victory column.” [UNC recap and ESPN interview excerpt](https://t.co/Y21lCXfbXl)
 
 The plays that decided it
 
 A mishandled TCU punt snap produced the safety that put UNC ahead 12–10  before halftime. Early in the third quarter, Melkart Abou Jaoude’s strip  sack and Jaylen Harvey’s recovery created the short field for Aeron  Burrell’s 28-yard field goal.
 
 The defense then protected that five-point lead twice deep in Carolina territory:
 
 - After Benjamin Hall fumbled at the UNC 24, Lewis and Isaiah Johnson  stopped Jeremy Payne for a loss on fourth-and-one at the five.
 - TCU’s final possession ended with an incomplete fourth-down pass from  the UNC 10. Carolina took over with 4:05 remaining and never surrendered  possession.
 
 Between those stands, a 70-yard UNC drive consumed nearly six minutes  despite ending with a missed field goal. [NC Football News game  breakdown](https://t.co/X1TY6kEcHa)
 
What the numbers say
 
 UNC outgained TCU 322–281, but the offense remained uneven: 90 rushing  yards, a 3-for-11 third-down performance and two lost fumbles. Edwards  threw no interceptions. Carolina committed three penalties for 20 yards,  compared with TCU’s 11 for 89.
 
 TCU converted only one of five fourth-down attempts. A late Horned Frogs  offside penalty on UNC’s fourth-and-one helped close out the game.  Derek McDonald led Carolina with 11 tackles. [Official box score and  play-by-play](https://t.co/dhWakdbvaA)
 
 Analysis: This was evidence that UNC can protect a narrow lead, not proof that its offensive problems are solved. Finishing drives, ball security and third-down efficiency should lead the follow-up coverage.
 
 Bill Belichick offered a similarly measured assessment: “We've got a  long way to go, but we certainly saw some good things tonight.” He highlighted fourth-down defense and avoiding controllable penalties.  [Lee Pace’s postgame report](https://t.co/Q2J8FVLn7m)
 
Staff, availability and reporting notes
 
Defensive coordinator Steve Belichick did not coach against TCU while on  medical leave. General manager Michael Lombardi remained on paid  administrative leave amid a university investigation into a personnel  complaint. Neither situation should be described as resolved by the  victory. [Front Office Sports](https://t.co/Y1Fk7KHeTZ)
 
TCU receiver Jordan Dwyer missed the game with a foot injury. [ESPN availability report](https://t.co/K8ba2vr9oC)
 
Next games
 
 UNC is idle over Labor Day weekend.
 
 - Sept. 12: HOME vs. East Tennessee State, noon Eastern, ACC Network.
 - Sept. 19: AWAY at Clemson, noon Eastern, ESPN — ACC opener.
 
 Carolina is 1–0 overall and 0–0 in conference play. [Official schedule](https://t.co/q5yGlSD0jS)

text:
self improvement culture is ruining us

to preface- I think there is a ton of merit to self improvement. before the internet, the way in which it was consumed was limited to books and in-person seminars.

Now, there is:
- Books
- Substacks
- Podcasts
- Reddit pages
- Twitter pages
- Instagram reels
- Titktoks
- Youtube channels
- ChatGPT/Claude
- Netflix mini series
- "Coaching" programs

None of these are inherently bad. But the pure rigor of stimuli that attacks our nervous systems every day from each of these platforms is unsustainable for most.

For anyone that's serious about improving themselves, there is pure paralysis of where to start because each source will offer a different recommendation or "hack" for how to improve yourself.

I'm learning lately that you can educate yourself on self improvement and that leads your mind to believe you're actually doing something to change. The reality is that you don't change until you take action.

Our lives improve then, not when we're reading books about how to talk to strangers, but when we actually go and talk to strangers and get data from the experience.

You can never read your way into having experience. It's just not possible.

Experience teaches us quickly because we get feedback on our actions. And rarely are experiences myopic - instead one experience can teach you many things.

Example: Training for a marathon makes you better in many facets of your life. You're forced to:
- Eat healthier
- Wake up early
- Overcome your mind when it wants to rest
- Learn your bodies limits

By actually doing you learn these things so much faster than you would reading a book about how to become more disciplined

text:
USDA Nebraska Weekly Livestock Auction Summary for the week ending August 29, 2026

For The Week
The Nebraska livestock market experienced sharp, broad-based downward pressure through the week ending August 29 as persistent CME board sell offs spilled over into regional cash markets. Statewide auction receipts jumped significantly to 9,000 head, driven by producers in drought-stricken regions, particularly around Crawford, marketing 2026 fall calves 2 to 3 months earlier than normal to preserve critical winter pasture for cow herds. 

While demand remained good for fresh unweaned bawlers, yearling feeders faced steady to lower trends, with 900 lb steers absorbing a heavy $15.00 pullback. Direct negotiated feedlot trade broke aggressively as packers capitalized on board weakness, forcing live cash down $5.00 to $225.00/cwt and dressed trade down $7.00 to $12.00 to settle between $355.00 and $356.00/cwt.

Price Trends by Class

Feeder Steers
Light fresh calves found good traction, while yearling steers from 600 to 900 lbs traded steady to $5.00 lower. Heavy yearlings over 900 lbs faced severe weight-based price pressure.

600 to 900 lbs: Traded generally steady to $5.00 lower across the bulk of yearling drafts.
810 to 846 lbs: Cleared active bidding from $338.50 to $354.50/cwt.
900 to 950 lbs: Faced steep discounts, selling $15.00 lower for the week with a bulk range of $319.00 to $344.00/cwt.
Over 1000 lbs: Heavy 1025-lb weights traded $9.00 lower, bringing $273.00 to $304.50/cwt.

Feeder Heifers
Heifer classes met moderate to good demand, with yearling offerings selling steady to mostly $5.00 lower across most weight breaks.

600 to 750 lbs: Cleared mostly steady to $5.00 lower under regular ringside bidding.
750 to 775 lbs: Bulk yearling load lots traded from $329.00 to $363.00/cwt.
815 to 850 lbs: Maintained a firm baseline, clearing from $311.00 to $337.50/cwt.

Slaughter and Negotiated Cash
Feedlot managers surrendered leverage under pressure from falling live cattle futures, allowing packers to secure northern inventories at cheaper baselines.

Live Sales: Dropped steady to $5.00 lower, settling the bulk of northern transactions at $225.00/cwt.
Dressed Sales: Fell $7.00 to $12.00 lower, liquidating delivered carcass inventories from $355.00 to $356.00/cwt.

Weekly Market Tops and Barn Highlights

Feeder Steer: $430.00 /cwt 520 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Steer: $354.50 /cwt 825 lbs, Valentine Livestock
Feeder Steer: $344.00 /cwt 912 lbs, Valentine Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $387.50 /cwt 580 lbs, Ericson Livestock
Feeder Heifer: $363.00 /cwt 760 lbs, Valentine Livestock

Feeder Heifer: $337.50 /cwt 835 lbs, Valentine Livestock

Regional Analysis

Early Calf Liquidation: Extremely dry, depleted pasture conditions across western grazing zones particularly around Crawford forced ranchers to wean and market 2026 fall calves early to conserve remaining grass and protect mother cow condition ahead of winter.

Weather and Storm Impact: Spotty rain showers brought little drought relief, while localized severe storms delivered heavy hail and wind damage to standing crops and regional farm infrastructure.

Feeder Breakdown: Feeder cattle comprised 93% of overall weekly auction offerings (49% steers, 51% heifers), with yearlings over 600 lbs representing 77% of total receipts.

Looking Ahead
The sharp pullback in fat cash prices down to $225.00 live and $355.00 dressed has compressed feedlot margin calculations, keeping order buyers cautious on heavy replacements. While lower feed grain prices offer cost of gain relief, early calf marketings and ongoing board volatility suggest backgrounders will maintain strict discipline on entry breakevens until cash fat markets establish a firm footing.

Buyer’s Analysis

Weight Discrimination: Bidders showed distinct caution on heavy 900+ lb yearlings (down $9.00–$15.00), preferring lighter green calves or mid-weight yearlings with shorter feeding windows.

Bawler Demand: Fresh, thin-fleshed calves off short pasture commanded active interest from backgrounders looking to utilize early silage and forage supplies.

Upcoming Sales

Valentine Livestock Auction: Thursday September 3, Special Feeder Sale.
Ogallala Livestock Auction Market: Thursday September 3, Regular Feeder Sale.
Burwell Livestock Market: Friday September 4, Special Calf and Feeder Auction. Weighups at 9 AM, regular auction at 11:30 AM.
Lexington Livestock Market: Friday September 4, Special Calf and Feeder Auction.

National Knife Day 2026: Celebrate the Blade with the Best EDC & Pocket Knives

Every August 24th, knife enthusiasts across the country come together to celebrate one of America's most enduring tools — the knife. National Knife Day isn't just a date on the calendar; it's a nod to the craftsmanship, heritage, and everyday utility that knives have represented for generations. Whether you're a seasoned collector, a dedicated outdoorsman, or someone who simply appreciates a well-made EDC blade, this is your day.

Why Knives Matter From the frontier days to the modern trail, knives have been indispensable. They're tools of survival, precision instruments of craft, and — for many — a daily companion that quietly gets the job done. The best knives aren't just functional; they're a reflection of the maker's art and the carrier's character.

What to Look for in Your Next Knife Not all knives are created equal. Here's what separates a great blade from a forgettable one:

Steel quality — CPM-154, S30V, and D2 are popular choices for their edge retention and corrosion resistance.

Blade geometry — Drop points for versatility, tanto for penetration, clip points for precision.

Handle ergonomics — G10, aluminum, and carbon fiber each offer a different feel and weight profile.

Locking mechanism — Frame locks, liner locks, and axis locks each have their strengths for EDC use.

Shop the National Knife Day Collection We've curated 235 knives for this year's celebration — spanning classic folders, lightweight EDC carry, rugged fixed blades, and iconic designs from the industry's most trusted brands including Benchmade, Kershaw, Spyderco, SOG, and more. Whether you're treating yourself or finding the perfect gift for a fellow enthusiast, there's something here for every style and budget.

text:
ROBOTAXI

NEW TODAY
- Testers (RobotaxiRadar): Here’s a list of all Cybercab sightings reported so far (Updated as of August 30, 2026) 🗺️ TEXAS 📍Austin (+ Giga Texas) 📍Dallas 📍Fort Worth 📍Houston 📍San Antonio CALIFORNIA 📍Los A…
- Testers (niccruzpatane): Tesla Robotaxi vs Waymo Service Area in Dallas, TX. Waymo launched public rides in Dallas nearly two months before Tesla. Tesla has already grown the service area since.
- Folder totals: Robotaxi 123 (+2) + Fleet 4 (0 new) → 127 unique
WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s paid autonomous ride service. You book a car in the Robotaxi app. The car drives. There is no human driver on unsupervised rides.
- Live cars today are mostly Model Y. The purpose-built Cybercab is the volume vehicle testers say Tesla is prioritizing.
- Camera-only vision. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy: no lidar, radar, or HD maps required for safe operation on this stack.
- This how-to merges the public Robotaxi service folder with Owning Robotaxi Fleet (owner / private-fleet economics). Not Cybercab-only bookmarks.

HOW IT WORKS
- Download the Tesla Robotaxi app and join the waitlist. Official robotaxi (Sep 2025): app is available to all; access expands over time.
- Book the ride in Tesla’s app. Elon: Tesla will not partner with Uber or Lyft. “We will have enough demand.”
- Unsupervised means no safety driver. Supervised cities still have a person in the car.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): service hours are 6am to 10pm, 7 days/week. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger. Upgraded vehicle distribution and routing so you wait less.
- Testers: you can change destination and keep the same trip for multiple stops.
- Cars return to a depot or homebase and park themselves (Houston footage).
- Ashok: FSD v15 is already running on Model Y robotaxis and will run on Cybercab.
- Testers: Tesla is limiting Model Y conversions to prioritize Cybercab, built with an unboxed modular process.
- Testers (Aug 24): Tesla expects Cybercab to replace Model Ys in the Robotaxi fleet over time and become the highest-volume vehicle there. Testers flag Sept 3 / 9/3 as the Cybercab strategy moment. Austin public Cybercab rides described as “imminent.”

HOW TO USE
- Official robotaxi: download the app, join the waitlist.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): rides run 6am to 10pm every day. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; routing upgrade is meant to cut wait time.
- Testers: booking is in the app. One Orlando rider paid with an X Money card.
- Tesla site (as quoted): app in 29 languages; service animals; space for some wheelchairs and assistive devices.
- Testers: vehicles in Nevada must be marked “Robotaxi.”
- After the Aug 20 Nevada approval, testers say Tesla still has to finish vehicle inspections, insurance, and published rates before paid rides start there.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).
- Fleet / chamath: intends to buy and deploy large fleets nationally when possible; expects payback and positive FCF in under 2 years (tester / investor claim, not Official Tesla).
- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.
- Fleet / tslaming (Mar 2026): then only 8 unsupervised Austin robotaxis — historical; do not use as current fleet size (Robotaxi dump Aug 23 tester: 908 total).
- Testers / Teslaconomics (Aug 25, Robotaxi folder): “owning your own Tesla Robotaxi fleet can one day make you financially free.” Still a tester slogan — no Official owner-earnings number in this dump.
- CONFLICT / caution: owner earnings, Cybercab sticker, ROI, and payback are tester models. Dump explicitly says none of it is guaranteed. Do not treat as Official Tesla guidance.

SERVICE AREA / CITIES
- Unsupervised (no safety driver), as listed May 2026: Austin, TX (launched Jun 22, 2025); Dallas, TX and Houston, TX (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Supervised (safety driver), as listed May 2026: SF Bay Area, CA (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Testers: Bay Area rides to and from SFO. Earlier: San Jose Airport pickup.
- Testers: an Orlando rider reviewed a live Robotaxi trip (Jul 2026). Aug 21 testers also list Orlando and Tampa as live; that is not on the May 2026 official city list.
- Testers (Aug 25 Teslaconomics): 7 metro areas live. Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa ramping unsupervised; Bay Area still safety-driver. Treat as tester city list, not Official May 2026 list.
- Testers (Aug 27 travel_invest): recap of Official hours post lists 6 target cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa. Tester translation, not a new Official city list.
- Nevada (Aug 20, 2026): full network permit for paid public service. Start small in Clark County / Las Vegas; Tesla can expand elsewhere in the state after notifying the commission.
- Testers (Aug 23): Nevada approved Tesla for up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles, up from a 10-car interim limit. Tesla said it would be “extremely happy” to have around 2,500 running within a year.
- Testers (May 2026) said Tesla was also aiming at Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa.
- Hiring and test-vehicle posts (treat as signals, not live service): Arizona, Florida, Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, California, D.C., plus a Germany Arzfeld pilot with a safety driver and Japan Kanagawa job listings.
- Ashok: expanding to a new city is getting cheaper; the end state is operating whole states, not city by city.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- Official: Robotaxi app waitlist. Access expands as cities open.
- Testers (Aug 27 WorldlyReviewer): received an email from Tesla advertising Robotaxi. Tester report of Tesla marketing, not a new Official service announcement.
- Elon (Feb 2026): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Testers (JPMorgan via folder posts): robotaxi operating cost about $0.50–$0.60 per mile vs $2.50–$3.00 for typical ride-hail; long-term platform goal $0.30 per mile. Older Morgan Stanley note used $0.81 per mile vs Waymo $1.36–$1.43.
- Folder testers argue Tesla scales on existing Model Y / Cybercab manufacturing and Superchargers, vs lidar-heavy custom cars.
- Testers (Aug 23): Waymo’s latest self-driving hardware reportedly costs around $20K.
- See OWNING / FLEET for private-owner economics from the Owning Robotaxi Fleet folder.

SAFETY
- Elon: scale as fast as possible, but do not harm anyone. One injury becomes a worldwide headline and a regulatory clampdown.
- Ashok (Jul 2026): zero notable incidents over 380,000 unsupervised miles, across six cities in two states. Cameras only.
- Testers on NHTSA ADS data (Jun 16, 2025–Jul 15, 2026): zero collisions initiated by the Model Y ADS. Two new incidents were other drivers hitting a stopped or parked Robotaxi (Austin red-arrow stop; Dallas parked). No passengers, no injuries, no tow.
- Austin: testers said 100% of tracked robotaxi rides in that NHTSA window were unsupervised.
- Testers: 7x safer than the average human driver is an FSD claim in this folder, not a Robotaxi-only official stat.

FLEET AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; upgraded intelligence in vehicle distribution and routing. Testers (tslaming) say that gain is backend ops (demand forecasting, fleet placement), not a self-driving software change.
- Testers (Aug 23): 908 robotaxis in the total fleet. Treat as the latest tester count, not official.
- Testers (Aug 19): about 97 Cybercabs at the Houston Robotaxi lot. Model Ys and Cybercabs still rotating in the geofence.
- Testers: Tesla plans 80 wireless chargers in Austin as Phase 2 of a Robotaxi charging hub.
- Testers: private (not public) V4 Supercharger depots, including 56 stalls in Chandler / Phoenix East Valley; a Dallas-area fleet depot; a Las Vegas Cybercab wash/service site.
- Testers: scale needs charging, cleaning, and maintenance automated, not only FSD.
- Fleet-size tweets in this folder are days-to-months apart and disagree. Do not treat an old 500–600 car count (or the Mar 2026 “8 unsupervised in Austin” fleet-folder snapshot) as current.

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- New city: download the Robotaxi app, join the waitlist, ride when your city opens.
- Live city: book in the Tesla app. Try a multi-stop trip if the app offers it.
- Airport: testers already used SFO and SJC where those pickups were live.

Thought of this way to introduce the tradeoff between a cash offer and a seller finance offer.

Writing it out here to see how it feels. Feedback welcome. Have not rolled it out with a seller yet:

Your house is a lottery ticket. 

Good news: you won.

Now, you know when you win the lottery, you get two choices on how you get the money, don't you? 

The lump sum and the annuity. 

With the lump sum, you get a pile of cash all at once.

And make no mistake. It's life changing money. 

But it's not the big jackpot number you see on all the billboards around town.

It's far less. 

To get that big jackpot number they advertise, you have to take the annuity.

That's where they send ya money in installments, and over time it adds up to that big jackpot number.

So on this house, you can cash in your lottery ticket either way. It doesn't matter to me. I'm just here to do what makes you happy.

You can take the lump sum (put hand at about chest height) and get a meaningful amount of money. 

Or (raise hand to just above head) you can go for the jackpot.

Which way do you want to get paid?
