Set in 1936, Raiders of the Lost Ark follows the globe-trotting archaeologist Indiana Jones as he races to find the biblical Ark of the Covenant before it falls into the hands of Nazi Germany, who believe its supernatural power will make Adolf Hitler's armies invincible.

Within the fictional Indiana Jones universe, the Ark of the Covenant is hidden inside Hangar 51, a top-secret U.S. government storage facility located in the Nevada desert.

The original medallion with the coordinates—officially known as the Headpiece to the Staff of Ra—is also kept by the United States government as classified material.

The Map Room was a chapel in Tanis, Egypt that revealed the location of the Well of the Souls, the resting place of the Ark of the Covenant, on a scale model of the city but only when sunlight passed directly through the headpiece to the Staff of Ra.

The room was commissioned by Shishak so that the Egyptian god Amun-Ra could know where the Ark was located in Tanis, without having to look at it.

During the events of Crystal Skull (set in 1957), Soviet infiltrators force Indiana Jones to navigate Hangar 51 to find a different artifact. During the ensuing firefight, a crate is smashed open, briefly revealing the Ark of the Covenant sitting inside the warehouse.

It was left behind in the wreckage and remains under strict military guard. After Indy successfully retrieved the Headpiece from Nepal and used it in the Tanis Map Room, the artifact was handed over to United States Army Intelligence alongside the Ark.

Because it reveals the exact geometric instructions needed to harness solar power and locate the Ark's original resting place, the medallion was classified as a high-security risk. It is stored away from public access to ensure no one can easily track the Ark's historical context. 

In the real world, nobody knows for sure where the actual biblical Ark of the Covenant is located. It vanished from the historical record over 2,500 years ago, and its current existence remains one of history’s greatest archaeological mysteries.

The text of the Hebrew Bible states that the Ark was kept in the Holy of Holies inside King Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem. However, when the Babylonians conquered Jerusalem and destroyed the temple in 586 BC, the Ark disappeared. 

It was not listed among the treasures carted off to Babylon, suggesting it was either destroyed, captured earlier, or hidden away beforehand.

The primary real-world theories regarding its location include:

The most famous claim comes from the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. They maintain that the true Ark was moved to Ethiopia millennia ago by Menelik I, the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

It is allegedly kept inside a secure chapel in Aksum. No historians, scientists, or outsiders are ever allowed to see it. It is guarded exclusively by a single, lifelong virgin monk who is forbidden from ever leaving the chapel grounds.

The church is named Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion (Aksum, Ethiopia). This may be it, @chrisbledsoeufo!

The life of the Guardian of the Ark is considered both a supreme holy honor and a lifetime confinement. He lives as the sole human protector of the relic within the Chapel of the Tablet at the Church of Our Lady.

Once a monk is anointed as the Guardian, he never steps foot outside the chapel grounds or its iron-fenced perimeter for the remainder of his life.

He spends his days entirely in isolation, praying, burning incense, and chanting the Biblical Book of Psalms before the relic. Food and water are brought directly to him by a few trusted high priests, but even they are barred from entering the inner room.

He is the only person on Earth permitted to look at the object believed to be the Ark. Not even the Patriarch (the head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church) or the country's political leaders are granted access.

The position is permanent. Typically, a reigning Guardian will personally select and train his successor from among the monastery's virgin monks as his own death approaches.

Local tradition views him not just as a guard, but as a spiritual prisoner. Once he accepts the mantle, his identity is absorbed into the role, and he will eventually be buried on the sacred grounds he protects.

Over the generations, journalists and travelers who have caught glimpses of the Guardians through the courtyard gates have noted that many develop severe eye cataracts. While science attributes this to intense desert sunlight and a lack of medical care, Ethiopian Orthodox tradition maintains a more supernatural explanation: the intense, divine "heat" radiating from the holy tablets slowly blinds the Guardian over time.

As his death approaches, the reigning Guardian will name a qualified, virgin monk to succeed him. 

Only when the new Guardian steps into the Chapel of the Tablet and takes physical custody of the Ark is the previous monk's soul considered fully relieved of its burden. The deceased Guardian is then buried directly on the sacred, gated grounds he protected.

An account documented by Smithsonian Magazine mentions a mid-20th-century incident where an appointed Guardian became terrified of the isolation and tried to run away. Church authorities tracked him down, apprehended him, and hauled him back to Aksum to fulfill his lifelong spiritual prison sentence.

The strict isolation of the Guardian is driven by two main reasons: spiritual purity and physical security.

The church believes that daily contact with the secular world—such as casual conversations, handling money, or interacting with people who have not fasted or prayed—would spiritually defile the caretaker.

By keeping him completely cut off from society, the church ensures he remains entirely focused on the divine, free from the temptations, conflicts, and distractions of ordinary human life.

On a practical level, the Guardian is the last line of defense for an object that countless people have wanted to steal, study, or destroy over the centuries.

If the Guardian were allowed to leave the grounds, go into town, or see his family, he would become vulnerable. Foreign governments, treasure hunters, or thieves could kidnap his relatives, blackmail him, or offer him millions of dollars to betray his trust.

Because he never leaves the fenced perimeter, the church always knows exactly where he is and exactly who is watching the Ark. His physical presence inside the chapel ensures that no one can breach the inner sanctuary without encountering him first.

The church explicitly teaches that the power of the Ark is tied to its mystery.

If scientists, archaeologists, or journalists were allowed to interview the Guardian freely, they might pressure him for details about the Ark's dimensions, materials, or appearance.

For the church, the Ark is an object of absolute faith, not academic study. Isolating the Guardian keeps a total wall of secrecy around the relic, ensuring it remains a holy mystery rather than a tourist attraction.

By changing the protocol from a human-enforced prison to a system-enforced rotation, the church would get the exact same level of airtight security and secrecy, but the monks would get their lives, their health, and their humanity back. @_SolFoundation

text:
I renovated 35 houses last year without stepping foot inside a single one of them

Not one walkthrough. Not one site visit. Not one trip to Home Depot. I managed every renovation from my laptop and my phone. The houses are in Ohio. I was not

People hear this and their first thought is either "you're lying" or "the work must be terrible." I've had 3 houses appraised above the top comp on the street. My appraisals don't come in low because my contractor sends me 147 photos per house and I approve every material choice before it ships

Here's the exact system:

The team: one general contractor in Ohio with his own crew, one project manager I pay $400 per project to physically inspect milestones, and one deal finder (wholesaler) who sends me properties

The deal: I buy sight unseen off the wholesaler's photos, the county assessor's records, and a $500 inspection report I order from a local inspector before I offer. If the inspection kills the deal, I'm out $500. If it confirms the deal, I just saved a $900 flight

The scope: I send my contractor a renovation template. Every house gets the same scope: full interior paint (Benjamin Moore Chantilly Lace, every house, every time), LVP flooring throughout, new kitchen cabinet fronts and hardware, quartz countertops, bathroom vanity and mirror, light fixtures, and any mechanical repairs flagged on inspection

Same paint color. Same flooring. Same cabinet style. Same countertop material. Every house. This isn't boring. This is why the numbers work. My contractor buys the same materials in bulk at distributor pricing because he knows the exact scope before he walks in the door. My material cost is 30-40% below what a one-off homeowner pays

The numbers on my last flip:

Purchase: $78,000 (3 bed, East Cleveland)
Inspection: $500
Renovation: $24,200 (same scope as always)
Holding costs (6 weeks): $2,400
Closing costs: $3,100
Agent commission: $5,640

Total in: $113,840
Sale price: $156,000
Net profit: $42,160

I never saw the house. Never met the buyer. Never shook the contractor's hand. The entire transaction happened through DocuSign, Venmo, and a group chat

The project manager sends photos at 4 checkpoints: demo complete, rough work complete, finishes installed, final punch list. I approve each stage in the group chat before the next payment releases. If something looks wrong in the photo, work stops until it's fixed. The contractor doesn't get paid for a stage until I approve the photo

Last year's 35 flips:
Average purchase price: $82,000
Average renovation: $23,400
Average sale price: $148,000
Average net profit: $31,200

That's $1,092,000 in net profit from houses I've never seen in a state I visited twice, both times for vacation

"But what if something goes wrong?"

Things go wrong constantly. A contractor found black mold behind drywall at a house in Akron. I got the photo, approved the $3,200 remediation within an hour, adjusted my sale price expectations by $0 because the mold was gone before the appraiser showed up. In person I would have panicked. Over text, I Googled the remediation cost, approved it, and went back to lunch

You do not need to live where you invest. You do not need to swing a hammer. You do not need to drive to job sites. You need a contractor who texts photos, a project manager who checks their work, and a system boring enough that nothing surprises you

I will teach you how to flip houses. Link in my bio, fill out the form and I'll hit you back

text:
The Hot South of Mars

Yes, there’s still a lot going on on Mars, and we’re constantly making interesting new discoveries!

Mars has two faces: smooth, young lowlands in the north, and ancient, crater-riddled highlands in the south—often three to five kilometers higher and with a crust about 25 kilometers thicker. Since the Viking images of the 1970s, researchers have been puzzling over this dichotomy. A giant impact or internal forces?

A study published in *Nature* on August 26, 2026, offers a glimpse into the planet’s depths. Alexander Berne (University of Arizona, formerly Caltech) and colleagues analyzed 16 years of tracking data from NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor, Odyssey, and Reconnaissance Orbiter probes. The method is called tidal tomography: Because Mars’s orbit is elliptical and its axis is tilted, the Sun causes seasonal deformation of the planet. The tiny change in the gravitational field reveals the stiffness of the mantle—it varies by more than 20 percent in a north-south pattern.

In the south, the mantle is 200 to 400 °C hotter than in the north and may be partially molten. The thermal boundary follows the visible dichotomy. The thick southern crust has been acting as an insulator for billions of years.

InSight confirms this: seismic waves dampen more quickly in the south. This explains the stronger magnetization in the south and the former water basins in the north. The recent volcanism in the north remains a paradox—the southern crust could be trapping magma.

The dichotomy extends deep into the interior. Whether an impact or convection triggered it remains unclear. Mars is just as divided internally as it is externally—a laboratory for planets without active plate tectonics.

text:
Lil Uzi Vert (Symere Woods) is suing a Malibu rehab facility after an employee allegedly recorded part of a private therapy session and the clip later leaked online‼️.

What happened (according to the lawsuit)⁉️

Uzi entered Oro House Recovery Centers’ Acadia Malibu location in February 2022 for substance-abuse treatment and spent several months there‼️. They did weekly individual and group therapy‼️. The suit claims employee Lynn Tumpa secretly recorded a portion of one session without consent, then shared the recording with her teenage nephew‼️. The clip surfaced on X in February 2024 and on Instagram in April 2024‼️. Uzi’s lawyers say Tumpa was “the source” of the leak, either directly or indirectly‼️.

Who is being sued⁉️
The June 2024 Los Angeles County Superior Court complaint names:
- Oro House Recovery Centers / Acadia Malibu
- Employee Lynn Tumpa
- Tumpa’s minor nephew‼️

The legal claims⁉️
The filing alleges violations of federal and California privacy laws (including the California Confidentiality of Medical Information Act), illegal recording of confidential communications, breach of contract, negligent hiring/supervision/retention, breach of fiduciary duty, invasion of privacy, and both intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress. Uzi is seeking compensatory, statutory, and punitive damages, with the amount to be decided at trial‼️.

Where the case stands⁉️
In June 2026 a judge denied the defendants’ request to force Uzi to sit for a deposition in California (they live in New York)‼️. The court said a non-resident cannot be compelled to appear in-state; deposition can happen in New York or by video‼️. Uzi’s attorney David Moreno has said Uzi was “extremely disappointed” and “distraught,” that trust was broken, and that the other side has not made a reasonable settlement offer, so they are heading to trial (reports from early July 2026 said October)‼️. There does not appear to be a public statement from the facility in the coverage‼️.

These remain allegations. The court has not ruled on whether the recording or leak actually happened as described‼️. Uzi has previously spoken positively about the rehab stay itself, saying the people there became like family and it helped them get sober‼️.

text:
Everybody in this business is bragging about response time. Almost nobody can tell you what those fast calls actually bought them.

Speed became the standard for a reason. The baseline was terrible. Studies going back years found the average first response to an online lead measured in hours, not minutes, and roughly half of inquiries never got answered at all. When that is what you are competing against, picking up fast feels like an edge.

It is not an edge anymore. It is table stakes.

There is a broker who kept a response time board on the wall. Ninety second average callback, green across the board. Somebody asked him how many of those leads he actually sat down with. He opened his calendar and it was mostly white space.

The sellers are not the problem. Ninety percent of them list with an agent because they need to be sold inside a window. New job, growing family, an offer already in on the next house. The intent is real. The leak is on our side.

So change the number you run on. Cost per lead is the easiest figure to pull and the most misleading, because a cheap lead that never lists is expensive. Cost per closed deal is the honest one.

Then fix the three things underneath it. Track time to appointment, not time to first touch. Qualify up front. Cover your phone outside of nine to five.

Slow still kills. But fast is not what separates you. The deal is won in the ninety seconds after hello.

Shoutout to HousingWire and Robyn Thompson DeSantos for some of the info in this reel 🙌

BHL Touch, a VA-approved web-based tool supporting measurement-based mental health care, now offers a new mode for Veterans to complete assessments anytime using their own device, in addition to traditional iPad entry in the office. This allows Veterans to receive and answer questions in advance of appointments, increasing the time they have with their primary care physician and reducing the time Veterans spend filling out paperwork when they arrive for their appointment. 
This new feature allows providers to text or email a secure link to a Veteran for convenient completion from anywhere. When the requested assessments are completed, the provider is immediately notified via email, and they can then review the results, track the patient’s progress over time, and seamlessly upload them to the electronic health record.
The benefits of this technology include:

increased overall patient and provider satisfaction

text:
This presents us with an interesting methodological problem.
Before refuting an argument, one must establish that an argument exists.
This is not merely pedantry. It is a foundational principle of intellectual hygiene. A sandwich requires bread. A triangle requires three sides. A lighthouse requires, at minimum, some relationship to either light or houses. Likewise, an argument generally requires premises, some form of inference, and a conclusion. Your tweet certainly contains words, and several of them appear to be nouns and verbs, but whether they collectively rise to the level of an argument is a separate empirical question.
We should therefore proceed cautiously.
Let us begin with ontology.
What exactly is a tweet?
Is it merely a sequence of characters transmitted electronically? Is it a proposition? A performance? A cry for help? A digital sneeze? Can a tweet meaningfully be said to “contain” an argument in the same way a jar contains olives, or is the argument instead an emergent property arising from the interaction between author, audience, platform, caffeine level, and Wi-Fi connectivity?
These questions cannot simply be brushed aside.
Philosophers have debated less important matters for centuries.
Next comes epistemology.
How do we know that you believe what you wrote?
Perhaps you do.
Perhaps you do not.
Perhaps you began typing one thought, were distracted by a notification, resumed several minutes later with another thought, and accidentally produced the intellectual equivalent of attaching the front half of a bicycle to the back half of a washing machine.
We simply do not know.
The data are insufficient.
This brings us naturally to statistics.
Suppose, purely for illustrative purposes, that we define the variable X as the amount of information contained in a randomly selected sentence of your tweet. We would then like to estimate E[X], the expected informational content.
Unfortunately, with such a small sample and such extreme variance, any estimator is likely to be unstable.
Indeed, there is a nontrivial possibility that the sample mean may be dominated by punctuation.
One might propose increasing the sample size by examining your previous tweets, but this introduces obvious ethical concerns for the research team.
Moreover, selection bias immediately becomes a problem.
Are we examining only tweets you considered sufficiently coherent to publish?
If so, then the observed dataset may represent an upper bound.
This is worrying.
We must also consider measurement error.
What unit should be used to quantify nonsense?
Decibels?
Kilograms?
Liters?
Perhaps nonsense should be measured dimensionlessly, like a coefficient of friction.
But then we face the calibration problem.
We would need a universally agreed reference unit.
For instance:
1 nonsense unit = the amount of confusion produced by a man confidently explaining something he learned twelve seconds earlier.
But even this standard has limitations.
Confidence varies.
So does broadband speed.
There is also the problem of causality.
You appear to suggest, if I understand you correctly—and I emphasize the conditional—that because A occurred before B, A caused B.
This is a very old mistake.
Roosters crow before sunrise.
Roosters do not manufacture the sun.
People carry umbrellas when it rains.
Umbrellas do not cause precipitation.
Firefighters appear at fires.
Firefighters are generally not considered the leading cause of combustion.
Likewise, your ability to place two events next to each other in a sentence does not automatically create a causal mechanism between them.
This remains true even if you use capital letters.
Capitalization is not a substitute for identification strategy.
Nor is punctuation.
Three exclamation marks do not triple the evidentiary strength of a claim.
Four question marks do not constitute peer review.
An emoji is not an instrumental variable.
A meme is not a robustness check.
And “everybody knows” is not a dataset.
Now, one might reasonably ask whether I am overcomplicating matters.
This is possible.
But since your original contribution managed to simplify the issue beyond the point at which recognizable reasoning survived, some compensatory complexity seems appropriate.
We should therefore broaden the inquiry.
Consider geography.
France is west of Germany.
Japan is east of China.
Australia is mostly south of Indonesia.
None of these observations is particularly relevant to your tweet, but they have the advantage of being independently verifiable.
This already puts geography ahead.
Consider zoology.
Octopuses have three hearts.
Giraffes have unusually long necks.
Penguins cannot fly.
Again, none of this bears directly on your claim, yet I find myself learning more from the penguins.
Consider agriculture.
Potatoes grow underground.
Apples grow on trees.
Rice cultivation requires specific environmental conditions.
A field left unattended tends to accumulate weeds.
The last point may actually have metaphorical relevance here, but I will resist overinterpreting it.
Consider maritime history.
For centuries, sailors navigated using stars.
Later came increasingly sophisticated instruments.
Eventually GPS revolutionized navigation.
At every stage, however, the fundamental objective remained the same: determine where you are.
Your tweet would benefit from a similar technology.
Consider engineering.
A bridge must bear load.
An aircraft wing must generate lift.
A pressure vessel must tolerate pressure.
A claim must tolerate scrutiny.
This is where the structural analogy becomes unfortunate.
Engineers sometimes speak of catastrophic failure.
I will leave it there.
Consider thermodynamics.
Entropy tends to increase.
This is one of the great laws of physics.
Your reply may represent supporting evidence.
However, we should avoid claiming scientific confirmation based on a single observation.
Replication would be required.
Preferably by someone else.
Far away.
Now let us examine the linguistic dimension.
Language is an extraordinary human achievement.
For thousands of years, civilizations developed increasingly sophisticated systems for recording thought.
Cuneiform.
Hieroglyphics.
Greek.
Latin.
Arabic.
Chinese.
The printing press.
Telegraphy.
Radio.
Digital communication.
All of this culminated, through an extraordinary chain of technological and intellectual development, in the possibility that you could instantly transmit that sentence to the entire planet.
History is magnificent.
Whether history considers this particular use of the technology a success remains uncertain.
We should also discuss economics.
Every activity has an opportunity cost.
The time spent reading your tweet could alternatively have been used for many things.
I could have made coffee.
I could have reorganized a drawer.
I could have looked through a window.
I could have counted ceiling tiles.
I could have investigated whether my refrigerator is making a slightly different noise than yesterday.
These opportunities are now gone forever.
Economists call this a sunk cost.
I call it Monday.
There is also the issue of scarcity.
Human attention is finite.
This makes attention valuable.
By consuming attention without delivering corresponding information, your tweet may be understood as a kind of unregulated cognitive inflation.
Too many words chasing too few ideas.
Central banks have no policy instrument for this.
Now to biology.
The human brain contains roughly eighty-six billion neurons.
It is one of the most complex structures known to science.
It allows us to reason abstractly, create art, develop mathematics, compose symphonies, explore distant planets, and understand the molecular basis of life.
I mention this only because it seems important to remember what equipment was theoretically available when the tweet was composed.
We must also consider evolution.
Natural selection operates over generations.
Traits associated with survival and reproduction become more common.
One therefore wonders what historical environmental pressure could possibly have favored the instinct to enter an online discussion with maximum confidence and minimum preparation.
Perhaps this remains one of evolutionary biology’s great unanswered questions.
Anthropology may offer clues.
Human beings are social animals.
Status matters.
Coalition membership matters.
Public displays matter.
In many societies, individuals signal competence through knowledge.
Online, an interesting inversion sometimes occurs: confidence itself becomes the signal, whether or not competence is present.
This creates what researchers might call the Peacock Problem, except that peacocks at least provide feathers.
Your tweet provides mostly volume.
Let us turn to probability.
There are several possible explanations for your comment.
Hypothesis H1: You genuinely believe it.
Hypothesis H2: You are trolling.
Hypothesis H3: You misunderstood the original point.
Hypothesis H4: You understood the original point but decided misunderstanding it would be more entertaining.
Hypothesis H5: Your phone was unlocked in your pocket and achieved sentience.
A rigorous Bayesian analysis would require priors.
I do not currently have priors for pocket sentience.
So we must remain agnostic.
One could perhaps infer likelihoods from writing style, but that risks overfitting.
And overfitting, as you may know—or perhaps as you may soon discover—is what happens when a model describes noise so enthusiastically that it mistakes randomness for understanding.
This analogy is becoming uncomfortable, so let us move on.
History also deserves consideration.
The Roman Republic produced Cicero.
Ancient Greece produced Aristotle.
The Islamic Golden Age produced Ibn Sina and Al-Khwarizmi.
The Enlightenment produced Hume, Kant, and Voltaire.
Modern science produced Einstein, Dirac, Feynman, and countless others.
Across centuries, humanity slowly developed traditions of logic, evidence, argument, criticism, and revision.
Then social media invented the quote-tweet.
Civilization is nonlinear.
Now, you may respond that I have still not addressed your point.
This criticism would be fair if a point had been conclusively established.
We are still at the detection stage.
Imagine radar operators staring at an empty screen.
Occasionally there is a flicker.
Is it an aircraft?
Atmospheric noise?
Birds?
A software glitch?
A sandwich placed too close to the equipment?
One must not jump to conclusions.
Similarly, I observed several clusters of words in your post.
They may represent meaningful intellectual traffic.
They may simply be weather.
Further monitoring is recommended.
We should perhaps appoint a committee.
The Committee for the Investigation of Whether Anything Was Actually Said.
Subcommittee A could examine syntax.
Subcommittee B could search for evidence.
Subcommittee C could determine whether the conclusion follows from anything preceding it.
Subcommittee D could bring snacks.
After eighteen months of hearings, the committee would release a 940-page report.
The executive summary would read:
“Results inconclusive.”
There would then be disagreements about the methodology.
A minority report would insist that the original tweet contained traces of an argument.
A dissenting member would claim these traces were contamination from another conversation.
The dataset would be archived.
A conference would be organized.
Nobody would attend the 8:00 a.m. panel.
Eventually a doctoral student would write a dissertation titled:
“Semantic Vacuum Formation in High-Confidence Digital Environments.”
The dissertation would be downloaded eleven times.
Six downloads would be the author.
Two would be the author’s mother.
One would be accidental.
One would be a bot.
And one would be me, still trying to determine what exactly you meant.
At this point we must address the elephant in the room.
Not a literal elephant.
That would complicate matters unnecessarily.
But since we have mentioned elephants, it is worth noting that African elephants are larger than Asian elephants.
This has nothing to do with the debate.
I simply wanted to establish one more uncontested fact before returning to the danger zone.
We should also discuss food.
Tomatoes are botanically fruits.
Cucumbers are fruits.
Peppers are fruits.
Culinarily, however, they are often treated as vegetables.
This illustrates something important: classification depends on context.
Your comment might therefore be classified differently depending on the disciplinary framework.
A linguist might call it a sentence.
A psychologist might call it behavior.
A statistician might call it an outlier.
A philosopher might call it a category error.
A plumber, after reading it, might simply return to the sink.
All interpretations deserve consideration.
Another relevant concept is signal-to-noise ratio.
In engineering and statistics, the signal is the meaningful component of observed data, while noise consists of irrelevant variation.
In ordinary conversation, the objective is generally to maximize signal relative to noise.
Your approach appears innovative.
You have inverted the optimization problem.
This may represent a new school of communication theory.
Instead of asking:
“How much information can I transmit using the fewest words?”
you appear to ask:
“How confidently can I arrange words while minimizing recoverable information?”
This is ambitious.
Perhaps even avant-garde.
Future scholars may study it.
Or they may mute you.
Science is unpredictable.
Now, before we proceed further, some housekeeping.
The Earth orbits the Sun.
Water freezes at approximately 0°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
A year contains approximately 365.24 days.
There are seven days in a week.
A dozen is twelve.
A baker’s dozen is thirteen.
None of these propositions has yet been disproven by your tweet.
Credit where credit is due.
We now arrive at the legal dimension.
If your argument were a witness, opposing counsel would have questions.
Where were you on the night of the inference?
Did you personally observe the evidence?
Can anyone corroborate your conclusion?
Were you under the influence of screenshots?
Did anyone pressure you to use the phrase “obviously”?
Did you consult a source?
What source?
Was the source another tweet?
Was that tweet yours?
At some point the judge might ask counsel to approach the bench.
After a whispered conversation, everyone would go home early.
There is also a theological angle, although we should tread carefully.
Many traditions have spent millennia wrestling with questions of existence, meaning, morality, and truth.
Your tweet has introduced another mystery:
How can something occupy so much confidence while containing so little uncertainty?
Perhaps this too belongs to the realm of faith.
Let us examine architecture.
A building generally begins with foundations.
Then come load-bearing structures.
Then walls.
Then the roof.
Your argument appears to have begun with the roof.
This is visually dramatic but structurally unconventional.
If your argument were a house, an inspector would arrive, stare silently for several minutes, remove his glasses, put them back on, and ask whether the house was intended to be upside down.
You would perhaps reply that everyone on the internet agrees the house is fine.
The inspector would write something on a clipboard.
We may never know what.
Now, weather.
Clouds form through condensation.
Wind results from pressure differences.
Thunder is caused by rapid expansion of air heated by lightning.
Fog reduces visibility.
The last phenomenon may be relevant.
Your tweet has a meteorological quality.
One enters with clear visibility and emerges unsure which direction the road goes.
Meteorologists issue advisories for less.
Astronomy offers another useful perspective.
The observable universe is vast.
There are hundreds of billions of galaxies.
Each may contain billions of stars.
Distances are so enormous that light itself takes millions or billions of years to cross them.
Against this cosmic scale, human disagreements appear tiny.
This is comforting.
Somewhere, millions of light-years away, there is almost certainly a region of spacetime entirely unaffected by your opinion.
I find that reassuring.
Geology also teaches patience.
Mountains rise over millions of years.
Continents drift centimeters per year.
Rock layers preserve ancient history.
Given enough geological time, perhaps the missing premise of your argument will eventually emerge.
Sedimentation is slow.
We should not rush it.
Music provides another analogy.
Harmony requires relationships among notes.
Rhythm requires structure through time.
Melody requires recognizable organization.
Randomly striking piano keys may still create sound.
Sound, however, is not automatically music.
You have produced sound.
The conservatory application remains under review.
Consider transportation.
A train requires tracks.
A car requires a road.
A ship requires navigable water.
An airplane requires sufficient lift.
An argument requires logic.
Every system has infrastructure.
Without it, one simply makes noise while going nowhere.
Which, to be fair, is also a recognizable form of transportation on Twitter.
Now, I anticipate a possible objection.
You may say:
“Why are you writing all this?”
Excellent question.
We have finally encountered one.
The answer is that your original comment inspired me to investigate whether sheer volume could compensate for lack of content.
I am conducting an experiment.
You supplied the control group.
For that, I am grateful.
Preliminary findings suggest that adding more words does not necessarily add more meaning.
This appears consistent with your result.
Replication strengthens confidence.
We should publish jointly.
Authorship order can be discussed later.
You may qualify for first author on the original demonstration.
I will handle the literature review.
The abstract might read:
“Background: Social media enables rapid transmission of information and non-information.
Methods: One tweet was observed.
Results: Words occurred.
Conclusion: More research is needed.”
Peer reviewers will complain that n=1.
They will be correct.
But perhaps we can obtain additional observations from your replies.
Please continue.
This could become longitudinal.
The funding prospects are unclear.
Government agencies may hesitate to support research with no measurable output, although this field already appears crowded.
We could seek private sponsorship.
Maybe a company that manufactures mute buttons.
At this stage, I would also like to acknowledge several entities that have contributed indirectly to this discussion:
the inventors of electricity;
the engineers who developed packet switching;
the mathematicians who built information theory;
the technicians maintaining server infrastructure;
the semiconductor industry;
the people who laid fiber-optic cables beneath oceans;
the software developers who built this platform;
and the unknown delivery driver who may at some point have transported part of the hardware involved.
Collectively, thousands of years of human ingenuity made your tweet possible.
Whether this should make humanity proud is outside the scope of the present analysis.
We can, however, ask whether technological progress always produces proportional intellectual progress.
The evidence here is mixed.
Let us briefly discuss cheese.
Cheddar originated in England.
Roquefort comes from France.
Parmigiano-Reggiano comes from Italy.
Halloumi is associated with Cyprus.
Cheese can be hard, soft, fresh, aged, blue, washed-rind, and many other things.
Why mention cheese?
No reason.
But importantly, I have clearly stated that there is no reason.
That alone improves transparency relative to your argument.
Transparency matters.
If one introduces an irrelevant point, one should identify it as irrelevant.
Otherwise readers may mistake irrelevance for profundity.
This happens more often than you might think.
Especially when Latin phrases are involved.
For example: post hoc ergo propter hoc.
There.
We have now used Latin.
This does not make the response more correct.
But it does make it look approximately 14% more serious.
Add a semicolon and we may reach 19%.
Scholars remain divided.
Now, perhaps the deepest issue is conceptual.
Disagreement is healthy.
People can reasonably disagree about complicated matters.
Different assumptions produce different conclusions.
Different evidence produces different posterior beliefs.
Different values produce different preferences.
All of this is normal.
But before disagreement becomes productive, participants must inhabit approximately the same logical universe.
If one person says, “Here is evidence A supporting proposition B,” and the other responds, “Yes, but dolphins are mammals,” the difficulty is not ideological polarization.
It is navigation.
We need coordinates.
Your tweet gives us none.
Therefore, before I can disagree with you, I first need to locate you intellectually.
Longitude unknown.
Latitude unknown.
Altitude concerning.
Please activate semantic GPS.
There is also a possibility that your comment is satire.
If so, congratulations.
You have successfully created a text indistinguishable from sincere confusion.
This is one of satire’s greatest technical achievements.
If, however, it was sincere, then congratulations again.
You have accidentally achieved the same thing.
Either way, the artifact is remarkably stable across interpretations.

Your tweet appears to exist.
It was posted.
It contains characters.
Some characters form words.
Several words form sentences.
The sentences are arranged in an order.
Beyond that, certainty declines rapidly.
I cannot exclude the possibility that somewhere beneath the confidence, punctuation, implication, and rhetorical exhaust there is a meaningful proposition waiting to be excavated.
Perhaps future generations, equipped with better instruments, larger language models, improved archaeological techniques, and considerably more patience, will uncover it.
Until then, I recommend preserving the tweet exactly as it is.
Do not edit it.
Do not clarify it.
Do not provide evidence.
Its scientific value lies precisely in its current state.
Museums preserve fossils.
Libraries preserve manuscripts.
Natural-history collections preserve unusual specimens.
The internet should preserve this.
Future students may stand before a screenshot and ask:
“Professor, did people really argue like this?”
And the professor will look toward the window, pause for a long time, and say:
“Yes.
And sometimes they paid for a blue checkmark.”
The class will fall silent.
Outside, a bird will land on a tree.
The bird will have no opinion on the matter.
This will immediately make it one of the strongest participants in the debate.
A light breeze will move through the leaves.
Somewhere, a refrigerator will hum.
Markets will open and close.
Tides will rise and fall.
The Earth will continue rotating at approximately 1,670 km/h at the equator.
And your argument, untouched by these developments, will remain exactly where we found it:
confident,
immovable,
and still waiting for a premise.

This presents us with an interesting methodological problem.
Before refuting an argument, one must establish that an argument exists.
This is not merely pedantry. It is a foundational principle of intellectual hygiene. A sandwich requires bread. A triangle requires three sides. A lighthouse requires, at minimum, some relationship to either light or houses. Likewise, an argument generally requires premises, some form of inference, and a conclusion. Your tweet certainly contains words, and several of them appear to be nouns and verbs, but whether they collectively rise to the level of an argument is a separate empirical question.
We should therefore proceed cautiously.
Let us begin with ontology.
What exactly is a tweet?
Is it merely a sequence of characters transmitted electronically? Is it a proposition? A performance? A cry for help? A digital sneeze? Can a tweet meaningfully be said to “contain” an argument in the same way a jar contains olives, or is the argument instead an emergent property arising from the interaction between author, audience, platform, caffeine level, and Wi-Fi connectivity?
These questions cannot simply be brushed aside.
Philosophers have debated less important matters for centuries.
Next comes epistemology.
How do we know that you believe what you wrote?
Perhaps you do.
Perhaps you do not.
Perhaps you began typing one thought, were distracted by a notification, resumed several minutes later with another thought, and accidentally produced the intellectual equivalent of attaching the front half of a bicycle to the back half of a washing machine.
We simply do not know.
The data are insufficient.
This brings us naturally to statistics.
Suppose, purely for illustrative purposes, that we define the variable X as the amount of information contained in a randomly selected sentence of your tweet. We would then like to estimate E[X], the expected informational content.
Unfortunately, with such a small sample and such extreme variance, any estimator is likely to be unstable.
Indeed, there is a nontrivial possibility that the sample mean may be dominated by punctuation.
One might propose increasing the sample size by examining your previous tweets, but this introduces obvious ethical concerns for the research team.
Moreover, selection bias immediately becomes a problem.
Are we examining only tweets you considered sufficiently coherent to publish?
If so, then the observed dataset may represent an upper bound.
This is worrying.
We must also consider measurement error.
What unit should be used to quantify nonsense?
Decibels?
Kilograms?
Liters?
Perhaps nonsense should be measured dimensionlessly, like a coefficient of friction.
But then we face the calibration problem.
We would need a universally agreed reference unit.
For instance:
1 nonsense unit = the amount of confusion produced by a man confidently explaining something he learned twelve seconds earlier.
But even this standard has limitations.
Confidence varies.
So does broadband speed.
There is also the problem of causality.
You appear to suggest, if I understand you correctly—and I emphasize the conditional—that because A occurred before B, A caused B.
This is a very old mistake.
Roosters crow before sunrise.
Roosters do not manufacture the sun.
People carry umbrellas when it rains.
Umbrellas do not cause precipitation.
Firefighters appear at fires.
Firefighters are generally not considered the leading cause of combustion.
Likewise, your ability to place two events next to each other in a sentence does not automatically create a causal mechanism between them.
This remains true even if you use capital letters.
Capitalization is not a substitute for identification strategy.
Nor is punctuation.
Three exclamation marks do not triple the evidentiary strength of a claim.
Four question marks do not constitute peer review.
An emoji is not an instrumental variable.
A meme is not a robustness check.
And “everybody knows” is not a dataset.
Now, one might reasonably ask whether I am overcomplicating matters.
This is possible.
But since your original contribution managed to simplify the issue beyond the point at which recognizable reasoning survived, some compensatory complexity seems appropriate.
We should therefore broaden the inquiry.
Consider geography.
France is west of Germany.
Japan is east of China.
Australia is mostly south of Indonesia.
None of these observations is particularly relevant to your tweet, but they have the advantage of being independently verifiable.
This already puts geography ahead.
Consider zoology.
Octopuses have three hearts.
Giraffes have unusually long necks.
Penguins cannot fly.
Again, none of this bears directly on your claim, yet I find myself learning more from the penguins.
Consider agriculture.
Potatoes grow underground.
Apples grow on trees.
Rice cultivation requires specific environmental conditions.
A field left unattended tends to accumulate weeds.
The last point may actually have metaphorical relevance here, but I will resist overinterpreting it.
Consider maritime history.
For centuries, sailors navigated using stars.
Later came increasingly sophisticated instruments.
Eventually GPS revolutionized navigation.
At every stage, however, the fundamental objective remained the same: determine where you are.
Your tweet would benefit from a similar technology.
Consider engineering.
A bridge must bear load.
An aircraft wing must generate lift.
A pressure vessel must tolerate pressure.
A claim must tolerate scrutiny.
This is where the structural analogy becomes unfortunate.
Engineers sometimes speak of catastrophic failure.
I will leave it there.
Consider thermodynamics.
Entropy tends to increase.
This is one of the great laws of physics.
Your reply may represent supporting evidence.
However, we should avoid claiming scientific confirmation based on a single observation.
Replication would be required.
Preferably by someone else.
Far away.
Now let us examine the linguistic dimension.
Language is an extraordinary human achievement.
For thousands of years, civilizations developed increasingly sophisticated systems for recording thought.
Cuneiform.
Hieroglyphics.
Greek.
Latin.
Arabic.
Chinese.
The printing press.
Telegraphy.
Radio.
Digital communication.
All of this culminated, through an extraordinary chain of technological and intellectual development, in the possibility that you could instantly transmit that sentence to the entire planet.
History is magnificent.
Whether history considers this particular use of the technology a success remains uncertain.
We should also discuss economics.
Every activity has an opportunity cost.
The time spent reading your tweet could alternatively have been used for many things.
I could have made coffee.
I could have reorganized a drawer.
I could have looked through a window.
I could have counted ceiling tiles.
I could have investigated whether my refrigerator is making a slightly different noise than yesterday.
These opportunities are now gone forever.
Economists call this a sunk cost.
I call it Monday.
There is also the issue of scarcity.
Human attention is finite.
This makes attention valuable.
By consuming attention without delivering corresponding information, your tweet may be understood as a kind of unregulated cognitive inflation.
Too many words chasing too few ideas.
Central banks have no policy instrument for this.
Now to biology.
The human brain contains roughly eighty-six billion neurons.
It is one of the most complex structures known to science.
It allows us to reason abstractly, create art, develop mathematics, compose symphonies, explore distant planets, and understand the molecular basis of life.
I mention this only because it seems important to remember what equipment was theoretically available when the tweet was composed.
We must also consider evolution.
Natural selection operates over generations.
Traits associated with survival and reproduction become more common.
One therefore wonders what historical environmental pressure could possibly have favored the instinct to enter an online discussion with maximum confidence and minimum preparation.
Perhaps this remains one of evolutionary biology’s great unanswered questions.
Anthropology may offer clues.
Human beings are social animals.
Status matters.
Coalition membership matters.
Public displays matter.
In many societies, individuals signal competence through knowledge.
Online, an interesting inversion sometimes occurs: confidence itself becomes the signal, whether or not competence is present.
This creates what researchers might call the Peacock Problem, except that peacocks at least provide feathers.
Your tweet provides mostly volume.
Let us turn to probability.
There are several possible explanations for your comment.
Hypothesis H1: You genuinely believe it.
Hypothesis H2: You are trolling.
Hypothesis H3: You misunderstood the original point.
Hypothesis H4: You understood the original point but decided misunderstanding it would be more entertaining.
Hypothesis H5: Your phone was unlocked in your pocket and achieved sentience.
A rigorous Bayesian analysis would require priors.
I do not currently have priors for pocket sentience.
So we must remain agnostic.
One could perhaps infer likelihoods from writing style, but that risks overfitting.
And overfitting, as you may know—or perhaps as you may soon discover—is what happens when a model describes noise so enthusiastically that it mistakes randomness for understanding.
This analogy is becoming uncomfortable, so let us move on.
History also deserves consideration.
The Roman Republic produced Cicero.
Ancient Greece produced Aristotle.
The Islamic Golden Age produced Ibn Sina and Al-Khwarizmi.
The Enlightenment produced Hume, Kant, and Voltaire.
Modern science produced Einstein, Dirac, Feynman, and countless others.
Across centuries, humanity slowly developed traditions of logic, evidence, argument, criticism, and revision.
Then social media invented the quote-tweet.
Civilization is nonlinear.
Now, you may respond that I have still not addressed your point.
This criticism would be fair if a point had been conclusively established.
We are still at the detection stage.
Imagine radar operators staring at an empty screen.
Occasionally there is a flicker.
Is it an aircraft?
Atmospheric noise?
Birds?
A software glitch?
A sandwich placed too close to the equipment?
One must not jump to conclusions.
Similarly, I observed several clusters of words in your post.
They may represent meaningful intellectual traffic.
They may simply be weather.
Further monitoring is recommended.
We should perhaps appoint a committee.
The Committee for the Investigation of Whether Anything Was Actually Said.
Subcommittee A could examine syntax.
Subcommittee B could search for evidence.
Subcommittee C could determine whether the conclusion follows from anything preceding it.
Subcommittee D could bring snacks.
After eighteen months of hearings, the committee would release a 940-page report.
The executive summary would read:
“Results inconclusive.”
There would then be disagreements about the methodology.
A minority report would insist that the original tweet contained traces of an argument.
A dissenting member would claim these traces were contamination from another conversation.
The dataset would be archived.
A conference would be organized.
Nobody would attend the 8:00 a.m. panel.
Eventually a doctoral student would write a dissertation titled:
“Semantic Vacuum Formation in High-Confidence Digital Environments.”
The dissertation would be downloaded eleven times.
Six downloads would be the author.
Two would be the author’s mother.
One would be accidental.
One would be a bot.
And one would be me, still trying to determine what exactly you meant.
At this point we must address the elephant in the room.
Not a literal elephant.
That would complicate matters unnecessarily.
But since we have mentioned elephants, it is worth noting that African elephants are larger than Asian elephants.
This has nothing to do with the debate.
I simply wanted to establish one more uncontested fact before returning to the danger zone.
We should also discuss food.
Tomatoes are botanically fruits.
Cucumbers are fruits.
Peppers are fruits.
Culinarily, however, they are often treated as vegetables.
This illustrates something important: classification depends on context.
Your comment might therefore be classified differently depending on the disciplinary framework.
A linguist might call it a sentence.
A psychologist might call it behavior.
A statistician might call it an outlier.
A philosopher might call it a category error.
A plumber, after reading it, might simply return to the sink.
All interpretations deserve consideration.
Another relevant concept is signal-to-noise ratio.
In engineering and statistics, the signal is the meaningful component of observed data, while noise consists of irrelevant variation.
In ordinary conversation, the objective is generally to maximize signal relative to noise.
Your approach appears innovative.
You have inverted the optimization problem.
This may represent a new school of communication theory.
Instead of asking:
“How much information can I transmit using the fewest words?”
you appear to ask:

This is ambitious.
Perhaps even avant-garde.
Future scholars may study it.
Or they may mute you.
Science is unpredictable.

The Earth orbits the Sun.
Water freezes at approximately 0°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
A year contains approximately 365.24 days.
There are seven days in a week.
A dozen is twelve.
A baker’s dozen is thirteen.
None of these propositions has yet been disproven by your tweet.
Credit where credit is due.
We now arrive at the legal dimension.
If your argument were a witness, opposing counsel would have questions.
Where were you on the night of the inference?
Did you personally observe the evidence?
Can anyone corroborate your conclusion?
Were you under the influence of screenshots?
Did anyone pressure you to use the phrase “obviously”?
Did you consult a source?
What source?
Was the source another tweet?
Was that tweet yours?
At some point the judge might ask counsel to approach the bench.
After a whispered conversation, everyone would go home early.
There is also a theological angle, although we should tread carefully.
Many traditions have spent millennia wrestling with questions of existence, meaning, morality, and truth.
Your tweet has introduced another mystery:
How can something occupy so much confidence while containing so little uncertainty?
Perhaps this too belongs to the realm of faith.
Let us examine architecture.
A building generally begins with foundations.
Then come load-bearing structures.
Then walls.
Then the roof.
Your argument appears to have begun with the roof.
This is visually dramatic but structurally unconventional.
If your argument were a house, an inspector would arrive, stare silently for several minutes, remove his glasses, put them back on, and ask whether the house was intended to be upside down.
You would perhaps reply that everyone on the internet agrees the house is fine.
The inspector would write something on a clipboard.
We may never know what.
Now, weather.
Clouds form through condensation.
Wind results from pressure differences.
Thunder is caused by rapid expansion of air heated by lightning.
Fog reduces visibility.
The last phenomenon may be relevant.
Your tweet has a meteorological quality.
One enters with clear visibility and emerges unsure which direction the road goes.
Meteorologists issue advisories for less.
Astronomy offers another useful perspective.
The observable universe is vast.
There are hundreds of billions of galaxies.
Each may contain billions of stars.
Distances are so enormous that light itself takes millions or billions of years to cross them.
Against this cosmic scale, human disagreements appear tiny.
This is comforting.
Somewhere, millions of light-years away, there is almost certainly a region of spacetime entirely unaffected by your opinion.
I find that reassuring.
Geology also teaches patience.
Mountains rise over millions of years.
Continents drift centimeters per year.
Rock layers preserve ancient history.
Given enough geological time, perhaps the missing premise of your argument will eventually emerge.
Sedimentation is slow.
We should not rush it.
Music provides another analogy.
Harmony requires relationships among notes.
Rhythm requires structure through time.
Melody requires recognizable organization.
Randomly striking piano keys may still create sound.
Sound, however, is not automatically music.
You have produced sound.
The conservatory application remains under review.
Consider transportation.
A train requires tracks.
A car requires a road.
A ship requires navigable water.
An airplane requires sufficient lift.
An argument requires logic.
Every system has infrastructure.
Without it, one simply makes noise while going nowhere.
Which, to be fair, is also a recognizable form of transportation on Twitter.
Now, I anticipate a possible objection.
You may say:
“Why are you writing all this?”
Excellent question.
We have finally encountered one.
The answer is that your original comment inspired me to investigate whether sheer volume could compensate for lack of content.
I am conducting an experiment.
You supplied the control group.
For that, I am grateful.
Preliminary findings suggest that adding more words does not necessarily add more meaning.
This appears consistent with your result.
Replication strengthens confidence.
We should publish jointly.
Authorship order can be discussed later.
You may qualify for first author on the original demonstration.
I will handle the literature review.
The abstract might read:
“Background: Social media enables rapid transmission of information and non-information.
Methods: One tweet was observed.
Results: Words occurred.
Conclusion: More research is needed.”
Peer reviewers will complain that n=1.
They will be correct.
But perhaps we can obtain additional observations from your replies.
Please continue.
This could become longitudinal.
The funding prospects are unclear.
Government agencies may hesitate to support research with no measurable output, although this field already appears crowded.
We could seek private sponsorship.
Maybe a company that manufactures mute buttons.
At this stage, I would also like to acknowledge several entities that have contributed indirectly to this discussion:
the inventors of electricity;
the engineers who developed packet switching;
the mathematicians who built information theory;
the technicians maintaining server infrastructure;
the semiconductor industry;
the people who laid fiber-optic cables beneath oceans;
the software developers who built this platform;
and the unknown delivery driver who may at some point have transported part of the hardware involved.
Collectively, thousands of years of human ingenuity made your tweet possible.
Whether this should make humanity proud is outside the scope of the present analysis.
We can, however, ask whether technological progress always produces proportional intellectual progress.
The evidence here is mixed.
Let us briefly discuss cheese.
Cheddar originated in England.
Roquefort comes from France.
Parmigiano-Reggiano comes from Italy.
Halloumi is associated with Cyprus.
Cheese can be hard, soft, fresh, aged, blue, washed-rind, and many other things.
Why mention cheese?
No reason.
But importantly, I have clearly stated that there is no reason.
That alone improves transparency relative to your argument.
Transparency matters.
If one introduces an irrelevant point, one should identify it as irrelevant.
Otherwise readers may mistake irrelevance for profundity.
This happens more often than you might think.
Especially when Latin phrases are involved.
For example: post hoc ergo propter hoc.
There.
We have now used Latin.
This does not make the response more correct.
But it does make it look approximately 14% more serious.
Add a semicolon and we may reach 19%.
Scholars remain divided.
Now, perhaps the deepest issue is conceptual.
Disagreement is healthy.
People can reasonably disagree about complicated matters.
Different assumptions produce different conclusions.
Different evidence produces different posterior beliefs.
Different values produce different preferences.
All of this is normal.
But before disagreement becomes productive, participants must inhabit approximately the same logical universe.
If one person says, “Here is evidence A supporting proposition B,” and the other responds, “Yes, but dolphins are mammals,” the difficulty is not ideological polarization.
It is navigation.
We need coordinates.
Your tweet gives us none.
Therefore, before I can disagree with you, I first need to locate you intellectually.
Longitude unknown.
Latitude unknown.
Altitude concerning.

There is also a possibility that your comment is satire.
If so, congratulations.

The comments mix some real events with a slant that doesn’t hold up. Arteta has not shown a pattern of distrusting or avoiding Hale End players. He has repeatedly given them early first-team exposure, publicly praised the academy, and kept several as core or emerging squad members. The sales and limited minutes for others are better explained by injuries, form, squad depth, PSR finances, and the jump in standards as Arsenal became title contenders.

Sales of Smith Rowe, Nketiah and Heaven
Emile Smith Rowe was a key part of Arteta’s early revival (especially 2020-21) before recurring injuries and competition from Odegaard, Rice, Havertz and others dropped him down the pecking order. He was sold to Fulham in 2024 for a fee that counted as pure profit. Arteta called it sad and said he felt he hadn’t got the best out of him. Eddie Nketiah wanted more regular starts and left for Crystal Palace around the same time for a similar fee. Both moves were typical squad-management decisions once they were no longer first-choice.
Ayden Heaven made one senior appearance (EFL Cup, October 2024) and trained with the first team. He rejected a professional contract at Arsenal and joined Manchester United in February 2025 for compensation of roughly £1.5 million. Reports indicated he wanted a clearer path to minutes; United’s setup (including a back-three system that suited him) offered that. Arsenal also had Marli Salmon emerging as another young defender. This was not a case of Arteta pushing him out.

Reiss Nelson’s contract
Nelson’s deal was mutually terminated in late August 2026. He was entering the final year (with an option), had been on multiple loans (Hoffenheim, Feyenoord, Fulham, Brentford), and was not in Arteta’s plans. The club and player agreed it was better for him to become a free agent so he could find regular football. Arsenal saved wages and accepted they would get no fee. This is standard for a 26-year-old fringe player, not evidence of personal dislike.

Minutes for Salmon, Dowman and Nwaneri
Marli Salmon (then 16) made his Champions League debut in December 2025 and started in the FA Cup. Arteta called him ready and versatile. Max Dowman became Arsenal’s youngest Premier League and Champions League player; he has been given starts and substitute appearances when fit (injuries have interrupted some periods). Both have been publicly praised.
Ethan Nwaneri received a genuine breakthrough in 2024-25 (goals, assists, starts). Minutes later dropped because of squad competition and Saka’s return. He was loaned to Marseille in January 2026 specifically for more game time; that loan produced limited minutes. Arteta has said Nwaneri needs regular football and that the situation can change quickly if he stays and performs. He is not being frozen out of distrust; he is competing in a stacked attacking midfield/wide group.

Lewis-Skelly
Myles Lewis-Skelly started the 2026 Champions League final, signed a long-term deal, and Arteta has publicly stated he is “100 per cent” confident the player will stay. There were summer rumours of interest from Chelsea and Manchester United and some discussion of a possible sale for PSR reasons, but the club and manager have not pursued it. Lewis-Skelly himself wants to remain. “Almost sold” overstates the situation.
Arteta’s record also includes giving Bukayo Saka a central role from a young age and moving his office closer to academy staff to stay involved. As the first-team level rose, some earlier graduates who plateaued were moved on — the same process that happens at most elite clubs. The comments isolate the exits and ignore the promotions, debuts and public comments that point the other way.

Join our Collections Aide, Tony, as he takes us Behind the Glass for an inside look at the Bird Room, one of The Hermitage’s most distinctive guest bedrooms—and one of the Mansion’s most remarkable examples of historic preservation.

Known for its exotic wallpaper, the Bird Room is 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦𝐬 in the Mansion where the original wallpaper from Andrew Jackson’s era remains preserved today. That makes this room part of something truly rare: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐡𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐩𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐜 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐬. More than a decorative detail, this remarkably preserved wallpaper offers a rare glimpse of the Mansion as Jackson and his guests would have encountered it nearly 200 years ago.

The Bird Room was one of the finest guest bedrooms at The Hermitage and was reserved for important visitors. Following the 1834 Hermitage fire, it received the 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 of the eight new beds purchased for the mansion. With only one bed, it also offered guests greater privacy than the other bedrooms.

Among those who visited were 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧 𝐕𝐚𝐧 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐧, 𝐉𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐊. 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐤, 𝐒𝐚𝐦 𝐇𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐫. The room also features a writing desk and several Napoleon-related items, including images of Napoleon’s brother, Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon’s trusted general Marshal Michel Ney, and a depiction of Napoleon’s death—reflecting Andrew Jackson’s admiration for Napoleon’s military skill and the historical figures who captured his interest.

Step Behind the Glass with Tony and discover the Bird Room, where original wallpaper, remarkable preservation, and the objects and people connected to the room offer a glimpse into the world of Andrew Jackson and his guests.

A man rammed a vehicle into Temple Israel and shot at a security guard, targeting a building with a preschool inside it, because Israel had killed four of his relatives in Lebanon the week before. Delaware is NOT a tax haven.

That distinction matters.

Delaware is a U.S. state and one of the world’s most established corporate jurisdictions. Its competitive advantage was built over more than a century through sophisticated corporate law, judicial precedent, institutional expertise and predictability.

A Delaware LLC does not place a business outside the U.S. tax system. Federal taxation, reporting, KYC/AML and other regulatory obligations still apply. And the owner’s country of tax residence may continue to impose its own tax obligations.

So why Delaware?

Because corporate structuring is about much more than tax.

Delaware offers a mature legal framework, investor familiarity, flexibility for international businesses, a highly developed corporate ecosystem and access to a financial environment understood by banks, investors, lawyers and institutions worldwide.

And there is an important distinction between Delaware and states such as Florida, Texas and California.

Florida and Texas have no personal state income tax, while California’s top individual rate can reach 13.3%. Delaware’s maximum individual state income-tax rate is 6.6%.

Yet Delaware remains one of the leading U.S. jurisdictions for companies because its principal advantage is not personal taxation.

It is corporate law.

Not by bypassing compliance.

By preparing for it properly.

By building structures that are legally coherent, professionally documented and appropriate to the client’s circumstances.

Not by selling a certificate.

By building a connection between the entrepreneur and the U.S. business ecosystem.

In international business, the difference between having a company and having a company that actually works can be enormous.

text:
Interesting...

Oh, and the Corporate officer was spying on children. 

There is no single official tally, because cases continue to surface as departments run audits, journalists review public logs, and Flock’s own “Audit Assistance” tool flags activity. Documented instances of abuse by people with access are in the dozens to low hundreds and growing; they are widely described as an undercount.

Law enforcement and other users with access
The most comprehensive recent figures (as of late August 2026) include:

The Washington Post identified at least 69 police officials accused, charged, or convicted of misusing Flock or other license-plate reader systems for unauthorized purposes. Flock was involved in the large majority of those cases. Many involved stalking current/former romantic partners, their new partners, or acquaintances; searches sometimes numbered in the hundreds or thousands.
The Institute for Justice’s public database catalogs well over 100 ALPR abuse incidents (Flock and competitors), including roughly 39 stalking cases plus other misconduct, wrongful stops from errors, and non-law-enforcement use. They explicitly call this an undercount.
InvestigateTV compiled more than 70 cases of officers, deputies, and law-enforcement agency employees placed on leave, fired, arrested, or convicted specifically for misusing the Flock system.

These include police chiefs (e.g., Braselton, GA), detectives, patrol officers, and supervisors across at least a dozen states. Georgia has seen a particularly high concentration after agencies began auditing.

Civilian employees and others with access (911 directors, crime-center supervisors, analysts, sheriff’s office staff) have also been caught. Examples include a 911 director who ran thousands of searches on an estranged husband’s and girlfriend’s vehicles, two civilian workers at Savannah PD (plus four officers), and a civilian employee in St. Charles County, Missouri. Several departments discovered mixed groups of sworn officers and civilian staff during the same audits. Some officers also improperly shared access or data with outsiders.

Journalists at USA TODAY and The Washington Post have independently identified additional suspicious search patterns in public logs that prompted departments to investigate officers they had not previously audited.

Flock corporate officers and employees
No documented cases match the pattern of law-enforcement personal abuse (stalking partners, etc.). Flock employees have access for support, sales demos, and system administration.

There was one notable controversy: Flock sales/exec staff accessed live camera feeds inside a Jewish Community Center (including a gymnastics room and pool areas) for product demonstrations. The CEO later apologized for “poor judgment”; the company denied claims of inappropriate personal conduct. This is not equivalent to the personal-use stalking cases involving police users.

Flock has acknowledged police misuse, rolled out mandatory auditing tools, shortened default data retention in some cases, and said more officers will be caught going forward.

Influencers who have openly supported Flock on X
Support is not widespread among major conservative or libertarian voices; many on the right have criticized the cameras as mass surveillance. A smaller number of accounts have explicitly defended them as a public-safety tool (often contrasting them with phone/app tracking or arguing they catch criminals and find missing people). Notable examples who have posted in support:

.@LauraLoomer — repeatedly stated “I am pro flock camera,” “I support Flock cameras,” and offered her firm’s services to the company.
@camhigby — has posted multiple times defending Flock, calling opposition “brainwashing” or “irrational,” and arguing people who destroy cameras are criminals.
@johnarnold (John Arnold of Arnold Ventures) — has written threads arguing cameras (including Flock) have crime-solving value and that the debate should focus on guardrails rather than removal.

Flock’s own accounts (@flocksafety, CEO @glangley, CSO @rahul) naturally promote the product. Broader “support” posts also appear from smaller accounts, some police-adjacent users, and people emphasizing stolen-vehicle or missing-person recoveries. Large accounts such as @JackPosobiec have posted mixed or sarcastic content rather than clear endorsement.

The numbers above reflect publicly reported cases as of late August 2026. New audits and records requests continue to produce additional names.

text:
Lionel Messi retires from international football, gives reasons.

Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football with Argentina after earning 207 caps.

Messi, who debuted for Argentina in 2005, won the World Cup in 2022 and was a runner-up in 2026 and 2014. Additionally, he secured two Copa América titles.

In a statement, he said: “It was a decision that hurt – and still hurts deep down – but I understand that the time has come. I swear to you that I always gave it my all – not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football.

“Time is fleeting, chapters come to an end, and this is one that deeply affects me. I love, have loved, and will always cherish being part of the national team. I’ve given everything I had; I have nothing left to offer, and moreover, there are some exceptional young players emerging who deserve this opportunity.”

The 39-year-old added that following the passing of his father, Jorge, this month, he had considerable doubts about whether he would continue for much longer.

He also disclosed the extent of his struggles during Argentina’s World Cup final loss to Spain in July. “My legs could no longer continue,” he stated. “This time I attempted to push myself beyond my physical limits, but I was unable to.”

Messi currently plays for Inter Miami, where his contract extends until 2028.

$GRAB KartaDashCam enhances Driver Productivity ✍️

As a tech company in Southeast Asia, we know we can rarely rely on off-the-shelf IT solutions. In many cases, we innovate and build products for the unique conditions of our region.

The latest addition to the series of smart devices we’ve designed to solve everyday challenges on our roads is the KartaDashcam (KDC).

KartaDashcam isn’t just another dashboard camera; it is a highly capable tool designed to support and protect our driver-partners in a variety of situations—whether that’s for better connectivity and navigation, or enhanced safety through the built-in alert and emergency call system.

How does the KartaDashcam work?
The KartaDashcam is a small device that is mounted to the dashboard of a vehicle. It captures road footage and (in some markets) it also records audio and video of what’s going on inside the vehicle based on passenger consent.

Unlike standard dashcams that simply record, the KartaDashcam has a built-in AI chipset that allows it to analyse video directly on the device, without needing to upload it to the cloud. This technology is called Edge AI.

Improved connectivity
Having a KartaDashcam on board offers drivers many practical advantages, such as improved connectivity while on the road.

At locations with poor or no mobile network coverage, drivers stay online through their KartaDashcam’s Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) and improved antenna. This means that the KartaDashcam acts as a Wifi hotspot for drivers, providing better connectivity by going through different network providers and connecting to the strongest one. This also ensures emergency calls and backend integrations are always active.

For Grab driver-partners, it has the added advantage of helping them stay connected and communicate easily with passengers on the app—even, for example, when navigating an area with weak signal—resulting in fewer trip cancellations

Location accuracy

The KartaDashcam also has an embedded GPS system which offers higher accuracy and coverage than a regular smartphone can. It helps drivers navigate more smoothly thanks to its precise positioning.

Drivers using the KartaDashcam also get to enjoy the device’s built-in dead reckoning (DR) algorithm which improves location accuracy in basements and other urban areas, such as tunnels, that have weak GPS connectivity, thus improving the overall navigation experience.

For Grab driver-partners, accurate and timely location data is important for staying productive on the road, because it helps allocate the rides best suited for their current position and route.

Enhanced safety on the road

The KartaDashcam is more than a practical productivity tool. Since it can “understand” video on the spot thanks to Edge AI, it enhances the road safety of the driver in multiple ways:

~It automatically saves footage of sudden braking or impacts, capturing evidence for incident resolution if required.
~In case of an emergency, the driver can alert Grab’s Safety Incident Response Team (IRT) by pressing an SOS button that can be installed alongside the cam. This sends an automatic emergency report to the Grab-IRT which is available for assistance 24/7. The Grab-IRT will also immediately receive video footage from the KartaDashcam which helps assess the situation visually.

With its safety features and ability to record evidence for protection, KartaDashcam is an especially useful companion for our women driver-partners. We’re currently rolling out complimentary KartaDashcams to women driver-partners across the region.

Beyond Grab: KartaDashcam’s many use cases

The KartaDashcam has many use cases that extend far beyond Grab’s ecosystem. For fleet operators, equipping vehicles with KartaDashcams can provide visibility into vehicle locations, driving events and recorded footage, helping fleet teams investigate incidents, coach safer driving and improve operational efficiency.

KartaDashcams can also support public transport operators, construction fleets and industrial vehicles by helping teams monitor vehicles across routes or worksites, identify risky driving events and review footage after incidents. This can strengthen safety oversight and operational control, particularly in complex or high-risk environments.

Looking ahead, we’re working on more features that build upon the KartaDashcam’s Edge AI capabilities.

For example,  real-time detection technology can give off an audio alert about risks like front-end collisions, lane departures, and pedestrians on the road.

In Karta Dashcams with an inward-facing camera, it could alert drivers in case it detects drowsiness or fatigue to keep drivers focused.

These devices are more than a cool gadget; They’re a vital part of the Grab ecosystem. By equipping vehicles with KartaDashcams, we aren’t just recording the road—we are building a safer, more connected Southeast Asia, one kilometer at a time.
