text:
Seattle Schools Superintendent Ben Shuldiner is publicly standing up to the Seattle Teacher's Union, their disinformation, and their "regressive" negotiating tactics that would make a mobster blush.

(The following is the letter he sent to Seattle Public Schools parents on Sunday)

Dear Seattle Public Schools Community,

I hope this newsletter finds you well. Not surprisingly, this edition will be much longer than usual because it is an important update about bargaining.

As you know the district is currently in negotiations with the Seattle Education Association (SEA), the collective bargaining group who represents many of our educators.

As you also probably know, SEA shares information consistently about the negotiations as well as their proposals. Both sides of bargaining are allowed to share information, this includes things like formal proposals from each side as well as any other information, like salaries or Time, Responsibility, and Incentive (TRI) pay.

Every now and then the union has shared their opinions (once with a poop emoji) about the district's proposals, which you are probably not supposed to do, but in general, most of the correspondence the union has sent out, up until last week seems to have been fine.

Many people have asked me why we, as a district, don't also share information about how things are going. Typically, school district lawyers are pretty conservative and generally advise against any communication to make sure that it doesn't cross the line of "bargaining in public," or "direct dealing," or any other problematic or "bad faith" action.

However, as many folks know, by not addressing things in public, only one side is being heard from. I have negotiated many contracts in my time, and I have never responded publicly about any of them. But that is also because I have never had a union or association share so publicly as SEA does. That is certainly their prerogative. I would never tell a union how to negotiate.
With this current bargain being so important and the community being so attuned with the machinations of the negotiations, I think it is important to follow suit with the union and explain a bit about what is going on. Yesterday, the district shared multiple parts of our latest offer as well as our rationale.

https://t.co/WyAIu9iYcn

In this update, I want to share some more information and try to address some outstanding concerns I have heard personally from families.

I want to start by saying, I care deeply about our educators and want what is best for them, as well as what is best for our students and our financial health. We, as a district, would never want to finalize an agreement that didn't make sense for our community. In my 100+ school visits, I went into over 1000 classrooms and saw amazing work being done by our staff. It has been an honor to be among such wonderful educators. Sometimes we lose sight of our mutual care and love of our entire community when things get difficult as they normally do in negotiations. But please know, these negotiations have only strengthened my resolve to try to help make SPS the best urban school district in the country.

The Beginning of Bargaining

On March 6th, the district asked to start bargaining. We were willing and ready to meet anytime, anywhere. However, SEA responded to our multiple entreaties with requests for data and did not commit to an actual meeting until June 25th, almost four full months since we initially reached out.

Since then, we have been meeting on a constant and consistent basis, sometimes going into the night, sometimes on the weekend. And of course, as a district team we have been meeting for hundreds of hours as well. I am currently writing this letter from the John Stanford Center, stepping out of yet another bargaining meeting.

During these sessions we talked about a lot of topics and were able to come to agreement around many of them, including hot button topics like Artificial Intelligence, Personnel Files, Safe School Zones and Protections for Students and Staff.

However, as you might've read or heard, there are many sticking points and the parties are still not at full agreement.

Salary Offer and Explanation of IPD

To put some things in perspective around our latest salary offer, on Wednesday night, August 26th, the Board voted to approve non-represented (non-unionized staff like coordinators and managers) a pay raise of "effective IPD" with two furlough days. This means that our non-repped staff is getting a 1.73% raise and must give back two days of pay totaling to less than a 1% raise for the 2026-2027 school year. In addition, many of these employees don't get overtime or extra compensation like TRI Day pay or stipends.

Note: Throughout bargaining, I am sure you have heard the term COLA (Cost-of-Living Adjustment) or IPD (Implicit price deflator). Seattle seems to use these terms interchangeably, so I won't really make a distinction. Each year, the state legislature gives school districts an IPD increase, which is great. However, this increase is based on the State's "prototypical model." The State funds us according to the way they think we should be staffed, how much we should pay our staff, and how much we should pay in transportation, among many other things.

For instance, we have Multilingual Learner Instructional Assistants in Seattle. The state doesn't fund those at all. So, when the state "gives us IPD" what they really are giving us is a dollar figure calculated by their model not our reality. What we get is "effective IPD." Thus, if you look at our entire district, we get about two-thirds the IPD rate. This is why the Board voted to give non-represented staff 1.73%. State IPD is 2.6% this year, multiply that by two-thirds and you get . . . 1.73%.

So, this means anytime a staff member asks for and receives the full IPD percentage, they are really getting much more than the State gives us. This is not a pass through; it is an added burden on an already burdened budget. And you might think, that 0.87% isn't a big deal, but it represents millions of dollars for the district writ large.

Nonetheless, we have offered SEA a minimum of an 8.8% raise over three years, with no furlough days. This 8.8% is based on the expected IPD rate for the 2027-2028 and the 2028-2029 school years. We have also promised that if IPD comes in higher, we will adjust, and if IPD comes in lower, we will let SEA members keep the extra, hence 8.8% being the minimum.

Time, Responsibility, and Incentive Pay

Additionally, as part of their contract many SEA members get the equivalent of about an extra 15% of their salary for "TRI" days (Time, Responsibility, and Incentive), as well as payment for 4 tech days and 5 PD days.

I was a teacher many years ago. I got paid for my time in the school. I got a salary for showing up to work and teaching the kids. Lesson planning, grading papers, and planning with my co-teachers after school was never part of what I got. Here in Seattle, our teachers get the equivalent of around 27 days of pay for all of these "responsibilities."

So, when you think a teacher isn't being paid to prepare "for school opening, including preparation for the classroom or workspace before, after, and during the school year" it's in there. When you think a teacher isn't being paid for "conferencing/communicating with students or parents/guardians at a reasonable time," it's in there. When you think that teachers are not being paid for "preparing, revising, or replacing materials," it's in there. Attending SPS and/or school-connected meetings and governance such as PTSA, participating in the development of the school plan or other building activities or committees, participating in a reasonable number of IEP and Section 504 meetings and communicating with parents/guardians and students, work connected with conclusion of the school year or grading period with grades and related paperwork, it is all in there.

I have never seen anything like this outside of Washington. I am not saying the teachers don't deserve this. I am only saying I wish I got this when I was a teacher. I also want to make sure that the community knows that this is already in their contract.

To put this in perspective, the salary line that the greatest number of teachers are in (1060 teachers), has a base wage of $118,716 for 180 days of work. Then they get $3,298 for 5 extra contractual days, another $2,638 for 4 "tech days" and then $17,932 for TRI days.

Thus, taking the total wage to $142,584. And this does not include any other benefits, retirement, stipends, extra hours, or other payments that some teachers receive.

And, just for clarification, in the current CBA, these "TRI" days are assumed to be done. There is no verification or paperwork for them. The TRI is in the check.
So, if the salary goes up by 2.6% than all of the parts of the salary: base pay, contractual days, tech days, and TRI days go up as well.

Special Education

Now the part of our proposal that has gotten the most interest is our Special Education proposal. I have received well over 500 emails expressing a very similar view (I assume these are form emails.) I get it. When you hear one side of the story, that is edited in a way to present a narrative it is going to rile folks up. I appreciate everyone’s engagement. As many of you know, I usually try to respond to all emails, but since so many of them are similar I will try to explain as best as I can and not respond individually.

In the six months I have been superintendent I have heard many concerns around Special Education. Generally, the issues revolve around services being provided, i.e. my child didn’t get this service, my child’s IEP wasn’t followed, etc. Much of this occurs because this district has thought of Special Education as a place and not a service. A child is “in Distinct” or “in Focus” rather than say “this wonderful student receives specific services as laid out in their IEP.” So much of what we do here is focused on ratios and class separation that we don’t do as strong a job in actually helping our students as we should.

And please don’t think this is a knock against our teachers or paras. I know how hard they work. It is a knock about how we are structured and organized. What makes this even worse is that we have a system that separates kids so much that many students with IEPs can’t go to their neighborhood school. The other major issue I see is that in many of our classrooms there are unmet behavior needs, because again, SPS has historically thought about Special Education as a place and not a service.

So, knowing all of that, our amazing and devoted Special Education team came up with a framework around what a new system could look like.

We are trying to address the need to have students stay in their neighborhood school and have teachers get additional behavioral support. By doing this, the district has also put on the table a Special Education proposal that would lead toward lower staff-to-student ratios for a majority of our Special Education students. And even the classes where the ratios might go up, we are creating extra supports. And again, the district is not tied to this or any other proposal. But we do want to try to do something.

We have proposed many different models with changes along the way based on feedback from SEA. However, even after meeting with SEA for many hours, over the last week, SEA has told us that they can’t respond in a formal way, because it is too hard or too difficult. In fact, their latest proposal to us just reads: “Special Education.”

When we asked them to explain, they said they worked really really hard, (which I know is true) but just couldn’t come up with anything to address the issues we discussed. And once they said that, I was flooded by hundreds of emails to “take Special Education” off the table. Sadly, that just means we can’t try to address the very real needs of our students. We are not wedded to our initial proposal nor any of the subsequent ones. But we are committed to try to find something that actually works better for kids, that keeps them at their neighborhood school, that gets the teachers the behavioral support they need, all while not bankrupting the district.

If the only response from SEA is “Special Education.” then by definition there is no discussion anymore. And to all of the folks that have suggested some kind of taskforce or working group, we have had those for years and as far as I have been told very little if anything moved. Others have asked why would we even talk about this during bargaining; that is because we have to if we want to make structural changes. As many of you know, I am a huge supporter of Special Education and have a deep background, especially as a Superintendent in leading large scale systemic change to better service students and their families. But if we can’t even negotiate things and we are being asked to “take it off the table,” that will only continue the situation we are in.

If folks want to have a deeper understanding of what we are trying to do around strengthening the services for our children, please don’t hesitate to reach out to our amazing Special Education department.

Other Parts of the Proposal

The district has also put on the table, as part of this total package, adding 6 Psychologists, having at least one full social worker or counselor at all schools with over 350 students. The district has also agreed to bringing in house many of the contracted BCBAs and BSPs. This would add to SEA's rolls. All of this is meant to support student needs. And all of this is a total package designed to better run SPS for students.

We have also agreed to set up VEBA accounts where the district would pay 10 dollars a month in year two of the agreement and $15 a month in year three of the agreement, if we can set the accounts up.

We have agreed to adding a training day for over a 1500 Paras and SAEOPs, which would be the equivalent to almost a 0.5% raise each year for those employees. We have even agreed to lowering the number of staff meetings from every week, to three times a month.

All of this has been done while also trying to balance a budget that is terrible and currently leading us to insolvency.
The District has tried its best to do right by students and staff in this bargaining.

Breakdown in Bargaining, Calling in a Mediator

And as you might've read that last night, union negotiations did break down. 
On Monday, August, 24th, the union gave us a "comprehensive" proposal. Within 24 hours, we turned around our response to that. In our response we agreed to some things, and not to others. And then we waited. We did not receive a response on the comprehensive proposal on Tuesday, or Wednesday, or Thursday or Friday. Finally, after waiting almost a week, we just countered our own proposal, giving more to the union, specifically adding money to the salary scale. And what did the union do? They gave us a comprehensive proposal that was millions more than their original proposal. They added numerous FTE, millions of dollars of extra pay, days, and time.

When we received this, we asked for clarification around all of these new to their Monday comprehensive proposal. They admitted that it was new to the comprehensive proposal and that in fact they knew it cost millions of dollars more. At that time, we said thank you very much, we understand and respect the union's position, but we believe that this is the definition of "regressive bargaining" and we informed the union we would call PERC, the Public Employment Relations Commission, to bring in a mediator. I left the room immediately to call PERC to try to get a mediator as soon as possible.

Because we believed the union’s offer was regressive, we couldn’t continue to negotiate around their new document. Because if we did, that would be accepting this new document as the starting point of negotiations. Please know we didn’t storm off or act upset in any way. We informed the union that we were going to call PERC to bring them in to help negotiations.

And to the credit of PERC, we had a mediator sent this morning. We now have a mediator assigned to us and we are deeply wanting to reengage with the union alongside a mediator so that we can get a deal done before the start of school.
We are very hopeful that with mediation now, we will be able to get to a deal before the start of school.

Additionally, I want to be very clear about what happens next.

Next Steps

I have a long history of fighting very hard for labor. In college, I co-founded the Progressive Student Labor Movement, I was part of the inaugural Union Summer program where I went door-to-door trying to unionize daycare workers in the Pilsen neighborhood of Chicago. I was an active member of both the teacher’s union and principal’s union in New York. I was even part of a professor’s union. I went to a summer camp where one year I slept in the Eugene V. Debs bunk and another year slept in the Joe Hill bunk. My grandfather started an apprentice union in the Brooklyn Navy Yard with Howard Zinn. Needless to say, I care very very deeply about worker’s rights and collective bargaining.

And, I made a promise to this community that I would always put students first. From my first newsletter to now, I have repeatedly said, I love our staff, but I am here for the kids. So let me be absolutely clear, SEA does not have to strike. Period, full stop. If they do, that is completely up to them. They have a contract that they signed and it will continue. The current contract they are working under remains in place. We are not the NFL owners who lock out our players trying to exact concessions or give-backs. We are good faith bargainers who are trying desperately to negotiate a contract that is good for staff and students. And the district has been clear that we would always be willing to provide retroactive pay, if they don’t strike, when a new contract is signed. There is absolutely no reason to strike other than to flex power. No one is “forcing” the union to strike. There is no Special Education agreement unless the union votes for one. There is only a desire to work together for the betterment of the district.

We are willing to meet with the mediator, morning, noon, and night. We are willing to pay retro once a deal is done, we are willing to adjust and compromise, but what I am not willing to do is play a game with our children’s education.

Our schoolroom doors will remain open as long as we can possibly do so. But if they close, that is because someone else is shutting them.

It is certainly my hope to have a contract before the beginning of the school year. But more importantly, it is my hope that we have school on Wednesday. And at this point, that is solely up to SEA.

Thank you all for believing in SPS. With your help and hard work, SPS truly will be the best urban public school district in the country.

Ben

Kemper founded Farmers & Stockmens Bank in 1946 to finance agriculture in the SW. It became Bank of Douglas, then Arizona Bank, Security Pacific, and finally Bank of America. BofA still makes ag loans, but the bank’s original ag-centered mission was lost to consolidation. The building is a historical landmark. 

My mom and dad said they went to his house in La Jolla one time with a presentation. If you got upside down, you just had to go to him and be honest and have a plan how to turn it around. If he liked the plan to make the money back, he'd give you more money. Shared features include 
the use of colored sand

ritual precision and

four-directional symbolism; 
the idea that the image

Navajo practice
 is embedded in a worldview

 on emptiness,

 the bodhisattva path; t
he mandala

One tradition 
is primarily narrative 
and identification-based; 
the other is geometric

One is typically

monastic and,

public.

Navajo (Diné) 
sand paintings

Cultural Context and 
Practitioners

Navajo sand paintings

Designs come

Nightway, 
Shootingway, or 
Mountainway.

Trained monks 
create them 
as part of

 dedicated to peace

 generation of merit. 

The practice

 tantric sources and

as a living, 
empowered sacred space 
rather than mere decoration, 
and both 
link the work to healing. 

Navajo practice 
is more tightly focused 
on an individual patient’s restoration 
within a specific mythic narrative; 

Tibetan practice
 is more explicitly cosmological, 
meditative, 
and oriented toward universal benefit.

Creation, Materials, and Technique

Navajo paintings 
are made on a smoothed bed 
of ordinary sand on the hogan floor. 

Colored materials
—crushed sandstone, 
gypsum (white), 
ochre (yellow), 
charcoal (black), 
and mixtures (blue)
—plus pollen, 
cornmeal, 
or flower petals
—are trickled from the fingers. 

Work is done from memory, 
often with taut strings for straight lines, 
and typically finished in a few hours 
by a small team. 

Paintings range from a foot or two across 
to 20 feet; 
most ceremonial ones average about six feet. 

They must usually be completed t
he same day they are started.
https://t.co/02b9vjsdqd

Tibetan mandalas 
begin with a consecrated platform and 
a precise geometric drawing 
(chalk lines, string, compasses). 

Monks then apply colored sand
—historically crushed stone, 
now often dyed
—using chak-pur funnels 
that vibrate to release a fine stream. 

Work proceeds from the center outward, 
often over days or weeks 
with several monks. 

Designs 
are highly geometric and architectural
.en.wikipedia.org

Navajo work is faster, 
more freehand and figurative, 
and uses local desert minerals. 

Tibetan work is slower, 
more instrument-mediated, 
and emphasizes exact sacred geometry.

Design and Symbolism

Navajo designs are stylized 
but largely figurative: 
Holy People 
standing on rainbow bars or earth bars, 
animals, 
plants, 
lightning, 
and directional guardians.

They are usually oriented 
with an opening to the east 
so the Holy People can enter. 

The four main colors 
correspond to the four directions 
and times of day 
(white/east/dawn, 
blue/south/midday,
yellow/west/twilight,
 black/north/night). 

The patient occupies the center 
and becomes part of the sacred scene.
https://t.co/e453UvzUoR

Tibetan mandalas 
are abstract and architectural: 
concentric circles and squares 
representing the universe, 
the deity’s palace with four gates, 
and layers of meaning (
outer cosmos, inner mind, secret union). 
A central deity or syllable sits at the heart. Colors and forms encode specific tantric symbolism rather than narrative figures from a single origin story.

Both often display 
four-fold symmetry
 and directional color coding, 
which has invited comparison, 
but the visual language differs:
 one is populated 
with anthropomorphic supernaturals 
from Navajo mythology,

 the other with geometric
 palace architecture 
encoding 
Buddhist cosmology.
https://t.co/OKOAVlDTyJ

Traditional Navajo sand painting
 showing Holy People figures 
(Mountain Chant example).
https://t.co/SS0wbXsdx8

Tibetan sand mandala 
showing geometric 
palace design with offerings.

Ritual Use and Destruction

In a Navajo ceremony 
the patient sits on the painting 
while the singer applies 
moistened sand 
from the figures 
to corresponding parts of the body. 

After the rite 
the painting is swept up 
(sometimes in reverse order of creation) 
and the sand 
is carried outside 
and returned to the earth, 
often in a prescribed direction. 

Lingering power 
must be released 
so it cannot be misused.
https://t.co/Wc8uZVaQYJ

In the Tibetan dissolution ceremony, 
invited deities 
are requested to depart. 

Sand is swept inward 
(or in a prescribed sequence), 
collected, 
and poured into a river 
or other moving water
 as an offering 
that spreads blessing. 

The destruction 
is an explicit 
pedagogical act 
demonstrating 
that even the most beautiful and
 laboriously made thing is transitory.

text:
THE WORST DAY EDISON INTERNATIONAL $EIX HAS HAD IN 25 YEARS WAS CAUSED BY A BLANK SPACE:

Edison International EIX at $54.07, -$16.11 / -22.95% today. The Rosemead, California company sells electricity to most of southern California. Almost a quarter of it is gone since Friday, and there was no fire, no earnings report, no accident. Lawmakers went home without writing down a number.

THE KID VERSION

You run the only lemonade stand on the street. A grown-up decides what you may charge - a nickel a cup, and you cannot raise it. Sometimes the stand tips over and scorches the neighbor's fence, and then you pay for the fence. So everyone agreed on a rule: there is a jar of money to pay the neighbors, and the most YOU have to put in is a written-down amount.

Saturday the grown-ups met about the jar. They agreed to pay the neighbors faster. They did not agree on how to refill it when it empties, and they never wrote your amount down. Your nickel did not change. The size of your worst possible day did.

THE REAL VERSION

California's legislature closed its session on Saturday, August 29, passing SB 492. The bill speeds up payments to wildfire victims and allows more borrowing for the state's wildfire fund. It left out a $6B ceiling on what a single fire can cost a company, and any way to refill that fund once it runs dry. So the largest bill these companies face - what they owe when their equipment starts a fire - still has no maximum.

Edison knows the shape of that bill. The Eaton Fire started January 7, 2025, killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,400 homes and buildings. Southern California Edison has made over 2,200 compensation offers worth more than $775M, with more than 30,000 claims still in court.

PG&E Corporation at $13.44, -$3.16 / -19.02% today, the Oakland company that delivers power across northern and central California, fell on the same news to its lowest price in a year. Both traded four to five times their usual daily volume.

A power company is meant to be the boring one: prices set by a regulator, customers who cannot leave, profit you can see coming years ahead. Saturday did not make Edison less able to pay a bill. It made the bill impossible to size, and a bill nobody can size frightens people more than a big one does.

WHERE THESE SIT

Neither is on any of the six Len5es. Edison is the tempting one, because the arithmetic looks generous: its dividend - the cash a company hands its owners each year - is $3.51 a share, or 6.5% of today's price against 5.0% on Friday. The payment did not change. The price fell, and it fell because of the exact thing that decides whether the payment stays affordable. The Income Len5 wants cash that reaches owners and is genuinely funded by the business, and only the first half of that is settled now. A real ceiling on the fire bill, with the payout intact, would settle the second. PG&E looks cheap at roughly 12 times a year of profit, the kind of gap the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 hunts for - but a discount nobody can measure is not one anybody can use. A law or a court settlement that finally attaches a figure would change both reads.

WHAT A GROWN-UP SHOULD WATCH

Not the share price. January 2027, when the first Eaton Fire case reaches a jury - the first time anyone outside a legislature puts a real number on one of these bills.

Not investment advice.

text:
Remembering 

Patricia Molly Owens  was a Canadian actress, working in Hollywood. She appeared in about 40 films and 10 television episodes in a career lasting from 1943 to 1968.

Owens moved from Canada to England as a child.  At 18, she made her motion-picture debut in the musical comedy Miss London Ltd. The following year, she had a small role in Harold French's social satire English Without Tears. Her career continued in this manner for a few years, Owens getting ever-larger roles in movies.

Her career received a boost when she was seen by a 20th Century Fox executive while performing in a stage production of Sabrina Fair, and was offered a screen test.  The result was a contract with the studio and a move to Hollywood. Her first American film was Island in the Sun (1957), followed by No Down Payment, both for Fox, after which Owens was lent to Warner Bros. to appear in the critically acclaimed drama Sayonara (1957).

Golden, British Columbia, Canada
DiedAugust 31, 2000 (aged 75)

Newsom asked lawmakers to bar insurance companies from suing the investor-owned utilities responsible for California's worst wildfires — utilities like PG&E, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric. Wildfire survivors put it bluntly: "𝘞𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘧𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘭𝘺 𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘧𝘶𝘭 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘪𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘥 𝘶𝘱 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘷𝘰𝘳𝘴," said Joy Chen, executive director of Every Fire Survivor's Network.

Newsom's own staff pushed to eliminate what's known as subrogation — the process that lets insurers who already paid wildfire victims' claims go after the utility that started the fire to recoup the money. When Democratic negotiators in his own party balked, his administration offered a fallback Friday night: cap insurers at recovering just 𝟓𝟎% 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬. Lawmakers rejected that compromise too, right up against the deadline that closed California's legislative session at midnight Monday.

The proposal would have protected the very companies whose downed power lines and faulty equipment torched entire neighborhoods, while leaving insurers — and by extension, the homeowners and businesses who pay their premiums — to eat the cost of someone else's fire. 𝐖𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬𝐨𝐦'𝐬 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐞𝐝: PG&E shares fell nearly 10%, Southern California Edison dropped about 5%, and San Diego Gas & Electric slid roughly 1%.

Newsom insisted the fight isn't over. "𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥𝘴 𝘧𝘶𝘭𝘭 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮 — 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘰𝘯𝘦. 𝘐 𝘶𝘳𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘓𝘦𝘨𝘪𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘥 𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘵 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘞𝘪𝘭𝘥𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘦 𝘍𝘶𝘯𝘥'𝘴 𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨-𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘮 𝘥𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺, 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦 𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘦𝘯𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘦 𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘶𝘯𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘦𝘥 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘢 𝘣𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘳𝘶𝘱𝘵𝘤𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨," he said — the same fire victims his own proposal would have left holding the bag this year.

Other pieces of Newsom's wildfire package did pass — faster payouts for victims, limits on attorneys' fees, a ban on utility CEO bonuses after a company starts a fire. But the one piece that would have let utility companies off the hook for their own wildfires d∗ed on his own party's desk. 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐚'𝐬 𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐛𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐭 — not this year.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

King George V of Britain and Tsar Nicholas II of Russia looked so remarkably identical that even their own families, servants, and foreign diplomats frequently mistook them for one another.

​The two monarchs were first cousins through their mothers, Queen Alexandra of Britain and Empress Maria Feodorovna of Russia, who were sisters and Danish princesses. Beyond sharing identical facial features, almond-shaped eyes, and matching groomed beards, they were close lifelong friends who called each other "Georgy" and "Nicky."

​At the wedding of the Duke of York (the future George V) in London in 1893, guests repeatedly approached Tsar Nicholas to offer congratulations, thinking he was the groom. On another occasion, a senior British royal attendant mistook the Russian Tsar for George and gave him orders, leaving Nicholas amused and the court embarrassed. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

​More Surprising Facts About George V & Nicholas II:

A. ​Matching Tattoos: During their youth in the late 19th century, both cousins visited Japan on naval tours and chose to get identical dragon tattoos inked onto their right forearms by local master tattooists, a trend popular among young sailors at the time.

B. ​Matching Outfits for Pranks: In 1909, during a royal gathering at the Cowes Regatta on the Isle of Wight, the cousins dressed in identical admiral uniforms, posed together for portraits, and took turns confusing court officials and photographers.

C. ​The Tragic Asylum Decision: When the Russian Revolution broke out in 1917, King George V initially offered asylum to Nicholas and the Russian imperial family. However, fearing that harboring the unpopular Tsar might spark anti-monarchist sentiment and revolution in Britain, George withdrew the offer. Tragically, Nicholas and his family were executed by the Bolsheviks in Ekaterinburg the following year in 1918.

text:
These two men were first cousins, and they look so much alike that people often mistake them for each other. One of them would be murdered by the Bolsheviks, along with his entire family. The other could have saved him, and chose not to...

The man on the right is King George V of Britain. The one who looks almost like his twin is Tsar Nicholas II of Russia. Their mothers were sisters, Danish princesses, and the two boys grew up close enough that in the private letters they sent each other all their lives they signed off as "Georgie" and "Nicky."

Then the world went to war, and Nicholas's own world fell apart with it. In March 1917 the Russian monarchy collapsed, Nicholas was forced to abdicate, ending 300 years of Romanov rule, and he and his wife and their five children were placed under house arrest. He was no longer a Tsar. He was a private citizen, a father, trapped with his family in a country turning against them.

At first, help seemed to be coming from the one place it should have. The British government offered the Romanovs asylum: if they could reach Murmansk on Russia's northern coast, a British warship would carry them out. For a moment his family had a way out...

Then George changed his mind. Frightened that sheltering an unpopular autocrat would turn British anger against his own throne in a time of revolution and war, he pressed his government to withdraw the offer. The National Archives hold the record of it: the asylum extended, and then, over the King's fears of anti-monarchy feeling at home, taken back. 

He chose his crown over his cousin.

By then the family's fate was in the hands of the Bolsheviks, who had seized power in Russia. On the night of 16 July 1918, Nicholas, his wife Alexandra, their four young daughters, and their thirteen-year-old son were woken and told they were to be photographed. Instead they were taken down to a cellar and shot. When the gunfire failed to kill the daughters, whose clothing was lined with hidden jewels that deflected the bullets, the killers finished them with bayonets...

When the news reached London, it broke George. In his diary, he mourned the cousin he had failed to save: "It was a foul murder. I was devoted to Nicky, who was the kindest of men and thorough gentleman: loved his country and people."

The selfie is not a picture. It is a portable altar.

We no longer look at the world; we look for ourselves in it, then offer the result to a machine that grades the sacrifice. The old icons pointed beyond the image. This one points only back and calls the loop identity.

What mass media made fungible, the algorithm makes liturgical. It does not merely predict our thoughts. It rehearses them until they feel like ours. A self that can be cropped, scored, and deleted was never a self. It was inventory.

They built the temple.
We mistook the glow for presence.
Now the worshipper is the offering.

And still, behind the feed, behind the profile, behind even the one watching the screen, something remains that was never uploaded and cannot be banned. The religion of man worships a reflection. What is real was never in the mirror. It is already free. It waits only to be noticed, once the offering finally stops.

text:
$GNS [UPDATE]

Reynolds (+ Genius Group Limited) v. Citadel Securities LLC et al

The legal filings detail a federal class action securities lawsuit brought against major market makers Citadel Securities LLC and Virtu Americas LLC. The lawsuit alleges that between April 2022 and May 2025, Citadel and Virtu engaged in a massive, illegal trading scheme known as "spoofing." By placing and almost immediately canceling over 1.3 million deceptive trade orders for Genius Group Limited stock, representing more than 139 million shares, the defendants allegedly created a false impression of heavy supply and market volatility. This artificially depressed Genius Group's stock price and widened its bid-ask spreads, allowing Citadel and Virtu to cover their own short positions and execute trades on highly favorable terms at the direct expense of regular investors.

The specific documents provided represent competing motions from three distinct individual investors seeking to be appointed as Lead Plaintiff for the overall class of damaged shareholders. Aron Reynolds, Jordan Dario Primo, and Duc To have each filed motions claiming to have suffered significant financial harm, with reported losses ranging up to $152,882. Each investor is asking the court to appoint them as the lead representative and to approve their chosen legal team including prominent law firms such as Grant & Eisenhofer, Pomerantz, and The Rosen Law Firm to manage the lawsuit on behalf of all affected Genius Group investors.

Keeping the lawsuit in the Southern District of Florida presents a strong legal case based on jurisdictional and factual ties. Citadel Securities maintains its global headquarters in Miami, Florida, making Florida the central hub where high-level corporate governance, executive decision-making, and algorithmic trading infrastructure reside. Furthermore, co-defendant Virtu Americas conducts substantial business operations within the state out of its Palm Beach Gardens office. Because a significant portion of the alleged market manipulation, trading strategy execution, and key witnesses are located within Florida, venue in the Southern District of Florida is proper and directly connected to the core locus of the alleged misconduct.

This litigation potentially benefits Genius Group and its shareholder base by bringing formal judicial scrutiny to predatory market practices that artificially suppressed the company's stock price. A successful outcome could result in monetary compensation for investors who traded at manipulated prices, while also helping to restore fair, supply-and-demand market mechanics to the stock. Furthermore, the willingness of major national class action law firms to commit extensive resources to this case offers strong external validation of the claims that Genius Group's valuation was distorted by unlawful trading conduct.

Moving forward, the federal judge presiding over the case in the Southern District of Florida will address the pending motion regarding venue transfer alongside the competing applications for Lead Plaintiff. Once the court resolves the location dispute and designates the official Lead Plaintiff and Lead Counsel, the current administrative stay on the case will be lifted. The action will then move into active litigation, where Citadel and Virtu will be required to formally respond to the allegations, followed by the discovery process, motions, and potential trial or settlement proceedings.

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

• $1 in the S&P 500 since 1950 (All Days): $463 
• Miss the 50 worst days: $11,074 
• Miss the 100 worst days: $69,582

The top chart makes cherry-picking look easy. The bottom chart explains why binary market timing is a statistical trap:

1.) Extreme Days Overlap: The 25 best and 25 worst daily sessions since 1990 cluster in the exact same liquidity washouts (2001, 2008, 2020). If you panic-sell to dodge the crash, you inevitably miss the violent rebound.

2.) The Calm Builds the Wealth: Look at the multi-year voids from 2003 to 2007 and 2011 to 2018. Zero extreme days. The quiet drift upward to 7,711.76 is where real compounding happens.

3.) Tactical Execution vs. Binary Timing: True macro management is not about jumping 100% in or out of the tape. It is about structured dollar-cost averaging, asymmetric rebalancing, and maintaining liquidity buffers so you never become a forced seller.

Do not confuse binary day-timing with disciplined tactical risk management. Budget your volatility, execute systematic rules, and let capital compound.

text:
I don't disagree.. when it's possible for a developer to offer such choices they definitely should.

But the reality is that is typically only possible when the limiting factor in the game comes down to GPU constraints and therefore you can just adjust the resolution and potentially dial back some of the graphical settings and offer that extra performance option.

But if your games fundamental core systems that make up its world are the problem. You end up with a CPU limited situation and it's a lot harder to justify a 60 FPS mode that could require fundamentally altering the game experience itself.

text: Long before Tesla, SpaceX, and fame, Elon Musk was a 23-year-old University of Pennsylvania student navigating college life and dating fellow student Jennifer Gwynne. The two reportedly met while working as resident advisers and dated from 1994 to 1995. Decades later, Gwynne decided to auction photographs and keepsakes from that period, turning a small collection of memories into a piece of tech history. In September 2022, 18 candid photographs and several personal items brought in more than $165,000 at auction. Among the most valuable pieces were a gold necklace containing a small emerald that Musk had given Gwynne, which sold for $51,000, a formal photograph featuring the couple that reached $42,000, and a birthday card signed by Musk that sold for nearly $17,000. Gwynne said she planned to use proceeds toward her stepson’s university education. The story offers a rare glimpse into Musk’s life before entrepreneurship made him globally known.

text:
Don’t lean on a cheap trick like the Sorcerer’s Stone. Even if you’re clumsy and dirty, lean on the friends beside you and trust the justice in your chest. That’s what the chessboard and the Great Hall proved. It’s the strongest magic people have, and what this story has yelled for twenty-five years.
It starts under the stairs. Harry is an unloved kid beaten by the Dursleys. A letter at eleven takes him to Hogwarts, where he meets Ron, Hermione, and Neville. Lonely kids drop their armor and start trusting each other. When they split candy, real magic is planted.
In the dungeon they stand as wizards alone. Hearts shake, then they wake up.
Ron has lived in hand-me-downs. On the chessboard he sees it: if he doesn’t throw himself in, Harry loses. “Harry, you’ve got to go on.” He bets his life and becomes a knight with his own pride.
Hermione armored herself with books. She watches Ron offer himself up and sends Harry on. “Friendship and guts matter more.”
Harry has always been the orphan who gets saved. He takes their sacrifice and walks in as a real wizard.
Neville stands shaking in front of his friends and won’t let Gryffindor look worse. That’s the real Gryffindor soul.
The Stone mirrors the hunger to never die. Voldemort and Quirrell fold. Harry doesn’t. It goes only to the one who wants to protect it, not own it.
Dumbledore says it takes as much courage to stand up to friends as to enemies. Neville gets the last ten points. The flag turns red.
Twenty-five years later the effects changed. The tears didn’t. The real magic was four clumsy kids getting hurt, still looking out for each other, and learning to believe in themselves. Don’t grab easy power. Lean on your friends. Trust yourself. Stand up.
⏬🙌🔎🔍👀👇

🇮🇷🇺🇸 Malcolm Nance: Iran may have already mined the shipping routes the U.S. just cleared

Why would Iran put mobile rocket launchers on tiny Larak Island when they could fire from the mainland?

Malcolm Nance thinks that's the key to understanding the U.S. strike.

The Fajr-5 launchers reportedly targeted can deploy specialized sea mines by rocket.

And according to Nance, their roughly 130-kilometer range means positioning them on Larak could allow Iran to reach far beyond the immediate Strait of Hormuz, potentially mining approaches used by tankers along the UAE coast and even around Fujairah.

That matters because CENTCOM had just announced that mines had been cleared from the Strait.

Nance's theory is that Iran quietly moved the launchers onto Larak specifically to put them back.

And there's a nastier possibility.

He believes the U.S. may only have discovered the launchers after detecting them firing.

If so, destroying the launchers doesn't solve the problem.

The mines could already be in the water, submerged and waiting for ships to pass overhead.

Nance estimates there could potentially be anywhere from one to two dozen mines already deployed, depending on the launchers involved.

So the U.S. may have successfully destroyed two Iranian launchers.

The considerably less comforting question is whether they had already finished their job.

@MalcolmNance

text:
Also… how are we helping others prepare for eternity?

I literally just got back from a family vacation with all of my children and grandchildren.

If you were to ask me what the highlight of my trip was—besides the incredible blessing of having all of my children and grandchildren together under one roof—it would be this:

One morning, I woke up in a beautiful bedroom overlooking the water and the mountains. Before long, I had an unexpected visitor—my almost 10-year-old grandson. He climbed right into bed between my husband and me, ready to wake us up for our next adventure of the day.

But I was just about to do my morning devotion using the @ourdailybread app.

I have been reading Our Daily Bread devotionals for almost 40 years.

When I was raising my own children, I would get up very early in the morning, sit at the kitchen table with my Bible open, and read my daily devotion and Scripture. My youngest son would often stumble out of his bedroom, still sleepy, and climb onto my lap while I read.

And now, all these years later, there I was with my grandson beside me.

I offered him one of my earbuds and decided to listen to the devotion on audio that morning. I normally read it myself, but that day, I wanted him to hear it with me.

So we listened together.

We lay there looking out at the beautiful water and mountains, sharing this quiet little moment with God. As we listened, my grandson looked up at me, smiled, and hugged me.

He looked so peaceful, so happy, and almost angelic.

And I was overwhelmed with gratitude that God had given me that moment with him.

Yes, we had a very busy and wonderful week. We visited national parks and lakes, went kayaking, saw the Space Needle, explored Seattle, and made countless family memories.

But that quiet morning with my grandson was the highlight of my trip.

Because in that moment, we weren’t just making a vacation memory.

We were investing in eternity.

It reminded me of this Scripture:

“These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” — Deuteronomy 6:6–7

Sometimes we may think teaching our children and grandchildren about God requires some great lesson or perfectly planned moment.

But often, it happens just like this—in a bed on vacation, sharing an earbud, looking at the mountains, listening to God’s Word together.

And perhaps that is something worth asking ourselves:

We spend so much time preparing our children and grandchildren for life… but how are we helping them prepare for eternity?

“I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” — 3 John 1:4

Dumbledore says it takes as much courage to stand up to friends as to enemies. Neville gets the last ten points. The flag turns red.
Twenty-five years later the effects changed. The tears didn’t. The real magic was four clumsy kids getting hurt, still looking out for each other, and learning to believe in themselves. Don’t grab easy power. Lean on your friends. Trust yourself. Stand up.

text:
Remember when astroturf required buses, matching shirts, printed signs, and enough warm bodies to fake a movement?

Now it needs a fucking ring light.

Welcome to Campaign Bus 2.0.

Some 24-year-old flips on TikTok, tilts the phone, gives you the concerned face and says, “I normally don’t talk about politics, but…”

Oh, absolutely. And McDonald’s normally doesn’t talk about hamburgers.

Then, by some miracle of civic awakening, forty other creators discover the same issue that morning. Same villain. Same emotional hook. Same suspiciously polished argument. Same sudden urgency.

What a beautiful spontaneous uprising.

Except somewhere upstream there may be a PAC, a marketing firm, an agency, three subvendors, a content brief, a payment schedule, and some asshole tracking engagement in a spreadsheet.

The campaign bus never disappeared. They shrunk it until it fit behind an iPhone.

That is what makes influencer astroturf so effective. Political advertising learned to dress like your roommate. The podium became a kitchen counter. The campaign surrogate became “just some guy online.” Talking points became “something I’ve been thinking about lately.”

And the disclosure?

Sometimes that apparently wandered off before filming.

One Michigan creator was reportedly offered money to discuss rising costs and told the paid-partnership label would not appear. She refused. Good for her. The interesting question is how many ring lights clicked on anyway.

So the next time your feed erupts with fifty deeply personal, totally independent revelations before lunch, enjoy the show.

Just remember you may be watching industrial political advertising wearing sweatpants.

The campaign bus is parked in the bedroom now.

And apparently it has excellent lighting.

Detailed:

• Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek convertible bonds and expanded their partnership so MediaTek can use NVLink Fusion to build custom XPUs that plug into Nvidia rack-scale systems. The deal also covers local AI PCs and automotive platforms and is Nvidia’s largest direct investment outside the United States. (Techmeme)

• The European Commission designated ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine and labeled Reddit and Roblox Very Large Online Platforms under the Digital Services Act after each crossed 45 million monthly EU users. The three services now face additional rules covering illegal content, minors, systemic risks and elections. (The Economic Times)

• A Chinese court froze up to $300 million of assets tied to Dutch chipmaker Nexperia after a filing by Chinese owner Wingtech. The freeze covers Nexperia stakes in four Chinese operations and runs through 2029, escalating the international fight over control of the semiconductor company. (Reuters)

• Huawei reported first-half revenue of 467.82 billion yuan, up 9.6%, while net profit fell 37% to about $3.5 billion. R&D spending jumped 25% to a record 121.38 billion yuan as Huawei continued heavy investment in chips, AI, devices and autonomous driving. (Wall Street Journal)

• OpenAI said ChatGPT Ads reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate about 200 days after launch and expanded self-serve Ads Manager access to India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. The milestone gives OpenAI a major new revenue stream beyond subscriptions and API usage.

• Tencent-backed AI chipmaker Shanghai Enflame priced its STAR Market IPO at 142.18 yuan per share and is targeting about $911 million in proceeds. The company plans to use the capital to develop next-generation AI chips as China pushes domestic alternatives to Nvidia. (Archive)

• Tim Cook completed his final day as Apple CEO, with hardware chief John Ternus taking over on September 1 while Cook becomes executive chairman. The transition puts a product-focused hardware leader in charge as Apple faces major challenges around AI, chips and its next generation of devices.

• Phil Schiller is stepping down from overseeing the App Store and Apple product events, with App Store responsibilities moving into Eddy Cue’s services organization. Carson Oliver and Ann Thai will take on operational responsibilities as John Ternus begins his first day as CEO. (The Verge)

• SLB agreed to acquire heat-management company Kelvion for about $3.4 billion in cash while assuming roughly $700 million of debt. The deal expands SLB into data-center cooling and is expected to create a combined data-center business generating more than $2 billion in 2026 revenue.

• Microsoft is investigating a widespread Exchange Online outage that caused email delivery failures, authentication errors and mailbox access problems. The incident affected multiple organizations and Microsoft has been investigating a failure pattern involving authentication and protocol connectivity.

• Instagram renamed its “AI Creator” tag to “AI-generated profile” and said unlabeled accounts featuring AI-generated people can lose recommendation reach across areas such as Reels and Explore. The policy specifically targets accounts presenting entirely AI-generated people as real profiles rather than ordinary posts created with AI tools. (9to5Google)

• SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won said SK hynix is reviewing potential locations across Japan for a possible memory-chip production facility or joint venture. No specific site, partner or investment has been finalized, but the move reflects the company’s search for additional capacity as AI demand drives demand for HBM and other memory. (The Japan Times)

• https://t.co/l3nfUDvApa reported first-half revenue of about $142 million, up roughly 400% year over year, driven by explosive growth in its cloud and API business. Its model-as-a-service ARR reached $1.6 billion by August 31 while R&D spending also climbed sharply as the Chinese lab scales its AI infrastructure. (South China Morning Post)

• Huawei opened China preorders for the Mate XT 2 tri-fold smartphone ahead of its September 7 launch. The new device uses a redesigned outward-opening “wing” folding structure and offers configurations reaching 16GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. (iTHome)

• The White House launched Project Watershed 250, a six-month Texas pilot bringing federal agencies, Texas Cyber Command and private cybersecurity companies together to protect water utilities from cyberattacks. Officials are positioning the program as a potential model for expanding critical-infrastructure protection nationwide. (Axios)

• Happiest Minds and ITC Infotech signed definitive agreements to combine their businesses into an Indian technology-services company targeting $1 billion in annual revenue by FY28. The combined organization is expected to have more than 19,000 employees, 800 customers and operations across more than 30 countries. (Happiest Minds)

• E2E Networks signed a roughly ₹1,000 crore term sheet with Sarvam AI to provide high-performance AI infrastructure and Nvidia Blackwell cloud GPUs in India through 2029. The deal highlights the rapidly expanding demand for domestic AI compute infrastructure. (The Economic Times Hindi)

• JetBrains confirmed unauthorized access to its Cadence cloud service and exposure of customer data. The company said the attacker accessed data contained in a 2024 Cadence server backup and that its investigation remains ongoing.

• Cloudflare launched Adaptive Intelligence, a bot-defense system that continuously generates short-lived detection rules from live traffic signals. The company says the system is designed to make automated attacks substantially more expensive by adapting defenses as attackers change tactics.

text:
THE OFFER I REFUSED: A LETTER FROM STOCKHOLM ON RECRUITMENT, LOYALTY AND THE MAN WHO SAID YES

By Kio Amachree

Let me tell you something my fellow Nigerians rarely hear said aloud. Many of us who were educated in the United States were approached, at one time or another, to work for American intelligence. I know, because I was one of them.

It was the 1980s. I had graduated from the University of Pennsylvania, completed my national service, and was beginning my career at Philip Morris. At the American Embassy in Lagos, a consular official — a Mr Bennett — evidently thought it would be a coup to recruit the son of Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC, Nigeria's first Solicitor-General and the first African Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations.

The offers were generous. To a less fortunate Nigerian they would have been highly attractive. I looked him in the eye and said no, thank you. He persisted. I repeated: no, thank you. I told him plainly that my father would never countenance it, that I understood exactly what such an arrangement entailed, and that I was loyal to my country. I was not some desperate man to be bought. I did not arrive at that embassy begging for anything.

Understand what they wanted. Not a spy in a trench coat — something far more valuable. An Ivy League-trained son of a Nigerian trailblazer, with an American stepmother, with access to the very top of both Nigerian and American society. Eyes, ears, and influence. Several of my friends from similar backgrounds were approached in exactly the same way. And nearly all of us said no.

Why? Because in those years the oil boom was at full blast. Nigeria was no pariah state. We begged no one for visas. The naira traded near parity with the dollar. We were a rising power — black and proud. Who in his right mind would sell out such a country for Yankee Doodle's shilling? Loyalty was not even difficult. It was the natural condition of a Nigerian who knew his worth.

Now consider a different case. It is documented public record that in 1993, a United States federal court in Chicago ordered the forfeiture of 460,000 dollars linked to accounts associated with Bola Ahmed Tinubu, in proceedings connected to a heroin trafficking investigation. That was a civil forfeiture, not a criminal conviction — I state that plainly. But ask yourself the question I have asked myself. When a man is caught with his hand in the cookie jar, facing the machinery of American narcotics enforcement, what options are placed before him? I refused my offer from a position of strength, privilege, and pride. What does a man do when the offer comes not as an invitation but as a lifeline?

I do not need a brain surgeon to work out the inference I draw, and I state it clearly as my opinion, formed as a citizen and commentator: the pattern fits a man who took the insider's deal. And observe what has happened since. In the FOIA litigation before Judge Beryl Howell in Washington — Greenspan versus the FBI and DEA — American agencies have fought with remarkable determination to keep records concerning this man sealed, more than thirty years after the fact, while the CIA declines even to confirm or deny that records exist. In my experience, that is not how bureaucracies treat matters of no consequence. That is how they treat assets.

Today the tables have turned. The economy is in free fall. Nigeria is no longer the belle of the ball. I do not doubt that there are Nigerians now who would line up to serve foreign intelligence services for far less than what Mr Bennett once laid on the table before me. That is what forty years of looted governance does to a proud people — it converts patriotism into a luxury good.

But I was raised differently. I was raised to love Nigeria, not to sell it to the highest bidder. Treason does not run in my family.

Release the files. Let Nigerians read the record and judge for themselves.

Disclaimer: This article is an opinion piece and personal testimony published under the press freedom protections of the Kingdom of Sweden. References to the 1993 Chicago proceedings concern a civil forfeiture in which no criminal charges were brought against Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Statements regarding any informant relationship are the author's personal opinion and inference drawn from publicly available records and ongoing litigation, not assertions of established fact.

text:
I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.

The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.

Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.

Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.

The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.

Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.

The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.

Lady Antebellum became Lady A.

Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”

Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.

Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.

Then there were the military bases.

Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.

Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.

Fort Benning became Fort Moore.

Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.

Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.

Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.

Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.

Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.

Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.

We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.

Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. 😎

text:
There is an uncomfortable sense that we have seen this movie before.

What is being presented as a strategy is, in reality, an operational plan, one that has been tried before. It produced some tactical gains, but it did not create the conditions for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. 

The fundamental problem is geography. Iran does not need a large naval force to keep disrupting maritime traffic. Small boats, drones, mines, and repeated harassment can impose risk faster than outside forces can eliminate it.

That leads to the much bigger question: What is the administration’s exit strategy for Iran?

The current limbo is not an exit strategy. Nor is a return to a limited military campaign. Another round of strikes is unlikely to compel Iran to abandon its nuclear program, relinquish its ability to threaten the Strait, or accept Washington’s broader strategic demands. Economic pressure will not accomplish that. Limited military pressure will not accomplish it either.

The administration clearly wants to avoid a wider war. The problem is that escalation is not controlled by Washington alone. Iran hs a word, too. Tehran has demonstrated a willingness to confront U.S. forces, and a limited exchange can quickly develop its own logic of escalation. Once American and Iranian forces begin trading strikes, the distinction between a carefully calibrated campaign and a broader conflict becomes increasingly difficult to preserve.

The status quo, meanwhile, is inherently unstable. A limited campaign is unlikely to change that underlying reality. But the broader the campaign becomes, the more substantial the Iranian response is likely to be. Washington therefore risks finding itself trapped between military action too limited to achieve its strategic objectives and military action extensive enough to trigger precisely the war the administration is trying to avoid.

That is why postponing the strategic decision is itself a decision. Avoiding a choice today may simply allow events, and Iran, to impose a less favorable set of choices on Washington tomorrow.

There is also a striking inconsistency in the administration’s recent behavior. Only days ago, it appeared determined to avoid being drawn back into direct confrontation, even showing restraint in response to Iranian attacks. Now it appears prepared to return to the same cycle of strikes. That reversal raises legitimate questions about the decision-making process in Washington and, more importantly, about whether there is a coherent political objective guiding the use of force.

The bottom line is straightforward: a limited military campaign is not an exit strategy. But a larger war offers no guarantee of solving the fundamental problem either. Even a substantially broader conflict would not necessarily eliminate Iran’s ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait.

Military operations can degrade capabilities and buy time. They cannot defeat geography, and they cannot substitute for a political end state.

Until the administration can explain what that end state is, and how the use of force actually gets the United States closer to it, the central problem with its Iran policy will remain unanswered.

text:
what Jesus Christ did for the sinner. Discipleship concerns what the saved man now does with the life Christ purchased. Reward concerns what survives the examination at the Judgment Seat. First Corinthians 3 does not say the believer’s Sabbath observance becomes the foundation. “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). The fire will try “every man’s work of what sort it is” (1 Corinthians 3:13). Doctrine, motives, faithfulness, sacrifice, stewardship, and service will meet the eyes of Jesus Christ. A man may build a massive religious haystack out of shadows, calendars, dietary pride, and arguments over pronunciations, but fire has never been impressed by acreage. Gold does not need to be large to endure, and hay does not need to be small to burn.

The law is holy. The law is just. The law is good. It is also unable to justify, unable to impart life, unable to perfect the flesh, and no longer the governing covenant of the Body of Christ. A Bible believer can say every one of those things without blinking. He honors the law’s origin without misusing its jurisdiction. He believes its accusations without seeking righteousness from its deeds. He studies its types without crawling back into its shadows. He receives its moral testimony without pretending that Israel’s national covenant has been transferred to Gentile believers. The fellow who cannot distinguish honor from submission will accuse you of hating the courthouse because you do not sleep in the jail.

Colossians 2 addresses the badges directly: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Paul does not say, “Let no unqualified man judge you, but find a Hebrew Roots teacher who will do it correctly.” He says, “Let no man.” Meat, drink, holy days, new moons, and sabbaths formed an identifiable covenantal calendar. They were shadows pointing toward Christ. The shadow is not evil; it is simply not the body. If the Man Himself has entered the room, only a confused guest continues holding a conversation with His outline on the wall.

A Christian may study the feasts and see Christ pictured in them. He may learn from Israel’s Sabbaths, sacrifices, priesthood, tabernacle, dietary distinctions, and national history. “For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Romans 15:4). Learning is not the same thing as covenantal subjection. Noah’s ark teaches us without obligating us to purchase gopher wood. The tabernacle teaches us without ordering a Gentile church to sew badgers’ skins. The Passover teaches us because “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7), but the lesson ends at the Lamb rather than at a religious identity built around the menu. We do not honor a signpost by camping beneath it after reaching the destination.

The Hebrew Roots movement often begins with something attractive: a desire to understand the Jewish background of Scripture, a rejection of genuine paganism, an interest in biblical feasts, or a wish to take obedience seriously. But error rarely knocks wearing horns and carrying a pitchfork. It brings a Hebrew dictionary, speaks solemnly about forgotten truths, and offers the believer an opportunity to become more authentic than the church down the road. Before long, Christ’s finished work is still verbally confessed while Christian assurance, fellowship, holiness, and spiritual maturity are measured by Sinai’s badges. The gospel remains printed on the brochure, but Moses is running the inspection department. A yoke does not become liberty because somebody carves a Hebrew letter into the wood.

• 2025–2026 — Grocery bills, energy costs, health costs, rent, insurance, and basic survival all crushing average Americans.

• 2025–2026 — Family business conflicts, crypto wealth, foreign ties, watchdog attacks, prosecutor pressure, retaliation allegations and court defeats — MORE presidential power with LESS oversight.

• September 2025 — A federal court found Trump unlawfully fired inspectors general without complying with the Inspector General Act.

• June 2025 — Trump deployed the National Guard to Los Angeles over California’s objections during immigration-raid protests, escalating disputes over military power, federalism and domestic enforcement.

• May 2025 — The administration accepted a Qatar-provided Boeing 747-8 for possible Air Force One use, raising ethics, security and foreign-influence concerns. Qatar denied seeking influence.

• April 2025 — Trump imposed sweeping tariffs through emergency powers, bypassing ordinary congressional processes and creating uncertainty for prices, businesses and trade.

• April 2025 — The administration terminated about $2.2 billion in Harvard research funding; a federal judge later ruled the cuts unlawful.

• March 2025 — Senior national-security officials discussed an imminent Yemen strike on Signal and accidentally included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg, exposing operational timing and strike details.

• March 2025 — Trump issued orders targeting law firms tied to critics, opponents and disfavored clients; judges blocked multiple orders as retaliatory or unconstitutional threats to legal independence.

• March 2025 — Other major firms negotiated with the White House, pledging hundreds of millions in pro bono work on administration-approved causes rather than risk similar retaliation.

• March 2025 — The government wrongfully deported Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador despite legal protection, then was ordered to facilitate his return.

• March 2025 — Trump used the Alien Enemies Act against alleged gang members, triggering litigation over removals without a meaningful chance to contest government accusations.

• February 2025 — DOJ ordered prosecutors to drop Mayor Eric Adams’ corruption case while citing his help with immigration enforcement. Senior prosecutors resigned; Trump denied directing the dismissal.

• January 24, 2025 — Trump abruptly fired inspectors general across major agencies. A judge later found eight removals violated federal notice and justification requirements.

• January 20, 2025 — Trump tried to end birthright citizenship by executive order, triggering repeated court blocks over whether a president can rewrite the 14th Amendment without Congress or an amendment.

He is accused of Raping White GB children but has not been convicted. Say that first, because the system hides behind it.
On 18 July 2024 Greater Manchester Police arrested Rukhsar Ahmed at Manchester airport. The suspicion: rape and trafficking of girls from Rusholme care homes in the early 1990s. Several women. He owned the Gujjar Palace on the curry mile. Detectives knew, while he was in the cells, that he was a Pakistani politician. They asked a judge for a travel ban. The judge said no.
That is the indictment. Not the allegation. The refusal.
Two years later he is an MP again for Shehbaz Sharif’s PML-N in the Azad Kashmir assembly. He missed a Manchester bail date. Too ill to fly, he told the police. The pictures showed rallies in Mirpur. The Mail found him at his desk in Khari Sharif. Would he return? In principle. A date? No. Legal team in London. Media out of order. Asked about the girls, he told the reporter to stop talking like that.
India, Pakistan and the Gulf reprinted the same sequence. Geo TV carried the denial. The Friday Times in Lahore noted the silence of his party. Nobody in Islamabad has offered him up. Why would they? Britain has just spent the summer begging Pakistan to take Shabir Ahmed, the convicted Rochdale ringleader, and being told the man was “spoiled” in Britain, not theirs.
What the law actually does
The Bail Act 1976 starts with a right to bail. A court may refuse it if there are substantial grounds to believe the defendant will abscond, offend, or interfere. Flight risk is written in. It is not a surprise. It is the first test.
For rape, automatic custody only kicks in under section 25 of the 1994 Act if the accused already has a listed homicide or serious-sex conviction. No such record was published here. So the judge had discretion. Discretion went to the passport.
Defence solicitors will tell you passport surrender is routine in child-sex investigations. This judge did not impose it. GMP wanted it. The bench did not. After that, “too unwell to fly” is not a medical miracle. It is what you say when the plane has already left.
The same architecture let two men accused of raping a woman in a Liverpool flat walk out with their phones still in their pockets. The same architecture has, in other weeks, put teenage rape defendants on the street until sentence, and let a remand rape suspect walk out of Wormwood Scrubs by clerical error and onto a second passport. These are not one rogue. They are the default when seriousness is treated as a factor among others, and foreign ties as a community connection rather than an exit.
The second failure is the destination
Even if a warrant comes, extradition is a negotiation with a state that will not take the convicted man. A suspect with a seat in Mirpur is a worse bargain. The girls, if the file is true, have waited thirty years. The system offered the suspect two more, a campaign and a legislature.
Singapore, using the old British toolkit this country discarded, would have kept the stamp at the desk. Britain kept the hearing, the conditions that were not imposed, and the press release that arrives after the man is already home.
He is still only accused. A jury has not spoken. That is not a defence of the bail decision. It is the reason the decision mattered. If the evidence is weak, he should not have been arrested at an airport and then waved toward another country. If the evidence is strong, the court had one job: keep him where a trial can find him. It did neither thing well. It left a date field blank, and called that justice.
