THE TRUMP RECEIPTS (updated daily)
The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

• August 31, 2026 — Treasury blocks major news organizations from G20 coverage: Treasury denied reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg credentials without publicly explaining why. The denials are established; viewpoint retaliation is not.

• August 30–31, 2026 — Iran fighting resumed as Trump posted an unsupported AI-generated attack video: U.S. forces struck Iranian launchers, Iran retaliated toward U.S. bases, and Trump posted a synthetic video claiming Kharg Island was being destroyed without corroborating evidence.

• August 30, 2026 — The administration deported dozens to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan man protected from removal to Afghanistan over Taliban threats. The removal is established; whether using a third country violated his rights remains unresolved.

• August 30, 2026 — Venezuela announced a 25-year U.S. oil deal covering 17 fields and targeting 1.5 million barrels daily. Trump claims U.S. partnerships gained majority control; Venezuela says it retains ownership. Corruption is not established.

• August 30, 2026 — Trump demanded FCC “punishment” of NBC’s Kristen Welker after she called his endorsement results mixed. The demand is documented; no FCC penalty or legal finding followed.

• August 29, 2026 — Administration escalates unsupported noncitizen-voting claims ahead of the midterms: DHS asserted without public evidence that up to 250,000 noncitizens may be on four states’ rolls. Experts say such voting is extremely rare and warn the method may produce false positives.

• August 29, 2026 — Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian imports under an untested Depression-era law after losing on his earlier tariff authority. Canada retaliated; the new legal theory remains unadjudicated.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS used a customs statute to obtain six months of journalist Georgia Fort’s phone records and seek data involving journalists, nonprofits and unions without prior judicial approval. The demands are documented; legality is unresolved.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge ruled that using immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation over pro-Palestinian advocacy or criticism of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

• August 28, 2026 — Regulators found White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez used advance access to Trump speeches for prediction-market trades; he must forfeit over $107,000, pay $65,000 and accept a three-year ban.

• August 28, 2026 — A judge rejected Trump’s effort to move his New York hush-money case to federal court, ruling the Stormy Daniels concealment was private conduct, not a presidential duty; his 34 felony convictions remain on appeal.

• August 28, 2026 — Trump renewed efforts to restrict birthright citizenship after his earlier approach was blocked. A judge denied an immediate block on procedural grounds; litigation continues.

• August 28, 2026 — The administration appealed continued Hudson Tunnel funding after Trump offered to release money if Democrats backed naming Dulles Airport and New York Penn Station after him. The proposal is documented; no criminal finding exists.

• August 28, 2026 — Border-wall work proceeded over Tohono O’odham Nation objections. A judge allowed work on the federal Roosevelt Reservation; the tribe alleges agents and contractors entered tribal land without permission, blocked tribal police and threatened sacred sites. Construction is established; alleged trespass remains unresolved.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge ruled the administration unlawfully rewrote farmworker wage rules, potentially cutting affected wages by up to $7 an hour and illegally deducting housing costs.

• August 27, 2026 — After a court blocked effectively renaming the Kennedy Center for Trump, allies pursued Trump branding and DOJ raised possible demolition or replacement if renovation plans were blocked. Trump said he was “not ripping it down.”

• August 27, 2026 — A judge barred the Pentagon from punishing Anthropic over its AI-use limits, finding unconstitutional retaliation, First Amendment and due-process violations, and an arbitrary “supply chain risk” designation.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge temporarily blocked core Trump mail-ballot rules as likely unconstitutional, citing no fraud evidence and an overwhelming disenfranchisement risk. The case continues.

• August 27, 2026 — ICE awarded a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 electric-shock gloves for arrests, transport and civil disturbances. ICE cites reduced force; critics warn of abuse and weak oversight.

• August 26, 2026 — A judge rejected DOJ’s request to erase Steve Bannon’s contempt conviction for defying the Jan. 6 committee, finding dismissal was not shown to serve justice. Bannon served four months; DOJ may try again.

• August 24, 2026 — ICE tightened international-student internship rules and warned noncompliant universities they could lose authorization to enroll foreign students. DHS calls it enforcement; universities call it a major restriction.

• August 2026 — A federal judge rebuked USPS for advancing a Trump-directed mail-voting rule despite an injunction, saying the agency failed to comply with the order.

• August 2026 — Six months into the Iran conflict, Iran had not capitulated, Hormuz traffic remained badly disrupted, U.S. munitions were strained, regional instability had grown and oil prices were sharply higher.

• August 2026 — DOJ turned investigations toward officials involved in earlier Trump cases, including FBI personnel connected to the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search.

• August 2026 — DOJ subpoenaed Letitia James’ office over earlier Trump cases; an appeals court upheld blocking them because the acting U.S. attorney was unlawfully appointed.

• August 2026 — The Pentagon dismissed the Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief, raising concern about political control of independent military journalism.

• August 2026 — The administration moved to ease firing career workers through new “suitability” and forced-ranking rules; unions sued, alleging a shift from merit service to political patronage.

• July 2026 — The administration increased wild-horse removals and sales; reporting indicates some protected horses may have entered the slaughter pipeline. BLM says it does not knowingly sell horses for slaughter.

• February 20, 2026 — The Supreme Court ruled Trump’s emergency statute did not authorize his sweeping tariffs. At least $133 billion had been collected, leaving businesses seeking refunds.

• February 2026 — Trump expanded lower-tariff Argentine beef imports to fight record prices, angering U.S. ranchers and Republican lawmakers who say the policy favors foreign beef over American producers.

• 2025–2026 — A federal judge found the administration unlawfully directed agencies to fire roughly 25,000 probationary workers en masse.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ fired or pushed out prosecutors and FBI personnel tied to Trump and Jan. 6 investigations, fueling concerns that law enforcement was being reorganized around political loyalty.

• 2025–2026 — ICE raids, violent enforcement operations, and families being terrorized in their own communities.

• 2025–2026 — Americans shot and killed during immigration enforcement while the government demands more power and less accountability.

• 2025–2026 — Expanded deportation operations repeatedly faced challenges over due process, detention, removals and extraordinary executive power.

• 2025–2026 — The administration sharply reduced the federal workforce, with about 317,000 employees expected to leave in 2025, raising concerns about lost expertise, weaker services and political control.

• 2025–2026 — Trump used federal funding as leverage against universities over leadership, DEI, campus protests and political culture.

• 2025–2026 — Cuts and freezes disrupted NIH grants, laboratories, medical research, staffing and graduate programs; courts repeatedly found parts of the funding actions unlawful.

• 2025–2026 — Vaccine chaos and public health policy being dragged into political extremism instead of science, safety, and trust.

• 2025–2026 — The administration rolled back climate, pollution, vehicle-emissions, wetlands and public-land protections while expanding drilling and fossil-fuel development.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s administration pursued investigations of people who investigated, prosecuted, sued, criticized or defeated him.

• 2025–2026 — The administration installed favored prosecutors without Senate confirmation; courts rejected several appointments, raising concerns about loyalists investigating Trump’s opponents.

• 2025–2026 — Millions of Epstein-related pages were released and Trump is referenced in the public record. Being named does not establish participation in Epstein’s crimes.

• 2025–2026 — A civil jury finding Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation while his movement still pretends morality matters.

• 2025–2026 — A desperate push to reshape voting rules, restrict access, and tilt the midterms before the people can respond.

• 2025–2026 — Rigging maps, erasing districts, and rewriting the rules to silence Black voters and diverse communities.

• 2025–2026 — Trump directed agencies toward new citizenship, mail-ballot, voter-data and election-administration restrictions, prompting litigation over intrusion into congressional and state powers.

• 2025–2026 — An unpopular war in Iran driving fear, instability, and higher gas prices while working families already struggle to survive.

• 2025–2026 — Congress abdicated core powers over war, spending, oversight, impeachment and executive abuse while the House waits for Trump’s approval and the Senate barely pushes back.

• 2025–2026 — Trump repeatedly froze, canceled or redirected congressionally appropriated money, reviving the constitutional fight over presidential control of Congress’ power of the purse.

• 2025–2026 — Capital One closed more than 300 Trump Organization-linked accounts after an anti-money-laundering review. The Trumps alleged persecution; the bank says it did not accuse the organization of money laundering.

• 2025–2026 — A nearly $1.8 billion taxpayer-funded “Anti-Weaponization Fund” for Trump allies drew warnings it could pay Jan. 6 defendants, including violent rioters, before Republican senators forced its rescission.

• 2025–2026 — Trump Media reportedly pitched Wall Street firms up to $100,000 monthly for faster access to Trump’s potentially market-moving Truth Social posts, monetizing presidential information for elite clients.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s family expanded World Liberty Financial and other crypto ventures while Trump controlled federal crypto policy, creating major presidential-family financial conflicts.

• 2025–2026 — A UAE-linked company reportedly bought a $500 million stake in Trump-family World Liberty Financial; months later the administration approved advanced AI-chip sales to the UAE. Senators sought review; no quid pro quo is established.

• 2025–2026 — Trump pressured the Federal Reserve for lower rates and tried to remove Governor Lisa Cook after disputed mortgage allegations.

• 2025–2026 — The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to remove Cook, protecting central-bank independence. Cook denies intentional wrongdoing; the allegations remain disputed.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ pursued former Olympic canoeist Davey Hearn on a felony charge carrying up to 10 years over alleged Reflecting Pool vandalism, then dropped it after evidence pointed to flawed contractor work.

• 2025–2026 — Attacks on the free press, subpoenas against journalists, and constant attempts to punish anyone who exposes the truth.

• 2025–2026 — The administration restricted Associated Press access over terminology while escalating lawsuits, license threats, regulatory pressure and investigations against news organizations.

• 2025–2026 — Twenty-three states sued over ideological conditions attached to Title X family-planning funds involving contraception, gender, DEI and abstinence. The claims remain unadjudicated.

• 2025–2026 — Grocery bills, energy costs, health costs, rent, insurance, and basic survival all crushing average Americans.

• 2025–2026 — Family business conflicts, crypto wealth, foreign ties, watchdog attacks, prosecutor pressure, retaliation allegations and court defeats — MORE presidential power with LESS oversight.

• November 2025 — After Trump pressured authorities against James Comey and Letitia James, a judge dismissed their prosecutions because the Trump-backed prosecutor was unlawfully appointed. Dismissals were without prejudice.

• September 2025 — A federal court found Trump unlawfully fired inspectors general without complying with the Inspector General Act.

• June 2025 — Trump deployed the National Guard to Los Angeles over California’s objections during immigration-raid protests, escalating disputes over military power, federalism and domestic enforcement.

• May 2025 — The administration accepted a Qatar-provided Boeing 747-8 for possible Air Force One use, raising ethics, security and foreign-influence concerns. Qatar denied seeking influence.

• April 2025 — Trump imposed sweeping tariffs through emergency powers, bypassing ordinary congressional processes and creating uncertainty for prices, businesses and trade.

• April 2025 — The administration terminated about $2.2 billion in Harvard research funding; a federal judge later ruled the cuts unlawful.

• March 2025 — Senior national-security officials discussed an imminent Yemen strike on Signal and accidentally included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg, exposing operational timing and strike details.

• March 2025 — Trump issued orders targeting law firms tied to critics, opponents and disfavored clients; judges blocked multiple orders as retaliatory or unconstitutional threats to legal independence.

• March 2025 — Other major firms negotiated with the White House, pledging hundreds of millions in pro bono work on administration-approved causes rather than risk similar retaliation.

• March 2025 — The government wrongfully deported Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador despite legal protection, then was ordered to facilitate his return.

• March 2025 — Trump used the Alien Enemies Act against alleged gang members, triggering litigation over removals without a meaningful chance to contest government accusations.

• February 2025 — DOJ ordered prosecutors to drop Mayor Eric Adams’ corruption case while citing his help with immigration enforcement. Senior prosecutors resigned; Trump denied directing the dismissal.

• January 24, 2025 — Trump abruptly fired inspectors general across major agencies. A judge later found eight removals violated federal notice and justification requirements.

• January 20, 2025 — Trump tried to end birthright citizenship by executive order, triggering repeated court blocks over whether a president can rewrite the 14th Amendment without Congress or an amendment.

• The government is not functioning for the people. It is functioning for one man, one movement, and one corrupt machine determined to keep power at any cost.

• Corruption, cruelty, arrogance, and authoritarian overreach becoming the daily operating system of this administration.

• People are angry. People are exhausted. People are awake. And people have had enough.

This song is a result of MAGA Trump supporters and the Trump administration pushing the average American beyond their personal limits.

You are in the FA stage and the FO stage at the ballot box is coming.

🚨TRUE PATRIOT: Most people know him as Indiana Jones and Han Solo—but few know Harrison Ford volunteered his personal helicopter to rescue a lost Boy Scout stranded in the freezing wilderness.

In July 2001, 13-year-old Boy Scout Cody Clawson became separated from his troop in the dense, freezing wilderness of Yellowstone National Park. As night fell and temperatures plummeted, local search and rescue teams scrambled to organize a massive aerial search mission.

Harrison Ford, an experienced pilot who lived nearby in Jackson, Wyoming, immediately offered his personal Bell 407 helicopter and volunteered his time to lead search flights at no cost to local authorities.

After hours of sweeping over rugged terrain, Ford spotted the missing boy sheltering under a rock ledge. Ford piloted the helicopter down into a tight clear landing spot, hopped out, and safely brought the cold, exhausted teenager aboard.

When Cody looked up and realized the Hollywood superstar himself had come to save him, he asked: "Are you who I think you are?" Ford simply smiled, handed him a bottle of water, and flew him straight to safety.

text:
One thing worth remembering with practice squads now that they’re being filled out (my understanding of the rules):

Teams can’t simply claim a player off another team’s practice squad. They have to offer/sign him to their 53-man roster, and the player has a choice in whether to leave.

That also gives the player/agent an opportunity to go back to his current team, which can try to retain him either by offering a 53-man spot, increased PS compensation, etc. There’s not an official “right to match” but there can certainly be a conversation.

PS players can get poached, especially as injuries pile up, but once you get a developmental player through waivers and back in your building, there’s more stability than any team just taking them away at any moment logic might imply.

text:
AUGUST IS BITCOIN'S WORST MONTH ON AVERAGE. ISHARES BITCOIN TRUST $IBIT JUST GAINED 25% IN IT:

iShares Bitcoin Trust IBIT at $44.64 (after hours), +$0.74 / +1.69% today. It is the largest US fund with one job: buy actual bitcoin, store it, and cut the pile into shares that trade in an ordinary brokerage account like a stock. That is what a spot fund is. "Spot" means it holds the real coin rather than a contract about it.

The bottom line: bitcoin just finished its best August since 2017, in the month that has historically been its worst. And three trading days did most of the work.

From the July 31 close of $35.64 to today's regular close of $44.675, this fund gained $9.035 / +25.4%. Now take only August 19, 20 and 21: $36.60 to $43.68, +$7.08 / +19.3%. Three sessions out of twenty-one carried roughly three-quarters of the month.

WHERE THE TWO BIGGEST COINS ARE RIGHT NOW

Bitcoin, ticker BTC, is at $78,784, +0.02% over the last 24 hours. Flat to the decimal. Ethereum, ticker ETH, the second-largest digital asset, is at $2,471, -1.17% across the same stretch.

WHY THE FUND IS UP 1.7% ON A COIN THAT DID NOTHING

Two numbers, two different clocks, and this catches out almost everybody who owns one of these funds.

Bitcoin trades every hour of every day. Nobody rings a bell and there is no closing price, so its "24 hours" runs from about this time yesterday to right now.

The fund trades on a US stock exchange, 9:30am to 4:00pm Eastern, Monday to Friday. Its day is measured against Friday's 4:00pm close. So everything the coin did across the entire weekend, a stretch the fund could not trade at all, lands inside one Monday number.

Both figures are correct. They are measuring different windows. Worth remembering every Monday, and every time a coin moves hard while the stock market is shut.

WHAT MAKES A 24% AUGUST STRANGE

August is normally when this market goes quiet and drifts lower. Since 2013 the typical August for bitcoin has been about -7%. This one gained roughly 24%, its strongest August since 2017, after early-month lows near $62,000 to $64,000 and a brief trip above $81,000.

That earns a caution rather than a cheer. A month behaving nothing like its own history is a reminder that seasonal patterns are descriptions of the past, not rules the future has agreed to follow. They break constantly. This one just did, in the pleasant direction.

The three routes an ordinary brokerage account offers into it, over the same month:

- iShares Bitcoin Trust: +$9.035 / +25.4%.
- Coinbase Global at $188.00 (after hours), +$9.36 / +5.24% today. The New York company runs a crypto exchange and is paid when somebody trades. Across August: +$41.81 / +28.6%.
- Strategy, the company formerly called MicroStrategy, at $133.05 (after hours), +$5.74 / +4.51% today. The Tysons Corner, Virginia company holds bitcoin and raises money to hold more of it. Across August: +$39.67 / +42.5%.

One coin, four different answers. And a fifth number that belongs beside them: even after all that, the fund sits $27.18 / 37.8% below the $71.82 it reached on October 6 last year.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED ON AUGUST 19

Not new buyers. Forced ones.

Some traders bet against a price by borrowing something and selling it, planning to buy it back cheaper. That is a short. It works until the price rises, and if it rises far enough the exchange closes the position for them and buys it back at whatever the market is asking. That forced buying is called a liquidation. It pushes the price up, which forces more of them, which pushes it up again.

On August 19 the crypto market saw about $2.99B of positions closed out that way, the eighth largest single day on record, and $2.74B of it, 91.6%, was shorts. Bitcoin rose 8.48% that day to about $69,686. Ether went considerably further, +18.16% to about $2,257. More than $1B of bitcoin shorts were closed inside roughly an hour.

The three stock-market routes show the same days from the outside, and the trading volume is the tell:

- iShares Bitcoin Trust: +5.96%, +6.24%, +6.02%. On the 19th it traded 140.8M shares against roughly 25M on the quiet days just before.
- Coinbase: +9.55%, +7.58%, +8.20%, on 17.0M shares that Wednesday against a usual 6M to 7M.
- Strategy: +12.68%, +7.81%, +6.10%, on 49.2M shares against 17M to 20M.

This matters for reading the month honestly. A price that rose because the people betting against it ran out of room is a different event from a price that rose because new money arrived. The first kind stops when the sellers are gone.

MONEY DID ARRIVE, AND MOSTLY AT ONE ADDRESS

US spot bitcoin funds took in more than $3B of net new money across August, their strongest month of 2026. Inside one eight-session run of inflows totalling about $2.8B, this single fund took $2.02B. Roughly 72 cents of every dollar.

Its size explains that. It holds about 782,000 bitcoin and is worth about $61.3B at today's price. The next-largest US spot bitcoin fund holds about $11.2B, so this one is more than five times anything else in the category.

The cost is a 0.25% annual fee, and it never sends a bill. The fee is paid by selling coin out of the fund, so each share stands on very slightly less bitcoin every year, by design.

THE PART OF TODAY THAT IS NOT ABOUT THE COIN AT ALL

Coinbase's move today has its own dated reason. This morning its derivatives exchange, Deribit, began listing perpetual contracts on ordinary US stocks and on funds tracking the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. A perpetual contract is a bet on a price that never expires: you hold it for as long as you keep paying to, rather than until a set date. They are quoted and settled in a dollar-linked digital token, run around the clock, and carry up to 10 times leverage on single stocks and 20 times on the funds. One of the contracts listed is on Strategy itself. Coinbase expects to finish moving its derivatives business onto that system by September 9.

Ten times leverage deserves the plain version: a 10% move against a position of that size wipes it out.

The business underneath is having a much harder year than the share price suggests. Its June quarter, reported July 30: revenue, the money coming in the door, was $1.22B against $1.5B a year earlier, and it lost $359.5M, or $1.36 a share, against the $0.17 loss analysts had modelled. Coinbase gets paid when people trade, not on where the coin finishes, so a quiet market is a bad quarter no matter what bitcoin does. These shares set the lowest price of their past year, $139.11, on July 31. One month ago.

Strategy is the third route and the strangest one. It holds 845,050 bitcoin, worth about $66.6B at today's price. The whole company is worth $51.1B, which is share price times share count and is what market value means. So the stock market prices the shares roughly $15B BELOW the coin sitting inside the company. That gap is not an oversight. Bonds and preferred stock rank ahead of ordinary shareholders, and the pile is not shareholder property until those are paid.

WHY A RATE DECISION LANDS ON A COIN PRICE

Bitcoin pays nothing for holding it. No interest, no dividend, no rent. Its real competition is whatever a savings account or a short-term government bond pays for taking no risk at all, and when that number goes up, holding something that pays zero costs more.

Which is why Friday mattered. At the Kansas City Fed's annual conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said he is committed to bringing inflation down. The Fed is the US central bank and its inflation target is 2% a year. Before that speech, futures traders put the odds of NO change at the September 15-16 meeting near 70%. After it, they put the odds of a quarter-point RISE at nearly 56%, per CME Group's FedWatch tool. In one afternoon the argument went from when rates get cut to whether they go up.

WHERE THESE THREE SIT

None of the three is on any of the six Len5 watchlists, and they miss for three different reasons.

The fund cannot be on one, and that is structural rather than a judgment call. All six weigh a business: what it earns, how fast it grows, what it hands back to owners. A vault with a fee attached has no earnings, no growth rate and nobody to pay. There is no development that would change that, which is worth saying out loud rather than leaving as a gap.

Coinbase misses both value styles on one shared fact. Quality-Value hunts a durable business at a fair price and Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a business priced under what it appears to be worth. Both need earnings to set a price against, and a company losing $359.5M in three months supplies none. Momentum is the closer miss, because that style watches a company climbing on news of its own and this one has certainly climbed: +28.6% in a month, +35% off a low set four and a half weeks ago. The climb is the coin price rather than the company's own results. What would change either read is trading volumes recovering far enough to reach profit, so the shares and the business finally move for the same reason.

Strategy settles fastest. Income watches cash genuinely reaching owners and genuinely funded by the business, and here the preferred holders receive cash while ordinary shareholders receive none. Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a discount, and the $15B gap between the coin pile and the market value is exactly the size of the claims standing in front of common shareholders, not a bargain hiding behind them. Those senior claims shrinking rather than growing, while the coin holds its ground, is the specific thing that would open it.

WHAT TO WATCH, AND NEITHER IS THE BITCOIN PRICE

First, the daily figure for money moving into and out of the spot funds, published every trading day. August's $3B-plus was real new money rather than forced buying, and it is the closest thing to a running count of whether American investors keep stepping in at these levels after a month like this one.

Second, Friday September 4 at 8:30am ET, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the August employment report, the government's count of jobs added or lost across the country. July lost 23,000 jobs, with unemployment at 4.1%. A weak August pulls the rate-rise case apart. A strong one props it up, and that lands on everything that pays its owner nothing.

THE RISK, AND IT IS NOT SMALL

Crypto is volatile and speculative, and nothing above forecasts where any of it goes. A market whose best month in nine years was largely three days of forced buying can hand it back in three days of the same machinery running the other way. All three of these shares moved further than the coin did in August, and that arithmetic does not politely reverse itself on the way down: a wrapper that turns a 24% month into 42% turns a 24% fall into something similar. Today's gains also came on lighter trading than usual, the fund 42.2M shares against a 78.0M two-week average, Coinbase 10.5M against 11.9M, Strategy 23.3M against 34.6M, on the last day of a month. That is a weak witness for anything.

Something crossed over today and it is worth sitting with. Stock investors have spent two years reaching into crypto through funds and shares that live in an ordinary brokerage account. This morning a crypto exchange started selling round-the-clock leveraged contracts on the biggest US stocks, settled in a digital token. The traffic runs both ways now, and one of the contracts it listed is on a company whose only business is owning bitcoin.

Not investment advice.

text:
PART 4 – ADOLF HITLER’S ALLEGED ESCAPE TO ARGENTINA The FBI would later use Eddie Senz’s portraits as supposed evidence of Adolf Hitler’s escape to Argentina (READ UNTIL THE END)

For years, the FBI was inundated with reports of Hitler sightings, some of which were actually investigated. He was spotted in a café in Los Angeles. He was living in Wisconsin, behaving erratically and playing the violin. He was a communist in Philadelphia; he lived in Miami and had undergone plastic surgery. He was in the Soviet Union, Argentina, and Denmark.

Even today, many people refuse to believe that Hitler died by his own hand in a bunker in April 1945; entire websites and books are dedicated to promoting the “truth” about his supposed escape to Argentina and other places. On some of these sites, one can find the images created with Senz’s assistance, offered as proof that the U.S. government knew Hitler was on the run and in disguise.

So let us examine the documentation produced by the FBI that is often cited as evidence of Hitler’s escape. We begin with an article from the Express, dated April 15, 2014, titled: “Are these classified FBI files proof Adolf Hitler escaped by submarine to Argentina?”

The article reproduces an FBI file dated September 21, 1945, marked “Hitler Hideout,” and quotes directly from it: “The astonishing documents describe how an Argentine fugitive claimed to have helped Hitler, two women, and other Germans disembark from a submarine in the South American country about two and a half weeks after the fall of Berlin in April 1945. Hitler and his companions then traveled by horseback to pack supplies at the foot of the southern Andes, and the plan was for the group of 50 people to relocate with German families to villages in the area.”

The unnamed Argentine informant, who provided the information to U.S. authorities in hopes of obtaining asylum, is not identified in the papers. He also gave directions to Hitler’s alleged location, stating: “If you go to a hotel in San Antonio, Argentina, I will arrange for a man to meet you there and locate the ranch where Hitler is staying. Naturally, it is heavily guarded, and you will risk your life by going there.”   
The information reached legendary FBI director J. Edgar Hoover, who forwarded it to the War Department.

Summarizing: Hoover’s FBI gave credence to an unnamed Argentine informant who was trying to secure entry into the United States. And if he was seeking asylum, it likely means he was a Marxist wanted by Argentina’s anti‑communist military government. Many high‑ranking “Nazis” did indeed flee to Argentina. But how would an unnamed informant know that the ranch belonged to Hitler? 
Either he was attempting immigration fraud, or he had simply repeated local gossip that “the German down at that ranch is Hitler.”
Toward the end of the Express article, we read that other “documented” tips to the FBI suggested Hitler was actually living in New York City—without his mustache. Others claimed he was hiding in Switzerland.

text:
It should go without saying, but I’ll say it again: this is a hard line college athletics needs to draw. The return of players who have already gone professional is exactly the kind of issue on which conference members have an obvious interest in establishing a clear boundary.

In part, that’s because no one should be naive enough to believe this is “a one-time deal.” The plaintiffs’ bar has made plain that no good deed goes unpunished here. Once you open this Pandora’s box, the next argument will be why the exception should extend a little further, and then a little further still. Years of eligibility litigation have made that abundantly clear.

The stakes are higher still because this goes directly to the viability of the self-governance model. It has taken a long time for member institutions to get past the learned helplessness of assuming that someone else--the NCAA, Congress, the courts--has to solve every governance problem for them. If a conference cannot collectively and unanimously adopt and enforce a rule on something this fundamental, it is hard to see how that model works at all.

Which is why I keep coming back to the same point: none of this ends well for LSU, and it's one of the dumbest fights I've seen in a long time.

As an aside, there is a genuinely interesting legal question lurking here: whether one member institution, armed with a Louisiana court order, can force the rest of a multistate association to compete under rules they collectively reject.

The University Should Teach Students to Forget Themselves
Commentary

Carlos Carvalho, president of the University of Austin, recently told his incoming students: “The whole world will keep telling you to find yourself. We’re hoping for something better: that you forget yourself and discover the durable joy of being absorbed in something greater than you.”
In that single sentence, Carvalho captured something essential about liberal education.

The modern university has increasingly placed the sovereign self at the center of its teaching. Students are encouraged to regard their feelings, identities, understandings, and “lived experience” as the primary measures of intellectual and moral significance.

The traditional questions, “What is true?” or “What do you think about this?” quietly give way to the therapeutic one: “How does this make you feel?”
Carvalho described the result with admirable economy. Universities, he said, have been offering students “a self-affirming mirror when what you need is a window.”

Related Stories
The Epoch Times
An Immense Study on the Universal Philosophies of Shakespeare’s Plays
The Epoch Times
Why America’s Universities Are Falling Apart
He has identified a fundamental dispute over the purpose of higher education. Is it meant to console students? To confirm and validate their identities and beliefs about the world?

Or is it meant to lead them beyond themselves into a world of new understandings, knowledge, achievement, and moral possibility that they neither created nor control?

Liberal learning embraces the latter view. Its purpose was never self-expression but self-transcendence. As the very name suggests, it is a “liberation” from the contingencies of our birth and from the necessarily parochial and time-bound understandings every generation must navigate, achieved through the disciplined encounter with truths, viewpoints, arguments, and achievements greater than oneself.

Liberal learning was never merely an accumulation of knowledge.

Cardinal John Henry Newman argued that a university education should cultivate the intellect rather than merely fill the mind with information. When pursued properly, it was transformative. It enlarged the mind, disciplined judgment, and liberated us from the ignorance with which each of us is born. Education concerns the kind of person one ideally might become.

Michael Oakeshott expressed a similar idea when he described education as an initiation into a civilizational conversation that began long before our arrival. The student enters an inherited world of philosophy, history, science, literature, and art.

That conversation is not organized around students’ feelings, nor does it pause to ask whether its contents please them or validate their identity. Its voices make claims on the student. They demand attention, open-mindedness, patience, humility, effort, and judgment.

One does not enter such a conversation by insisting that one’s voice be heard first. One begins by listening to what has already been said.

This is the paradox that Carvalho’s address illuminates. Students are endlessly advised to “find their voice.” Yet a voice worth hearing is not found by looking inward; it is formed through disciplined attention to voices wiser, stranger, more powerful and more accomplished than one’s own.

As Northrop Frye put it, “Nobody is capable of free speech unless he knows how to use language, and such knowledge is not a gift; it has to be learned and worked at.”

The ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” was inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, where it counseled humility and an honest recognition of one’s limits. But “know thyself” was never an imperative to embark on an inner journey.

For the Greeks, knowing oneself meant engaging with the world and asking, “What is this thing?” or “Who are these people?” or “What does this mean?”

It was a recognition of the ancient paradox that we find ourselves by first forgetting ourselves; by directing our energies outward toward something much greater than our limited self.

To forget oneself, in this context, does not mean erasing one’s individuality or submitting uncritically to authority. Nor does it mean that education should be indifferent to the circumstances students bring with them. It means escaping the prison of perpetual self-reference. It means recognizing that the world contains realities independent of our approval and truths that remain true regardless of how they make us feel.

A mathematical proof does not accommodate our identity. An unsettling historical fact remains true even when it offends our sensibilities. Plato, Shakespeare, and Dostoevsky did not write to affirm our preconceptions. Their value lies partly in their power to disturb them.

Among liberal education’s greatest enemies is self-absorption. The student who approaches every text by asking, “Where am I in this?” reduces education to an exercise in narcissism.

The better questions are more demanding: “What is this text asking me to see that I could not before? What does it reveal about the world? About others? About the human condition?”

Such encounters can be humbling. That is precisely their value. As Carvalho told his students, a genuine education should humble without humiliating and challenge without flattering. It should reveal both the limits of our knowledge and the possibility of expanding it.

There is also joy in this discipline, though not always the immediate gratification promised by a culture of self-affirmation. Carvalho’s phrase “durable joy” is apt. The pleasures of flattery are brief because they leave us where they found us.

The pleasures of absorption—in a difficult book, an intricate problem, a scientific discovery, a work of music, or a demanding conversation—are more enduring because they carry us beyond ourselves.

Anyone who has taught will recognize the moment when a student stops performing for a grade or calculating an exercise’s usefulness. It becomes clear when the subject itself captivates and commands the student, who is absorbed in the argument, the poem, the historical puzzle, the scientific equation, or the question of justice. At that point, education has begun.

This is why liberal learning is more than acquiring skills or credentials. It teaches us that we inhabit an intellectual and moral world we did not create and cannot fully possess. That inheritance invites our participation, but not on our terms alone.

Among the university’s deepest purposes is to help students become more fully themselves. But it does so not by affirming their existing prejudices and presumptions, but by initiating them into a civilizational conversation that broadens their understanding, chastens their certainties, and ultimately transforms them.

The world will continue telling young people to find themselves. Liberal learning should offer the more demanding—and ultimately more liberating—invitation: forget yourself for a while. Attend to something worthy of your attention, even if it is alien to you, or maybe, particularly if it is. You may discover, in doing so, not only a durable joy, but a larger and more wondrous world, and a far richer life within it.

text:
Before Harriet Tubman became one of the most famous conductors of the Underground Railroad, she was married to John Tubman, a free Black man living on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. They married around 1844, when Harriet was still enslaved and known as Araminta Ross. Their marriage existed under a brutal legal reality. John was free, but Harriet remained the property of another person, and marriage offered her no protection from being sold or separated from her family. Any children they had could also have inherited Harriet’s enslaved status under Maryland law.

In 1849, fearing that she might be sold, Harriet escaped Maryland and eventually reached freedom in Pennsylvania. She later returned for John and reportedly hoped he would leave with her, but she discovered that he had married another woman, Caroline, and he refused to go north. Harriet did not allow that painful chapter to stop her. Instead, she continued returning to Maryland and helped relatives and other enslaved people escape, risking capture and possible death each time. John remained in Maryland and was killed in 1867 during an altercation with a white man. Harriet later married Civil War veteran Nelson Davis in 1869 and remained with him until his death in 1888.

text:
A $55 MILLION deal closed on ONE PAGE, with no audit, on a HANDSHAKE, and 6 years later the 95 YEAR OLD woman who sold it opened a rival store right across the street.

Warren Buffett trusted her word once. It cost him the second contract.

Her name was Rose Blumkin, known to everyone as Mrs. B. She arrived in America from Russia with no formal education and learned English from her own daughter. In 1937, she used $500 to open Nebraska Furniture Mart. Her rule never changed: sell cheap, tell the truth.

When suppliers tried to cut her off for underpricing the established retailers, she just found new suppliers elsewhere. By 1983, a single Omaha location was generating more than $100 million a year, more than all its local competitors combined.

Buffett had been watching that number for years.

On August 30, 1983, his own 53rd birthday, he made her a cash offer. Mrs. B was 89. Berkshire didn’t count the inventory. Didn’t verify the receivables. Didn’t check a single property title.

She gave him her word. He wrote the cheque.

Buffett himself later said buying a company with no audit at all was almost unheard of, even for him.

Mrs. B stayed on as chairman, working alongside her son Louie and her grandsons Ron and Irv. Then in May 1989, at 95 years old, a dispute with her own family pushed her out the door.

3 months later, she opened Mrs. B’s Warehouse directly across the street from the company she’d just left.

At the end of 1992, now 99, she rejoined Nebraska Furniture Mart, and this time she signed a non compete.

Buffett called skipping that clause the first time around a real mistake.

She never broke her word once. There was just nothing on paper stopping her from walking out the door and starting again.

Save it while you can ⭣

text:
< Be Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
< Born 1841, Boston. Your father is the most famous writer in America.
< He names you after himself. You will spend decades escaping that shadow.
< Harvard College, Class of 1861. You graduate into a war.
< Three months later, you enlist. Massachusetts 20th Infantry.
< Ball's Bluff. A bullet passes through your chest. You survive.
< Antietam. Shot through the neck. Left for dead in a cornfield.
< Fredericksburg. Shrapnel tears through your heel. You walk with a limp forever.
< Three wounds in three years. You are twenty-three years old.
< You return to Harvard. This time for law.
< Graduate 1866. Start practicing in Boston. Find it tedious.
< So you do something no American lawyer has done before.
< You spend three years editing the twelfth edition of Kent's Commentaries.
< Then you write The Common Law. Published 1881.
< "The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience."
< One sentence. It rewrites American jurisprudence.
< Harvard offers you a professorship. You accept.
< Twenty years on the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court. Ten as Chief Justice.
< 1902. Theodore Roosevelt nominates you to the Supreme Court.
< You are sixty-one years old. Most men would be winding down.
< You serve for thirty years.
< You dissent. And dissent. And dissent again.
< Lochner v. New York. You call the majority opinion economic theology, not law.
< Abrams v. United States. You invent the marketplace of ideas.
< The Great Dissenter, they call you. Your dissents become tomorrow's majorities.
< Then comes Buck v. Bell. 1927.
< Virginia wants to sterilize Carrie Buck. She is "feebleminded," they say.
< You write the opinion. Eight to one.
< "Three generations of imbeciles are enough."
< The Nazis will cite it at Nuremberg.
< You retire in 1932, aged ninety. The oldest justice in history.
< You die three years later. No children. No regrets, you say.

The man who gave America free speech also gave it forced sterilization.

Eight words in Buck v. Bell. They outlived every dissent he ever wrote.

The Great Dissenter's majority opinion is the one we cannot forget.

text:
Last month, Virginia became the first state in the country to launch a bulk-purchasing campaign for rooftop solar — a move that promises to bring down the cost of installing panels for households across Old Dominion.

The idea behind the program, called Switch Together, is simple: Solar panels come cheaper by the dozen. Trusted solar installers can pool demand to purchase equipment in bulk and pass the discounts on to participants.

Solar United Neighbors, the nonprofit running the initiative, has for years used this model on a local scale in communities around the U.S. But it’s now expanding statewide in Virginia at the urging of the office of Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, who is looking for ways to lower energy bills as utilities jack up rates in the world’s data center capital. Rooftop solar both slashes power costs for homes that install it and can drive down expenses for utility customers at large.

“If more people go solar, that’s less strain on the grid, and there’s less need to build costly infrastructure that the entire rate base would actually pay for,” said Brandon Praileau, SUN’s Virginia program director, who joined the group in 2023 after rooftop solar helped his church in Norfolk cut utility bills by a quarter.

The state is not providing any funding for Switch Together, though its partnership promises to amplify the reach of the bulk-purchasing effort, which is focused on solar but also offers residents access to cheaper home batteries, EV chargers, and, in some locations, heat pumps.

Since Spanberger announced the initiative in July, more than 4,300 residents, small businesses, and nonprofits have put their names down to receive more details, and 120 have signed contracts, according to SUN.

The campaign is set to end Oct. 15. By the time the bulk-purchasing drive is over, Praileau expects those figures will swell to 5,000 requests for info and about 500 signed contracts. ​“We’re talking about a utility-scale amount of solar with those numbers,” he said. ​“Almost 4 megawatts.”

text:
That is the official position. The gap is between the official position and what actually happens in parishes, informal deliverance circles, or when a priest is presented with a distraught, devout parent and a child who is “acting out.” Informal prayers of deliverance, charismatic practices, or a well-meaning priest who does not recognize the family-systems pattern can occur with far less scrutiny. A parent who is already isolating the child has a strong incentive to present the situation as a spiritual emergency rather than as a custody conflict.

Some Catholic writers and at least one Irish bishop have named parental alienation as a form of abuse and have urged that children not be cut off from a parent after marital breakdown. That awareness exists. It is not yet widespread training for clergy who encounter these families.

Why congregations and dioceses often miss it
Several structural features make this easy to miss:

- Clergy and parish staff are rarely trained in high-conflict divorce dynamics, coercive control, or the specific tactics of parental alienation. They see a present, involved, religiously committed parent and a child who appears troubled. The absent or rejected parent is easy to pathologize.
- Churches tend to treat family matters as private unless there is obvious physical or sexual abuse. Psychological isolation and reality-distortion do not trigger the same reflex.
- A parent who frames everything in spiritual terms can look like the more faithful party. Questioning that framing can feel like questioning the faith itself.
- Mental-health language and spiritual language compete. If the first interpretive frame offered is “this child has a demon,” medical or psychological evaluation can be delayed or subordinated.
- The child’s own testimony is often discounted because the child has been coached, frightened, or made to feel that loyalty to the favored parent is a religious duty.

The result can be that a congregation or a priest becomes an unwitting amplifier of the alienation rather than a check on it.

The legitimate questions this raises
Welborne’s account is one data point, not a claim that most Christian communities do this. It does, however, point to concrete gaps:

- Do dioceses and denominations train clergy and pastoral staff to recognize when religious language is being used to isolate a child from a parent?
- When a parent requests spiritual intervention for a minor’s “dark thoughts” or behavioral problems after a divorce, is medical/psychological screening required first, and is the other parent’s perspective sought?
- Are there clear policies that distinguish a child’s right to a relationship with both parents from a parent’s right to transmit religious belief?
- Do safeguarding protocols for minors in deliverance or exorcism settings treat possible coercion by a parent as a red flag, not just possible coercion by a cleric?

Religious communities that take the protection of children seriously already have language for this: the child’s welfare is not subordinate to a parent’s preferred spiritual narrative. The same caution that the Church applies to distinguishing mental illness from possession can be applied to distinguishing a child’s genuine spiritual struggle from a parent’s campaign to rewrite the child’s reality. The teachings themselves do not require the outcome Welborne described. The absence of awareness about how those teachings can be conscripted in a family war does.

Note: Grok AI was used as part of the textual basis for these observations

text:
most [technical] founders think distribution means becoming an influencer.

but here are 10 faceless, $0 distribution tactics you can run behind a screen:

1. buy abandoned communities instead of building one

there are thousands of dead FB groups, Discord servers, and subreddits where the admin quit in 2022.

dm the owner, offer $50 to take over mod rights, and revive the room with actual utility.

2. build 30-second free tools around your main product

spin out tiny standalone utilities on separate subdomains with pure SEO titles: calculators, generators, widgets.

people search the micro-problem, use the tool in 30 seconds, and see your main app in the footer.

3. turn other people’s weekly chores into distribution

make free templates for things people already have to send to their bosses, investors, or clients.

a clean investor update generator where every exported PDF has "generated via [Your App]" at the bottom.

4. engineer screenshots into your product loop

people love screenshotting receipts, test scores, Spotify Wrapped summaries, and personality breakdowns.

format your key outputs into clean 1:1 cards. if the screenshot looks aesthetic, users distribute you for free.

5. seed answers on the internet, not ads

search Google for "site:https://t.co/tWhSfcFi7C" or "site:https://t.co/EDZujJ7dXl" in your niche from the last 30 days.

write the most detailed, genuine reply solving their exact problem, with your product casually mentioned as one option among three.

6. build hyper-niche comparison pages

create landing pages for every competitor query: "[competitor] alternative for [niche]" or "[tool A] vs [tool B]".

these only get 100 searches a month, but searchers have their wallets out ready to switch today.

7. create the public database nobody wants to maintain

curate an open Airtable or Notion directory of niche tools, investor lists, grant deadlines, or salary benchmarks.

everyone bookmarks and shares comprehensive directories because nobody wants to manually clean 200 rows.

8. hijack offline behaviour

find physical spots where your exact target audience gets bored or waits around.

coworking boards, tech coffee shops, campus laundry rooms, event lanyards. a simple QR code on a laminated card with a provocative question beats digital ads.

9. build something people can flex with

people love displaying proof of their taste, streak, or competence.

give users a badge, tier status, or customized audit score they can drop into their bio, portfolio, or GitHub readme. status is the fastest distribution engine.

10. manufacture a recurring internet event

create a weekly index, monthly teardown, or niche leaderboard published strictly from a brand account.

when you rank the top 20 projects or people every Friday, the 20 people featured will retweet it to their audience every week.

the question i ask before building any feature:

"what useful or funny artifact can this tool produce that a user already has an excuse to share?"

distribution gets easier when you stop forcing yourself to be an influencer and let the product speak for itself sometimes  :)

text:
Washington State 

FAIR CHANCE ACT

Washington Background Check Requirements in Effect Now for Large + Medium Employers and in January for Small Businesses

Monday, August 31, 2026

Washington State Fair Chance Act Amendments Criminal History
Related Practices & Jurisdictions
Labor Employment, Election Law Legislative News

Washington’s amended Fair Chance Act prohibits employers from requesting an individual’s criminal background information before a conditional offer of employment is made and also limits an employer’s ability to take tangible adverse employment actions against both applicants and employees because of their arrest or conviction records. 
Medium and large employers are covered by new requirements effective July 1, 2026, with the next effective date for small employers, January 1, 2027.

Employers should be proactive in understanding what steps they need to follow, including adding the new Washington State Attorney General’s Guide along with their required written notification to a candidate in the event of voluntary disclosure of a criminal conviction prior to a job offer and if they are subject to a background check after  conditional offer of employment.

Washington State’s 2025 expanded Fair Chance Act, imposing additional limits on employers’ criminal information inquiries, went into effect for medium and large employers (15 or more employees) beginning July 1, 2026, and will be effective for small employers (fewer than 15 employees) beginning January 2027.

Employers with employees in the City of Seattle are already one step ahead under local law. The changes to state law will supplement those Seattle requirements and apply to employers throughout the state.

Timing of Inquiries

Unless otherwise required by law, only post-offer criminal history inquiries and criminal background checks will be permitted. Previously, an employer could potentially inquire earlier, after a candidate was deemed “otherwise qualified.”

Additionally, if an employer discloses to the applicant that the position is subject to a background check after a conditional offer of employment, or a candidate voluntarily discloses a conviction prior to any offer, the employer must immediately provide written notification of the law and the recently updated Attorney General’s Guide (AG’s Guide) for employers and job applicants. The AG’s Guide restates the law, as well as provides instructions and a link on how to file a complaint with the State Attorney General’s office.

According to the AG’s Guide, providing a separate written notification of the law includes informing the applicant in writing that:

An employer may not ask for or receive information about an applicant’s criminal history, orally or in writing, until after making an initial determination that (a) the applicant is otherwise qualified for the position and (b) making a conditional offer of employment; 
 
An employer may not implement policies or practices that automatically or categorically exclude job applicants with a criminal record, including rejecting applicants for failure to disclose a criminal record prior to receiving a conditional offer of employment; 
 
An employer may not carry out a tangible adverse employment action based on an applicant’s or employee’s adult arrest record of juvenile conviction record, provided the individual is not out on bail or released on their own personal recognizance pending trial; and 
 
An employer may not carry out a tangible adverse employment action solely based on an applicant’s or employee’s adult conviction record, unless the employer has a legitimate business reason for taking such action.
Even if an applicant voluntarily discloses a conviction prior to an offer and the employer immediately provides the required written notification alongside the AG’s Guide, the employer should still refrain from taking the conviction into consideration before a conditional offer is made.

September self-care challenge: Intentional movement

This month’s self-care challenge is to incorporate intentional gentle movement into each day, in a way that feels supportive, safe, and sustainable for you. Aim for at least ten minutes of movement daily. This can include stretching, walking, yoga, dancing, Tai Chi, or any activity that helps you reconnect with your body. The goal is not intensity or performance, but consistency and awareness. Notice how even small amounts of movement can impact your mood, energy, and overall well-being. Choose what feels good, honor your body’s needs, and celebrate each day you show up for yourself.

September is National Recovery Month

National Recovery Month began in 1989 to promote awareness that recovery from mental health and substance use challenges is possible. It’s a time to celebrate the achievements of individuals in recovery, recognize service providers, and reduce stigma through education and community engagement.

SAMHSA has teamed with community partners, providers, people with lived experience, and other experts to create a toolkit for this key month.

text:
#D4VD #CelesteRivasHernandez 

The more information that comes out about #D4vd’s legal situation, the more questions I have — and I think we need to be very careful about separating what we KNOW from what we’re assuming.

Let’s start with the assets.

#D4vd reportedly transferred 2 Texas properties into a trust connected to his mother.

Separately, according to reported testimony from Benjamin Greger, who worked with D4vd’s management team, D4vd had allegedly discussed using a Texas property as possible bail money and advised Greger to transfer other properties into his mother’s name to protect his money from a potential civil lawsuits.

Why were D4vd’s properties transferred into the trust? What exactly do the trust documents say?
Can those assets be used to pay D4vd’s legal expenses?

If they can, are they being used?

If they aren’t, why not?

And if the properties remain in the trust and haven’t been sold, what does that tell us — if anything — about the sudden change in his legal representation?

Then we have Blair Berk and D4vd’s former private defense team withdrawing.

That raises another set of questions.

Was this financial?

Was it strategic?

Was there a disagreement?

Were plea negotiations ever happening behind closed doors?

If D4vd was considering an early plea, did Berk attempt to negotiate one?

Was anything offered?

Was anything rejected?

We simply don’t know.

And now we get to the public defender.

I keep seeing people automatically equate “public defender” with “bad representation.”

Public defenders are licensed criminal-defense attorneys, and many spend their careers handling serious felony cases. Heavy caseloads and limited resources can absolutely be legitimate concerns within public-defense systems, but that does NOT mean an individual public defender is incompetent.

The change in representation creates another major issue: the death-penalty decision.

District Attorney Nathan Hochman has said the change in D4vd’s representation does not impact the prosecution.

He also said D4vd’s former attorneys were given the opportunity to submit a mitigation packet explaining why prosecutors should NOT pursue the death penalty — but according to Hochman, that packet was not submitted before they withdrew.

Now DA says new counsel will be given additional time to submit mitigation if they choose.

So I have questions.

How much additional time?

Is there a deadline?

Why wasn’t the original mitigation packet submitted?

Was it being prepared before the attorneys withdrew?

Does new counsel start the mitigation process from scratch?

And if the change in attorneys does not impact the prosecution, how much should it be allowed to delay the DA’s decision. 

The DA has made one thing clear:

The death-penalty decision has NOT been made.

Why not?

What information is the DA still waiting for?

How significant are the aggravating factors prosecutors say they must weigh?

How much weight could a mitigation packet actually carry?

Then there’s the trial timeline.

New attorneys potentially have to review an enormous amount of evidence, understand the previous defense strategy, conduct their own investigation, evaluate experts, prepare mitigation and decide how they intend to defend the case.

Could this push an eventual trial back significantly? ABSOLUTELY 

Could another private attorney eventually enter the case — possibly even pro bono because of the extraordinary publicity surrounding it?

Maybe.

And that’s my biggest point:

QUESTION EVERYTHING — BUT DON’T TURN QUESTIONS INTO FACTS.

The trust deserves scrutiny.
The property transfers deserve scrutiny.
The timing deserves scrutiny.
The change in attorneys deserves scrutiny.
The mitigation situation deserves scrutiny.
And the continued delay in deciding whether to seek the death penalty DEFINITELY deserves scrutiny.

What is happening behind the scenes that the public still doesn’t know?
