The Economist
June 20th–26th 2026

Briefing | The unverified state
The Economist June 20th 2026

Who goes there?

One month after a single piece of software stopped working, Britain cannot say who its citizens are. The rest of the world is discovering what that was holding up

Paris, Delhi, Beijing and Washington, DC

Your correspondent left England in the second week of what the government still calls an outage, in a rigid inflatable boat, from a beach between Dungeness and Hythe, having paid €4,000 in cash to a man who did not give his name and did not need to know hers. The crossing took five hours. She mentions it not for colour but because it is the most efficient available summary of the position: the only functioning identity system on the Channel this summer belongs to the people-smugglers, who have never required documents and have simply reversed the direction of travel. Their rates going north have collapsed. Going south they have tripled.

It is worth recalling what Britain was arguing about on May 19th. The newspapers, then still printing, were exercised by the number of vape shops on the high street, the licensing regime for pavement tables and whether a cabinet minister had been rude to a select committee. This is not offered as satire. It is the standard condition of a rich, stable, elaborately governed country, and it is what a month ago looked like the natural order of things.

On May 20th an intruder with privileged access reached https://t.co/VWJ2Le8avK One Login, the verification system through which, by then, 250 online public services and some 23m citizen accounts passed. Britain had spent four years consolidating identity onto it and closing every other route as an economy: the civil-service telephone helplines, the counters, the paper forms. On May 21st the government could no longer establish, online, that a citizen was who he claimed to be. Since online was where the services had been moved, the qualification was academic.

Sauve qui peut
A month on, the tally is easier to state than to absorb. HMRC receives money it cannot attribute and issues no repayments. Employers deduct tax at source and hold it; something over £25bn a month now sits in business current accounts that will not all survive to hand it over. New benefit claims are not being established. Companies House processes nothing.

That last is worth dwelling on, because it is misunderstood abroad. Britain introduced director verification only in 2025, having run for a century and a half a corporate register that required no proof of anything and was, in consequence, a recognised instrument of fraud. Optimists therefore argued that One Login's failure merely returned the register to its previous condition. This has proved wrong in practice. The alternative route—verification through an authorised corporate service provider—is paid, thinly supplied, and widely believed by British privacy campaigners to route back to One Login regardless. Free-at-the-point-of-use crowded out the alternatives before it failed, which is what free-at-the-point-of-use does.

The pound is down by roughly a fifth on a trade-weighted basis. Two gilt auctions have failed. The Bank of England is buying, and saying little. What began as a verification failure has become a fiscal one, and is becoming a monetary one.

Scotland's brief immunity has ended. Holyrood kept its own arrangements and its devolved services worked for a fortnight, to considerable local satisfaction. But tax, benefits, borders, company law and financial regulation are reserved, and a Scot is no more able to file a return or start a claim than anyone in Kent. Devolution protects a jurisdiction from London's decisions. It does not protect it from London's absence.

Devolution protects a jurisdiction from London's decisions. It does not protect it from London's absence

The kindness of strangers
Who gains? From Washington, the answer is: nobody deliberately, and America substantially by accident. General counsel who spent June rewriting choice-of-law clauses are choosing New York, and contractual jurisdiction does not migrate back on the strength of an apology. The administration has offered assistance and will expect terms. It has also, more quietly, compartmented intelligence sharing—not as a rebuke but because British vetting cannot presently be assured, and no competent service would do otherwise.

From Beijing, the read is longer. China has the capacity to underwrite a country of Britain's size and no incentive whatever to hurry. Officials speak, without embarrassment, of the difference between assisting a nation that is embarrassed and one that is exhausted. What is on offer, when it comes, will not principally be money. It will be the reconstruction of a digital state, on Chinese infrastructure, inside the G7—a prize that no amount of lending could buy and that Britain has now placed on the table itself.

Moscow's position is more comfortable still. Attribution remains unresolved and may stay so. It scarcely matters: a Britain that cannot pay its soldiers' families or renew their clearances is a Britain distracted from NATO's eastern flank, where it leads the battlegroup in Estonia—a country of 1.3m people that has run a working national identity system since 2002 and, when a flaw appeared in 2017, switched it off and told its citizens. The comparison is being made in Tallinn with more tact than it deserves.

Pyongyang is the case that analysts find instructive rather than alarming. North Korea does not want to govern Britain; it wants revenue, and it has spent a decade perfecting two techniques. One is ransomware, which took down parts of the NHS in 2017. The other is the placement of operatives inside Western companies using fabricated identities. A state whose speciality is manufacturing people who do not exist has been presented with an economy that has lost the ability to check. Nobody knows the scale. That is the point.

Which brings one to Romania, now the most awkward subject in Whitehall. Development work on One Login was subcontracted to staff working in Bucharest for the programme's prime contractor, Deloitte. The Government Digital Service did not consult the National Cyber Security Centre before the arrangement was made; its own head recorded, in a review conducted after the fact in 2022, that he was uncomfortable with the clarity of offshore oversight. Ministers later assured Parliament that a handful of people were involved, that none had access to the production environment and that all code was checked. Those assurances are now a load-bearing element of a forensic investigation, which is not a position anybody intended them to occupy. Britain spent four years describing One Login as sovereign infrastructure. It cannot presently say with confidence who had access to what while it was being built.

Brussels, meanwhile, can do less than it would like and rather less than Dublin requires. Ireland has the deepest exposure and no responsibility at all—the crisis's Icelandic depositors. The EU has no instrument for a neighbour's administrative collapse, having spent a decade being told by that neighbour that it required nothing, and it is now absorbing British arrivals under a legal framework built on the assumption that traffic moves the other way.

Institutions of last resort, so called
The IMF is the wrong tool and everybody in Washington knows it. The Fund lends to governments that can execute a programme. Britain's difficulty is not a financing gap—the tax base is intact, the wheat is in the fields—but the absence of an administration capable of being a counterparty. There is no conditionality one can usefully impose on a state that cannot count its own citizens. In 1976 Britain went to the Fund with a balance-of-payments crisis and a functioning Treasury. It now has a functioning-Treasury problem.

The UN is stranger. Britain is a permanent member of the Security Council, which means it holds a veto over any resolution concerning its own condition. The humanitarian machinery—OCHA, the WFP—is built for states that lack capacity and accept help. Britain lacks capacity and has not yet found a form of words in which to accept anything. Officials in New York describe the file, privately, as the most delicate they have handled, and note that India has views about the seat.

The Commonwealth cannot lend. It can, however, do something more pointed. India, Singapore, Estonia (not a member, but offering anyway), Pakistan and Kenya possess between them most of the world's practical expertise in building national identity infrastructure at scale. From Delhi, the offer of technical assistance has been made warmly and in public, which is itself the message. The UIDAI has authenticated identity for over a billion people; NADRA pays welfare to millions in Pakistan and exports the technology; Singapore has run Singpass for two decades. The direction of capacity-building has reversed, and everyone involved is being extremely polite about it.

A state whose speciality is manufacturing people who do not exist has been presented with an economy that has lost the ability to check

The experiment nobody would have funded
Among economists, and it is unbecoming how many have said so, this is the most interesting month of their professional lives. The counterfactual that no ethics committee would approve has been run: remove a modern state's administrative capacity, leave every physical asset in place, and observe.

Three findings so far. First, the order of collapse follows transaction costs, exactly as Coase would predict. Activity requiring verified strangers to trust one another failed within days—mortgages, insurance, employment of anyone new, cross-border trade. Activity between people who already know each other barely paused. The corner shop extends credit; the wholesaler does not.

Second, substitution was faster than any model allowed. Informal exchange, scrip issued by market traders, and reciprocal labour appeared within a fortnight. Britain has not reverted to barter, which is a journalist's word; it has developed a dozen local monies and a great deal of credit based on reputation.

Third, and least comfortable for the profession, a measurable fraction of recorded British GDP appears to have been the administrative overhead of a state verifying things about itself. Nobody yet knows how large that fraction is. The suspicion that it is not small is doing quiet damage to a good deal of previous work.

The Birmingham anomaly
Which brings one to the case now being examined by every political scientist with a flight booked. Across several wards of east Birmingham, daily life is functioning better than in any comparable British city: food is distributed, disputes are settled, elderly people are checked on, and violence is markedly below the national picture.

The institutions doing this are, in the main, mosques and their associated charities, operating a system of arbitration and mutual aid that some participants describe with the word sharia and that the few remnants of the British broadcast media have reported with the excitement one would expect. The reality is duller and more interesting. No legal code has been imposed on anyone; jurisdiction extends only to those who consent to it, as with the Beth Din. Non-Muslim residents of those wards report the same improvement and use the same food distribution.

And the mechanism is precisely the subject of this article. These institutions can act because they can identify people. They hold membership rolls, they occupy premises, they handle cash, and above all their members know one another by face—which is to say they possess, without a database, the capability the British state has lost. The same has happened, with less publicity, around Sikh gurdwaras whose langar kitchens are feeding whole districts, in England's thriving evangelical churches, in a handful of Orthodox Jewish communities, and in those rural parishes where the Anglican church still functions as anything at all.

The comparative literature is unambiguous: when a state withdraws, whatever possesses dense mutual recognition inherits the ground. Mogadishu in 2006 got the Islamic Courts Union and, briefly, the safest streets in twenty years. Beirut has lived the arrangement for decades. That the British example is producing decent outcomes is a fact about social capital, not about theology, and it will remain true only for as long as the arrangements stay voluntary—which is the thing nobody can guarantee and which historically does not last.

The dog that did not bark
One observation is owed to a decade of anxious commissioning. Britain built an institute to examine whether artificial intelligence might destabilise the state, convened the world at Bletchley Park to discuss it, and published declarations on frontier risk. Successive governments treated the question as the defining technological threat of the age, and on the available evidence they were sincere.

The state was then brought down by a sign-in page procured in 2021. Nothing was superintelligent. Nothing was even clever. A supplier let a certificate lapse, a red-team finding went eighteen months without being closed, development was offshored without asking the cyber-security agency, and somebody walked in through privileged access that the monitoring could not see. The catastrophe arrived from the direction nobody was funding, wearing the clothes of routine IT, and it was boring all the way down.

The means of verification
British Marxists have had a disappointing month. The temptation to read this as capitalism's implosion is strong and does not survive contact with the evidence: the factories stand, the capital stock is unimpaired, the market continues in degraded form. What failed was the state, and it failed while performing its most basic function.

There is a Marxian account available, and it is better than the one being offered. For two decades British public administration transferred hundreds of millions of pounds to itself and to consultancies for work it had lost the capacity to specify, assess or absorb. The consultancies were the visible half and took the blame; the officials who commissioned them, rotated out before delivery and were promoted on the announcement rather than the outcome, were the larger half. A rentier class extracting from the state until the state could no longer do the thing it existed to do. Marx would have recognised the pattern. He simply located it elsewhere.

Weber is the better guide. This is a crisis of rational-legal authority: the bureaucracy's claim to legitimacy rested on impersonal, reliable procedure, and the procedure stopped. What has filled the gap in east Birmingham is, precisely as he would have predicted, traditional and charismatic authority—the mosque, the elder, the man everyone knows.

But the century's contribution to political economy may be simpler. Marx asked who owns the means of production. Britain has spent a month establishing that there is a prior question, which nobody thought to ask because the answer had been stable since 1538: who owns the means of verification. Britain gave the answer away to a single piece of software, at a medium assurance level, on a certificate due to expire in October, and has not yet been told when it might get it back.

Your correspondent will return when there is a means of proving she is entitled to. ■

This is an imagined magazine briefing written by Claude at the user's request, exploring a hypothetical scenario. It is not a real Economist article and is not real reporting. The May 2026 attack and every consequence described — including the Birmingham arrangements, the correspondent, the market and currency movements, and all quoted official positions — are invented. Real background referenced: the 2025 introduction of Companies House director verification under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act and the authorised corporate service provider route; Computer Weekly's reporting that One Login development work was subcontracted to staff in Romania without prior NCSC consultation, that the then head of GDS recorded discomfort about offshore oversight in an after-the-fact 2022 review, and that ministers subsequently gave Parliament assurances about the scope of that access; the UK's 1976 IMF programme; the 2017 WannaCry attack on NHS systems and North Korea's documented use of fabricated identities to place IT workers in Western firms; UK leadership of NATO's battlegroup in Estonia; Estonia's 2017 ID-card certificate suspension; Aadhaar, NADRA and Singpass; the Beth Din's consensual jurisdiction in English law; the Islamic Courts Union's control of Mogadishu in 2006; the 2023 Bletchley Park AI safety summit and the UK's AI safety institute; the requirement for English parish registers from 1538; and One Login's DVS register certification at medium assurance expiring on 30 October 2026. The depiction of community institutions filling a governance vacuum draws on the comparative state-collapse literature and is speculative fiction, not a prediction about any real community.

text:
This is not a case for an alliance. It is an oath of political submission.

Allies can share interests; they do not share identities. When a former vice president declares that a foreign state’s cause, values, and fight are America’s, he is surrendering the first duty of statecraft: deciding independently what to defend, whom to fight, and what price one’s citizens should pay. Under Pence’s formula, Israel defines the conflict and America inherits it.

His historical argument is built on a bait-and-switch. The Pilgrims reading Hebrew scripture, the Liberty Bell quoting Leviticus, and George Washington defending American Jews from bigotry establish a religious inheritance and a promise of equal citizenship. They establish no perpetual allegiance to a foreign state founded in 1948.

Respect for Judaism is not obedience to an Israeli government. American religious liberty is not an Israeli security guarantee.

Even Pence’s modern history is false. He says Israel’s Arab neighbors invaded in 1967. The U.S. State Department’s own history records that Israel launched pre-emptive military operations against Egypt on June 5, while contemporary American assessments did not regard an Arab attack as imminent. In 1973, Egypt and Syria fought to recover the Sinai and Golan Heights—territories Israel had seized in 1967. One may debate the crises surrounding those wars; one cannot reverse who struck first and call the result moral clarity.

His appeal to “liberty over tyranny” is more grotesque still. The International Court of Justice concluded that Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful. The UN Security Council states that Israeli settlements have no legal validity and constitute a flagrant violation of international law.

A state cannot advertise itself as the embodiment of liberty while permanently ruling millions who do not choose the power controlling their land, movement, borders, and security. The word “democracy” does not disinfect occupation.

Pence then uses antisemitism as political armor. Hatred of Jews is real; it does not make an Israeli government sacred, convert criticism of occupation into bigotry, or require Americans to finance every Israeli policy. Conflating Jewish safety with immunity for Israeli power does not protect Jews. It protects a state from accountability and turns foreign policy into a loyalty test.

For the Middle East, Pence’s doctrine is a blank cheque. If Israel’s fight is automatically America’s, every Israeli escalation arrives in Washington already sanctified. American power ceases to balance its own interests and becomes the military insurer of decisions made elsewhere.

That does not produce “peace through strength.” It rewards escalation with a superpower guarantee.

Pence’s conclusion removes any remaining disguise. He does not close with treaty obligations, reciprocal interests, or measurable benefits to the United States. He invokes Genesis: bless Israel and be blessed; curse it and be cursed.

That is not conservative statecraft. It is biblical blackmail made foreign policy.

The U.S. Treasury is not a tithe. The Pentagon is not an offering. American soldiers are not instruments of Mike Pence’s private exegesis.

A real alliance is conditional, reciprocal, and subordinate to national interest. Pence offers identity fusion instead: Israel chooses the fight; America supplies the weapons, diplomatic cover, and bill.

That is not an alliance between sovereign states. It is the voluntary surrender of a superpower’s judgment to a smaller state’s agenda.

text:
Cooper Kupp came out of Davis High School in Yakima with two scholarship offers. Idaho State and Eastern Washington.

That was it. Two.

He took Eastern Washington and went to Cheney, a small college town with a red turf football field.

The summer before one of those seasons, he tried working landscaping in the afternoons on top of morning workouts. By the time the season started he was exhausted. He realized he couldn't do both.

So football and school had to be the full-time job. Which left one problem.

Somebody still had to pay for their life.

Anna Croskrey had met Cooper at a track meet back in 2012, their senior year of high school. She handed him a medal. They started dating not long after.

She started college at Arkansas. He was in Washington. Neither of them liked the distance, so she transferred to Eastern Washington to be near him.

Then she got a job at a teriyaki place in Cheney called Rokko's and went to work.

Full-time. While also being a full-time student.

After practice, Cooper would drive his white Nissan Pathfinder across campus to the restaurant. That truck broke down constantly. Teammates who rode with him treated every trip as a coin flip.

He'd get there and she'd be behind the cash register, or packing orders into styrofoam containers.

"I supported us monetarily through college," Anna told ESPN, laughing about it years later, almost like she couldn't believe she'd pulled it off. "I was working full time so that he didn't have to worry about that, so that he could focus."

They got married in 2015. He was 21. Still in college.

Here's the moment that tells you exactly where they were financially.

After the wedding, they went to the bank to merge their accounts. Anna's father came along, since he was a co-signer on hers.

The teller pulled up Cooper's balance and said it out loud, in front of his brand new father-in-law.

Three dollars.

That was the whole account. Three dollars, a broken down Pathfinder, and a wife working a cash register so he could chase something that two colleges in America had been willing to bet on.

He has never once pretended he did it himself.

"Without a doubt, there's no doubt in my mind, not only would I not be here where I am today without her," Kupp said. "I really believe I may not be in this. I may not be in the NFL if it wasn't for her and what she has inspired in me and pushed me to do."

The Rams took him 69th overall in 2017.

He won Offensive Player of the Year. He won the receiving triple crown in 2021, leading the league in catches, yards and touchdowns. He won Super Bowl LVI and was named MVP of it.

Then, after eight years, Los Angeles released him.

Anna posted about it publicly. Not bitter, just honest about how disorienting it was.

"Wherever we go, wherever we land, is going to be so lucky to have you in their building."

Where they landed was Seattle. Three years, $45 million, back in the state where the whole thing started, about four hours from Cheney.

And last season, the Seahawks beat the Rams in the NFC Championship game on their way to winning the Super Bowl.

The team that let him go watched him go get another ring.

A kid nobody recruited, a truck that wouldn't start, three dollars in the bank, and a woman working doubles at a teriyaki counter so he wouldn't have to think about any of it.

My daughter and I got to visit the Museum of the Bible today in Washington, D.C. What a beautiful museum. Loved it!

Behind me is the remarkable Megiddo Mosaic, discovered in Israel and dating to about A.D. 230—nearly a century before the Council of Nicaea. It formed the floor of one of the oldest Christian worship sites ever discovered. 

One of its Greek inscriptions says that a woman named Akeptous offered a table “to God Jesus Christ.” The table stood in the center of the room and was likely used for the Lord’s Supper. The mosaic also mentions a Roman centurion who helped fund the floor and includes an early Christian fish symbol. 

What makes this especially significant is that it provides extraordinary archaeological evidence that Christians were openly worshiping Jesus as God in the early third century—long before Christianity was legalized in the Roman Empire and long before the Council of Nicaea in A.D. 325. Amazing to see this piece of early Christian history in person!

text:
Xi and Putin in Bishkek: What a Handshake Summit Tells Us About the New World Order

The images from Bishkek on August 31 were predictable in their choreography and precise in their intention. Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan — smiling, shaking hands, exchanging rhetoric about a partnership whose "foundations will become ever stronger."

This was not a breakthrough summit. It was not designed to be.

What Actually Happened — and Why It Matters

The Bishkek bilateral is best understood as a consolidation meeting, not an initiation. The consequential agreements between Moscow and Beijing were signed at their May 2026 Moscow summit — energy frameworks, defense-industrial cooperation, Rosatom nuclear reactor agreements covering four units entering Chinese service between 2026 and 2028, plus joint fusion and quantum technology research. Bishkek added one durable institutional commitment: Putin's offer to make the China-Russia visa-free travel regime permanent, backed by a 43% surge in people-to-people travel in the first half of 2026.

That single move deserves more attention than it has received. People-to-people ties are the connective tissue that survives sanctions cycles, leadership transitions, and diplomatic ruptures. Institutionalizing them is how you build a partnership that outlasts the individuals who constructed it.

The Real Audience: Not Putin, Not Xi

Xi's language at Bishkek — carefully formulaic, strategically timed — was not directed at Putin. Putin already knows where China stands. The language was directed at the 30+ heads of state gathered in Bishkek: Central Asian leaders managing geography between Russia and China, South Asian states navigating US pressure, Middle Eastern governments watching the Iran war reshape the regional order.

The message: the Sino-Russian axis is durable, deliberate, and not going anywhere.

This is what the Kremlin made explicit — framing the summit as proof that "Putin personally is not isolated geopolitically." That framing, sourced to UK geostrategy firm Gatehouse, is almost certainly accurate as a description of Russian intent. When you are entering your fourth-and-a-half year of a war that has cost hundreds of thousands of lives, you need to project normalcy to the governments you want in your corner. Bishkek provided that stage.

The Strategic Context Washington Cannot Ignore

The Bishkek summit occurred against a specific backdrop that makes its timing analytically significant:

Russia is deep into its full-scale Ukraine war, under comprehensive Western sanctions, dependent on Chinese trade, components, and diplomatic cover.
Iran is six months into an active war with the United States and Israel — the most acute test yet of whether the non-Western order can absorb direct military pressure from Washington.

Trump has simultaneously disrupted the US-ROK alliance, antagonized European partners, and imposed tariffs that pushed India toward strategic hedging.

The unspoken message to Washington from Bishkek is structural: you are isolating your own partners faster than you are isolating ours.

The Nuclear Dimension — The Partnership's Most Durable Layer

China's deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia is the part of the relationship that receives the least public analysis and carries the most long-term strategic weight. Four Russian-designed reactors entering Chinese service over the next two years are not reversible on diplomatic timelines. Rosatom's agreements on fusion technology create a shared research dependency that will persist for decades. This layer of the partnership is the least susceptible to political disruption — not because the two governments are ideologically aligned, but because the technical interdependencies are now structural.

For those tracking Chinese energy security and technology self-sufficiency: Sino-Russian nuclear cooperation is a hedge against both Western sanctions and domestic technology gaps. Beijing is not accidentally deepening this relationship while pursuing semiconductor independence and AI parity. These moves are part of the same strategic logic.

Xi's Broader Sprint — And the Tension Inside It

Bishkek was one stop in a multi-leg diplomatic sprint that includes Egypt, India (BRICS), and Washington for the September 24 Trump-Xi summit. This is the analytically interesting tension in Xi's current posture.

Beijing is positioning itself as the indispensable broker between the Western and non-Western orders simultaneously — the leader who can talk to both Putin and Trump, who can attend the SCO and then fly to Washington, who can deepen nuclear cooperation with Russia while negotiating AI safety frameworks with the United States.

That posture is strategically brilliant and structurally fragile. If the Trump-Xi summit produces a significant US-China alignment — particularly around trade or technology — it will immediately strain Sino-Russian trust. Moscow will be watching Washington closely for signals of a bilateral deal that comes at Russia's expense. Beijing knows this. Which is why Xi's language at Bishkek was as reassuring to Putin as it was signaling to Washington.

The SCO Development Bank: The Sleeper Agenda Item

Lost in coverage of the Xi-Putin bilateral is the SCO's proposed Development Bank — an institutional financing mechanism for non-Western infrastructure that, if operationalized, would compete directly with World Bank and ADB channels. This is not a near-term story. Operationalizing a multilateral development bank takes years and requires resolving significant governance disputes among SCO members with competing interests (India and Pakistan are both members; China and India maintain active border tensions).

But over a 3-to-5 year horizon, a functioning SCO Development Bank would represent something qualitatively different: a parallel institutional architecture for infrastructure finance outside Western conditionality. That is the summit's most consequential long-term economic agenda item, even if it generated the least headline coverage.

The Bottom Line

What Bishkek actually demonstrates is the maturation of a partnership that no longer needs dramatic deliverables to project durability. The foundations — nuclear cooperation, permanent people-to-people mobility, energy interdependence, shared anti-Western institutional architecture — are now deep enough that a consolidation summit is the message. The signal to the non-Western world is that this axis is reliable. The signal to Washington is that diplomatic disruption of the US alliance network is not going unnoticed or unexploited.

The September 24 Trump-Xi summit will be the more consequential test. But understanding what Xi said to Putin three weeks before that meeting — and why — is essential context for reading whatever comes next.

text:
I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”
Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?
The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.
The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.
Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.
Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.
The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.
Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.
The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.
Lady Antebellum became Lady A.
Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”
Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.
Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.
Then there were the military bases.
Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.
Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.
Fort Benning became Fort Moore.
Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.
Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.
Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.
Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.
Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.
Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.
We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.
Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.
And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.
For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.
Okay.
Apparently there was an asterisk:
This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.
Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.
Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.
But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.
So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:
Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. — copied

💰🇦🇫🇺🇸Taliban want one more shot with their ex

Five years after forcing the US out of Afghanistan, the Taliban are inviting Washington back. Not with troops, but with chequebooks.

"Relations should not be assessed through the lens of the past 20 years of war, but rather on the basis of future co-operation," Taliban Foreign Minister said.
🔍 What's on offer

Afghan copper, lithium, iron ore and rare-earth minerals are estimated to be worth at least $1 trillion. The Taliban have already signed over $7 billion in mining deals with China and Iran.

At the same time, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan are deepening trade ties with Afghanistan — over 90 trade agreements worth more than $1.4 billion were signed in the first half of 2026 alone. 

The US has also been invited to the table, but it's showing up late, and the seats are mostly taken.

👀 What they really want

The Taliban's ultimate goal is sanctions relief and access to $7 billion in frozen overseas assets held in the US. 

Taliban officials also want the US embassy in Kabul reopened, claiming the capital is now "very vibrant and attractive".

text:
THE TRUMP RECEIPTS (updated daily)
The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

• August 31, 2026 — Treasury blocks major news organizations from G20 coverage: Treasury denied reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg credentials without publicly explaining why. The denials are established; viewpoint retaliation is not.

• August 30–31, 2026 — Iran fighting resumed as Trump posted an unsupported AI-generated attack video: U.S. forces struck Iranian launchers, Iran retaliated toward U.S. bases, and Trump posted a synthetic video claiming Kharg Island was being destroyed without corroborating evidence.

• August 30, 2026 — The administration deported dozens to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan man protected from removal to Afghanistan over Taliban threats. The removal is established; whether using a third country violated his rights remains unresolved.

• August 30, 2026 — Venezuela announced a 25-year U.S. oil deal covering 17 fields and targeting 1.5 million barrels daily. Trump claims U.S. partnerships gained majority control; Venezuela says it retains ownership. Corruption is not established.

• August 30, 2026 — Trump demanded FCC “punishment” of NBC’s Kristen Welker after she called his endorsement results mixed. The demand is documented; no FCC penalty or legal finding followed.

• August 29, 2026 — Administration escalates unsupported noncitizen-voting claims ahead of the midterms: DHS asserted without public evidence that up to 250,000 noncitizens may be on four states’ rolls. Experts say such voting is extremely rare and warn the method may produce false positives.

• August 29, 2026 — Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian imports under an untested Depression-era law after losing on his earlier tariff authority. Canada retaliated; the new legal theory remains unadjudicated.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS used a customs statute to obtain six months of journalist Georgia Fort’s phone records and seek data involving journalists, nonprofits and unions without prior judicial approval. The demands are documented; legality is unresolved.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge ruled that using immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation over pro-Palestinian advocacy or criticism of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

• August 28, 2026 — Regulators found White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez used advance access to Trump speeches for prediction-market trades; he must forfeit over $107,000, pay $65,000 and accept a three-year ban.

• August 28, 2026 — A judge rejected Trump’s effort to move his New York hush-money case to federal court, ruling the Stormy Daniels concealment was private conduct, not a presidential duty; his 34 felony convictions remain on appeal.

• August 28, 2026 — Trump renewed efforts to restrict birthright citizenship after his earlier approach was blocked. A judge denied an immediate block on procedural grounds; litigation continues.

• August 28, 2026 — The administration appealed continued Hudson Tunnel funding after Trump offered to release money if Democrats backed naming Dulles Airport and New York Penn Station after him. The proposal is documented; no criminal finding exists.

• August 28, 2026 — Border-wall work proceeded over Tohono O’odham Nation objections. A judge allowed work on the federal Roosevelt Reservation; the tribe alleges agents and contractors entered tribal land without permission, blocked tribal police and threatened sacred sites. Construction is established; alleged trespass remains unresolved.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge ruled the administration unlawfully rewrote farmworker wage rules, potentially cutting affected wages by up to $7 an hour and illegally deducting housing costs.

• August 27, 2026 — After a court blocked effectively renaming the Kennedy Center for Trump, allies pursued Trump branding and DOJ raised possible demolition or replacement if renovation plans were blocked. Trump said he was “not ripping it down.”

• August 27, 2026 — A judge barred the Pentagon from punishing Anthropic over its AI-use limits, finding unconstitutional retaliation, First Amendment and due-process violations, and an arbitrary “supply chain risk” designation.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge temporarily blocked core Trump mail-ballot rules as likely unconstitutional, citing no fraud evidence and an overwhelming disenfranchisement risk. The case continues.

• August 27, 2026 — ICE awarded a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 electric-shock gloves for arrests, transport and civil disturbances. ICE cites reduced force; critics warn of abuse and weak oversight.

• August 26, 2026 — A judge rejected DOJ’s request to erase Steve Bannon’s contempt conviction for defying the Jan. 6 committee, finding dismissal was not shown to serve justice. Bannon served four months; DOJ may try again.

• August 24, 2026 — ICE tightened international-student internship rules and warned noncompliant universities they could lose authorization to enroll foreign students. DHS calls it enforcement; universities call it a major restriction.

• August 2026 — A federal judge rebuked USPS for advancing a Trump-directed mail-voting rule despite an injunction, saying the agency failed to comply with the order.

• August 2026 — Six months into the Iran conflict, Iran had not capitulated, Hormuz traffic remained badly disrupted, U.S. munitions were strained, regional instability had grown and oil prices were sharply higher.

• August 2026 — DOJ turned investigations toward officials involved in earlier Trump cases, including FBI personnel connected to the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search.

• August 2026 — DOJ subpoenaed Letitia James’ office over earlier Trump cases; an appeals court upheld blocking them because the acting U.S. attorney was unlawfully appointed.

• August 2026 — The Pentagon dismissed the Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief, raising concern about political control of independent military journalism.

• August 2026 — The administration moved to ease firing career workers through new “suitability” and forced-ranking rules; unions sued, alleging a shift from merit service to political patronage.

• July 2026 — The administration increased wild-horse removals and sales; reporting indicates some protected horses may have entered the slaughter pipeline. BLM says it does not knowingly sell horses for slaughter.

• February 20, 2026 — The Supreme Court ruled Trump’s emergency statute did not authorize his sweeping tariffs. At least $133 billion had been collected, leaving businesses seeking refunds.

• February 2026 — Trump expanded lower-tariff Argentine beef imports to fight record prices, angering U.S. ranchers and Republican lawmakers who say the policy favors foreign beef over American producers.

• 2025–2026 — A federal judge found the administration unlawfully directed agencies to fire roughly 25,000 probationary workers en masse.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ fired or pushed out prosecutors and FBI personnel tied to Trump and Jan. 6 investigations, fueling concerns that law enforcement was being reorganized around political loyalty.

• 2025–2026 — ICE raids, violent enforcement operations, and families being terrorized in their own communities.

• 2025–2026 — Americans shot and killed during immigration enforcement while the government demands more power and less accountability.

• 2025–2026 — Expanded deportation operations repeatedly faced challenges over due process, detention, removals and extraordinary executive power.

• 2025–2026 — The administration sharply reduced the federal workforce, with about 317,000 employees expected to leave in 2025, raising concerns about lost expertise, weaker services and political control.

• 2025–2026 — Trump used federal funding as leverage against universities over leadership, DEI, campus protests and political culture.

• 2025–2026 — Cuts and freezes disrupted NIH grants, laboratories, medical research, staffing and graduate programs; courts repeatedly found parts of the funding actions unlawful.

• 2025–2026 — Vaccine chaos and public health policy being dragged into political extremism instead of science, safety, and trust.

• 2025–2026 — The administration rolled back climate, pollution, vehicle-emissions, wetlands and public-land protections while expanding drilling and fossil-fuel development.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s administration pursued investigations of people who investigated, prosecuted, sued, criticized or defeated him.

• 2025–2026 — The administration installed favored prosecutors without Senate confirmation; courts rejected several appointments, raising concerns about loyalists investigating Trump’s opponents.

• 2025–2026 — Millions of Epstein-related pages were released and Trump is referenced in the public record. Being named does not establish participation in Epstein’s crimes.

• 2025–2026 — A civil jury finding Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation while his movement still pretends morality matters.

• 2025–2026 — A desperate push to reshape voting rules, restrict access, and tilt the midterms before the people can respond.

• 2025–2026 — Rigging maps, erasing districts, and rewriting the rules to silence Black voters and diverse communities.

• 2025–2026 — Trump directed agencies toward new citizenship, mail-ballot, voter-data and election-administration restrictions, prompting litigation over intrusion into congressional and state powers.

• 2025–2026 — An unpopular war in Iran driving fear, instability, and higher gas prices while working families already struggle to survive.

• 2025–2026 — Congress abdicated core powers over war, spending, oversight, impeachment and executive abuse while the House waits for Trump’s approval and the Senate barely pushes back.

• 2025–2026 — Trump repeatedly froze, canceled or redirected congressionally appropriated money, reviving the constitutional fight over presidential control of Congress’ power of the purse.

• 2025–2026 — Capital One closed more than 300 Trump Organization-linked accounts after an anti-money-laundering review. The Trumps alleged persecution; the bank says it did not accuse the organization of money laundering.

• 2025–2026 — A nearly $1.8 billion taxpayer-funded “Anti-Weaponization Fund” for Trump allies drew warnings it could pay Jan. 6 defendants, including violent rioters, before Republican senators forced its rescission.

• 2025–2026 — Trump Media reportedly pitched Wall Street firms up to $100,000 monthly for faster access to Trump’s potentially market-moving Truth Social posts, monetizing presidential information for elite clients.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s family expanded World Liberty Financial and other crypto ventures while Trump controlled federal crypto policy, creating major presidential-family financial conflicts.

• 2025–2026 — A UAE-linked company reportedly bought a $500 million stake in Trump-family World Liberty Financial; months later the administration approved advanced AI-chip sales to the UAE. Senators sought review; no quid pro quo is established.

• 2025–2026 — Trump pressured the Federal Reserve for lower rates and tried to remove Governor Lisa Cook after disputed mortgage allegations.

• 2025–2026 — The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to remove Cook, protecting central-bank independence. Cook denies intentional wrongdoing; the allegations remain disputed.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ pursued former Olympic canoeist Davey Hearn on a felony charge carrying up to 10 years over alleged Reflecting Pool vandalism, then dropped it after evidence pointed to flawed contractor work.

• 2025–2026 — Attacks on the free press, subpoenas against journalists, and constant attempts to punish anyone who exposes the truth.

• 2025–2026 — The administration restricted Associated Press access over terminology while escalating lawsuits, license threats, regulatory pressure and investigations against news organizations.

• 2025–2026 — Twenty-three states sued over ideological conditions attached to Title X family-planning funds involving contraception, gender, DEI and abstinence. The claims remain unadjudicated.

• 2025–2026 — Grocery bills, energy costs, health costs, rent, insurance, and basic survival all crushing average Americans.

• 2025–2026 — Family business conflicts, crypto wealth, foreign ties, watchdog attacks, prosecutor pressure, retaliation allegations and court defeats — MORE presidential power with LESS oversight.

• November 2025 — After Trump pressured authorities against James Comey and Letitia James, a judge dismissed their prosecutions because the Trump-backed prosecutor was unlawfully appointed. Dismissals were without prejudice.

• September 2025 — A federal court found Trump unlawfully fired inspectors general without complying with the Inspector General Act.

• June 2025 — Trump deployed the National Guard to Los Angeles over California’s objections during immigration-raid protests, escalating disputes over military power, federalism and domestic enforcement.

• May 2025 — The administration accepted a Qatar-provided Boeing 747-8 for possible Air Force One use, raising ethics, security and foreign-influence concerns. Qatar denied seeking influence.

• April 2025 — Trump imposed sweeping tariffs through emergency powers, bypassing ordinary congressional processes and creating uncertainty for prices, businesses and trade.

• April 2025 — The administration terminated about $2.2 billion in Harvard research funding; a federal judge later ruled the cuts unlawful.

• March 2025 — Senior national-security officials discussed an imminent Yemen strike on Signal and accidentally included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg, exposing operational timing and strike details.

• March 2025 — Trump issued orders targeting law firms tied to critics, opponents and disfavored clients; judges blocked multiple orders as retaliatory or unconstitutional threats to legal independence.

• March 2025 — Other major firms negotiated with the White House, pledging hundreds of millions in pro bono work on administration-approved causes rather than risk similar retaliation.

• March 2025 — The government wrongfully deported Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador despite legal protection, then was ordered to facilitate his return.

• March 2025 — Trump used the Alien Enemies Act against alleged gang members, triggering litigation over removals without a meaningful chance to contest government accusations.

• February 2025 — DOJ ordered prosecutors to drop Mayor Eric Adams’ corruption case while citing his help with immigration enforcement. Senior prosecutors resigned; Trump denied directing the dismissal.

• January 24, 2025 — Trump abruptly fired inspectors general across major agencies. A judge later found eight removals violated federal notice and justification requirements.

• January 20, 2025 — Trump tried to end birthright citizenship by executive order, triggering repeated court blocks over whether a president can rewrite the 14th Amendment without Congress or an amendment.

• The government is not functioning for the people. It is functioning for one man, one movement, and one corrupt machine determined to keep power at any cost.

• Corruption, cruelty, arrogance, and authoritarian overreach becoming the daily operating system of this administration.

• People are angry. People are exhausted. People are awake. And people have had enough.

This song is a result of MAGA Trump supporters and the Trump administration pushing the average American beyond their personal limits.

You are in the FA stage and the FO stage at the ballot box is coming.

1. Everywhere Jesus traveled, He was followed by crowds of people. Some wanted Him to feed them or to heal their diseases. Others wanted Him to give them political freedom from the Romans. Not very many of them thought about their spiritual needs. Only a few realized that their greatest need was for Salvation from sin, Satan, and death. What do you want from Jesus? Think about that during this lesson.

2. Jesus and His disciples were traveling to Jerusalem. On the way, they came to the village of Bethany, where His friends Mary, Martha, and Lazarus lived. Not long before this, Jesus had raised Lazarus from the dead. Jesus sent two of His disciples ahead into the village. He told them they would find a young donkey tied up there, and they were to untie it and bring it back to Him. The disciples found the donkey and untied it. Some people asked them what they were doing. The disciples said, as Jesus had told them, that the Lord needed it, so the people let them take the donkey. (Mk. 11:1-6)

3. Jesus sat on the young donkey and rode into Jerusalem. (Mk. 11:7-10) Many people came and shouted praises to Him as He rode. They praised Him as the One Who came in the name of the Lord to bring back the kingdom of David. They covered the road with garments and with tree branches. This was foretold by the prophet Zechariah 500 years before it happened.(Zec. 9:9, Mt. 21:4-5)

4. Unfortunately, most of the cheering crowd did not believe that Jesus would save them from sin, from Satan’s power, and from God’s punishment. They just wanted Jesus to give them freedom from the cruel power of the Romans.

5. The Jewish leaders were afraid that the Romans would be angry about people following Jesus as a new king. They thought the Romans might bring an army to destroy Israel. The Jewish leaders lived a comfortable life in cooperation with the Romans, and they didn’t want to lose their position. They began to make plans to kill Jesus, but they were afraid of the people, who had seen Him do many miracles, and considered Him to be a great prophet of God. (Mk. 14:1-2)

6. The Jewish leaders tried to find a way to catch Jesus when He was away from the crowds. One of the disciples, Judas Iscariot, came to them and offered to help them find and capture Jesus if they would give him money. They happily promised to pay him if he would betray Jesus. (Mk. 14:10-11)

Source: UK PULSE

 “#Captain #JimPhilippson did not want a desk. He wanted to be where his soldiers were — & on 11th June 2006 that decision took him into a firefight from which he would never return.” 🇬🇧

James Anthony Philippson, known to those around him as Jim, had already built a reputation as an officer who threw himself wholeheartedly into whatever challenge stood before him. Born in 1977 & from St Albans, he studied at Plymouth University before joining the Army in January 2001. After #Sandhurst, he was commissioned into the #RoyalArtillery. 🎖️

From the beginning, those who trained and served with him saw qualities that would define his short career: sharp intelligence, determination, physical stamina and an infectious enthusiasm. He was selected for 29 #Commando Regiment #RoyalArtillery, where he completed demanding Commando training and served for three years. His combination of professionalism, confidence and an easy sense of humour earned the respect of the soldiers and officers around him. His career took him to Iraq and on exercises in Norway, the United States and Cyprus.

Jim then wanted another challenge.

He left 29 Commando for 7 Parachute Regiment Royal Horse Artillery, spending six months in the Falkland Islands before joining the regiment in February 2006 as it prepared for Afghanistan. The Ministry of Defence later described him as a pivotal member of the team responsible for training and mentoring the Afghan National Army. His patience, technical ability and maturity made an impression on both British colleagues and the Afghan soldiers he worked alongside.

His commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel David Hammond, remembered an officer who combined confidence with humility — a man with commitment and drive, but also enthusiasm, wit and a willingness to learn. He described Jim as a gifted commander and a “rising star” who had a huge amount still to offer.

Then, in June, the reality of Helmand caught up with him.

On the evening of 11 June 2006, a British mobile patrol in the Sangin area came under attack from suspected Taliban fighters. Two soldiers were seriously wounded. A rapid reaction force was sent to help them, and Jim was among those who went forward. As the force moved to evacuate the wounded men, it came under fire itself. Jim was hit in the head and fatally wounded. He was 29.

He became the first British soldier killed in action in Helmand after British forces had taken responsibility for security in the province.

The circumstances surrounding his death would later become the subject of a highly critical inquest. Evidence was heard that troops had faced shortages of equipment, including night-vision equipment and certain weapons, & the Oxfordshire coroner recorded a verdict of unlawful killing. An Army Board of Inquiry subsequently reached a different conclusion, stating that lack of training or equipment had not directly contributed to Jim's death. That distinction is important, & his story should not be simplified beyond what the evidence establishes.

What remains beyond dispute is the impression Jim left on the people who knew him.

He was an #officer who loved soldiering, a #warrior who brought humour into difficult circumstances, a #commander whose men respected him. His father, Anthony, said Jim had loved the Army & had been killed doing exactly what he wanted to do — because, as his father put it, he could never have worked behind a desk.

On 11 June 2006, in the #Sangin valley, that commitment cost him his life.

A soldier. A son. A brother. A friend. A Royal Artillery officer whose career had barely begun to reach its full potential.
His grave carries four simple words that say what a longer tribute never could: “Soldier, Son, Brother, Friend.” 🕊️

• ASTS opened around $57.4 and initially fell to $56.50, putting the $55 concern back on the table. Buyers then stepped in aggressively, driving shares to $59.40 before the $59.10 close.

• That intraday reversal matters. ASTS recovered roughly 4.6% from the session low and finished near the high despite the broader market closing red.

• The broader tape offered little help. S&P 500 -0.3%, Nasdaq -0.1%, Dow -0.7%, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 4.75%.

• No major new AST SpaceMobile operational announcement appears to have driven Monday's rebound. The latest material company development remains the recently completed $1B convertible senior notes offering.

• I am leaving directional options flow out because I could not verify sufficiently reliable Aug. 31 flow data to characterize positioning as bullish or bearish.

Technical Takeaway:

Monday was constructive after Friday's 5.52% decline.

Buyers defended $56.50 and pushed ASTS back above $59, reducing the immediate threat of a break below $55.

But one green session does not reverse the recent downtrend.

Bulls now need to reclaim and hold $60, followed by $61.50 to $62. The $56.50 to $55 area remains the critical downside zone.

text:
BY: MICHAEL SMITH
Several years ago and because I recommend placing this book in the hands of every high school junior and senior in America, I wrote this review to help parents understand why doing that is necessary - and now that we are seeing the lack of awareness in our kids weaponized by collectivists, I thought I would post it here for all to read.
The God That Failed is a 1949 collection of six essays by Louis Fischer, André Gide, Arthur Koestler, Ignazio Silone, Stephen Spender, and Richard Wright, the common theme of the essays is the authors’ disillusionment with, and abandonment of, communism.

In the mold of C.S. Lewis’s idea that “No man knows how bad he is till he has tried very hard to be good”, Richard Crossman, the editor of “The God that Failed”, wrote:
“But no one who has not wrestled with Communism as a philosophy, and Communists as political opponents, can really understand the values of Western democracy. The Devil once lived in Heaven, and those who have not met him are unlikely to recognize an angel when they see one.”
It has been said that the impulse of the left is totalitarian. An honest review of the historical performance of the left indicates that statement is more than mere words because history has a way of settling arguments that ideology tries to keep alive.

In 1949, six former Communist believers published The God That Failed, a slim volume that landed like a quiet thunderclap. Arthur Koestler, Ignazio Silone, Richard Wright, André Gide, Louis Fischer, and Stephen Spender were not offering policy prescriptions. They were offering confessions—accounts of how a movement that promised justice, dignity, and equality had instead delivered coercion, conformity, and moral rot.

At the time, many dismissed the book as Cold War propaganda or the sour grapes of apostates.

Seventy-five years later, history has rendered its verdict.

They were right.

What these writers understood—long before the Berlin Wall fell or Soviet archives were opened—was that Communism fails not primarily as an economic system, but as a moral one. It demands ideological obedience over individual conscience. It elevates abstract collectives above real people. And it justifies cruelty in the language of progress.

They saw it firsthand. Koestler described how independent thought becomes heresy once a movement claims moral monopoly. Silone recognized that revolutionary politics replaces compassion with theory, turning workers into symbols rather than human beings. Wright discovered that even racial justice becomes transactional under Party discipline. Gide witnessed a society built on fear, surveillance, and forced cheerfulness. Fischer and Spender chronicled the quiet terror of dissent inside a system that treats doubt as betrayal.

What they diagnosed was not a temporary corruption of a noble idea. They identified something structural: when a political ideology claims total authority over truth, it inevitably suppresses freedom.

And history confirmed it.

The Soviet Union collapsed under the weight of its own lies. Mao’s China left tens of millions dead. Cambodia’s killing fields, Cuba’s prisons, North Korea’s hereditary tyranny, Venezuela’s economic implosion—each followed the same pattern. Grand promises. Centralized power. Crushed dissent. Human suffering.

These were not accidents. They were features.

Defenders of socialism still argue that “real communism has never been tried,” as though every failed experiment were merely a misunderstanding. But when the same outcomes recur across continents and cultures, we are no longer dealing with implementation errors. We are confronting design flaws.

The contributors to The God That Failed understood this early because they had lived inside the machinery. They saw how revolutionary movements begin by speaking the language of empathy and end by enforcing obedience. They watched moral certainty harden into authoritarian control. They learned that once ideology becomes sacred, people become expendable.

Their warning was not limited to Marxism. It was broader and more unsettling: any system that subordinates the individual to an abstract vision of the future will eventually justify atrocity.

That lesson feels painfully relevant today.

We live in an era of renewed ideological fervor—where dissent is policed, speech is regulated, and moral virtue is increasingly measured by conformity to approved narratives. Once again, we hear calls to subordinate liberty to collective outcomes. Once again, critics are told that resistance proves their moral deficiency. Once again, complex human problems are reduced to slogans.

The same psychology is at work.

What makes The God That Failed enduring is its insight into how good intentions become instruments of control. The authors were not cynics. They were idealists who learned—at personal cost—that utopian politics inevitably collide with human nature. You cannot engineer virtue. You cannot mandate equality of outcome without coercion. And you cannot abolish freedom in the name of justice without destroying both.

Capitalism is imperfect. Liberal democracy is messy. Markets produce inequality and cultural friction. But history shows that societies anchored in individual rights, voluntary exchange, and decentralized power generate prosperity—and prosperity creates space for moral choice. People can disagree without disappearing. They can fail without starving. They can dissent without imprisonment.

That is not trivial. That is civilization.

Many years ago, long time 60 Minutes commentator Andy Rooney opined:

“Communism got to be a terrible word here in the United States, but our attitude toward it may have been unfair. Communism got in with a bad crowd when it was young and never had a fair chance… The Communist ideas of creating a society in which everyone does his best for the good of everyone is appealing and fundamentally a more uplifting idea than capitalism. Communism’s only real weakness seems to be that it doesn’t work.”

The writers of The God That Failed did not claim to possess all answers. They simply refused to surrender their conscience to ideology. In doing so, they offered one of the most important lessons of the twentieth century: when politics becomes religion, freedom becomes heresy.

In our current political climate, at least half of America has succumbed to what Daniel Boorstin, the noted American historian, described when he wrote in 1962:

“We risk being the first people in history to have been able to make their illusions so vivid, so persuasive, so ‘realistic’ that they can live in them. We are the most illusioned people on earth. Yet we dare not become disillusioned, because our illusions are the very house in which we live; they are our news, our heroes, our adventure, our forms of art, our very experience.”

That “we” applies to the psychologically damaged and abused left, the children of the God that failed, and continues to fail every time it is tried.

History has proven them right.

The tragedy is not that they were correct.

The tragedy is how often we still need reminding.

text:
This is how Claude explains the situation;

Presale buyers paid $0.015 and $0.05 between October 2024 and March 2025, and only 20% of those tokens became unlockable around September 1, 2025, with the May 2026 governance vote placing the remainder behind a two-year cliff followed by two more years of vesting. That leaves their capital immobilized until roughly 2028 while the token trades near $0.058 — flat against the $0.05 round and about 87% below the $0.46 print on day one. Throughout that lockup, World Liberty is spending WLFI to buy distribution for USD1, a product whose reserve interest accrues to the issuer rather than to token holders: Bybit is running a 38 million WLFI pool through September 17, Binance ran a $13 million campaign from May 15 to June 12, MEXC put up 15 million tokens in April, and Aster's USD1 RWA Boost allocates 125 million WLFI from August 31 through December 31 out of a roughly $28 million pool. Each of those programs hands near-free tokens to short-horizon traders who can sell the same day, while the people who paid cash for the identical asset cannot. Governance offers little recourse, since the top four wallets control roughly 40% of voting power and some proposals have passed with more than 76% of the weight coming from ten addresses. The company's answer is that this spending grows USD1 adoption and that fee-funded buybacks and burns return value to holders — but individual buybacks have run in the low seven figures while the incentive programs distribute hundreds of millions of tokens, so the dilution is arriving considerably faster than the offset.

text:
A hung jury means the 12 jurors cannot reach the unanimous verdict Massachusetts law requires. It is neither a conviction nor an acquittal.

Immediate court process
The judge will first send the jury back with additional instructions (often a Tuey-Rodriguez charge) urging them to keep deliberating and re-examine their views. If they still report they are hopelessly deadlocked, the judge declares a mistrial on the charges they cannot resolve. If they have agreed on some counts but not others, the court can accept the completed verdicts and declare a mistrial only on the remaining ones.

What happens next
The charges remain pending. Double jeopardy does not apply because there was no final verdict.
The Plymouth County District Attorney decides whether to:Retry the case before a new jury (most common when the first trial produced strong evidence and a close split).
Offer a plea deal.
Dismiss the charges (with or without prejudice).

Lindsay Clancy would stay in custody at Tewksbury State Hospital while that decision is made. Release pending a possible second trial is considered unlikely.
A second trial would start from scratch: new jury selection, same evidence presented again. Prosecutors in similar high-profile Massachusetts cases (such as the first Karen Read trial) have chosen to retry. Legal observers covering the Clancy case have said they expect the same if the jury hangs.
As of August 31, 2026 the jury has been deliberating for several days with no verdict reported. A hung jury remains one of the possible outcomes given the complexity of the mental-health defense and the available verdict options (first-degree murder, second-degree murder, manslaughter, or not criminally responsible).

text:
We’ve Got Trouble: With a Capital T, and That Rhymes with P, and That Stands for Proposition | Yavapai County’s Growing Tax Layer Cake

Friends, we’ve got trouble.

Not necessarily with a capital “T,” and probably not because somebody installed a pool table in River City. But Yavapai County voters will find plenty of propositions on the November ballot asking them to consider how much government should collect—and what taxpayers should receive in return.

Taxes rarely arrive with a marching band. They usually show up a fraction of a cent at a time. A quarter-cent for jails. Half a cent for recreation. A temporary tax for pensions. A school override here, a bond there.

Each proposal gets its own sales pitch. But taxpayers pay the combined bill. So before the band starts playing, let’s look at how we got here.

Start with the Cities & Towns
Prescott’s Transaction Privilege Tax (TPT)—Arizona-speak for what most people call a sales tax—stood at 1% until 1996, when it doubled to 2%. In 2018, Prescott added a temporary 0.75% tax to attack its PSPRS public-safety pension debt. Give credit where due: that tax actually went away when its job was done.

The intermission didn’t last long. Voters later approved Prop 478, adding a 0.95% public-safety tax. Prescott’s municipal TPT now stands at 2.95%.

Other communities followed their own paths.

Prescott Valley gradually increased its municipal rate from 2% to 2.83% and now asks voters through Prop 493 for another half-cent to support an aquatics and recreation facility.

Cottonwood moved from 2% to 3.5% over several decades.

Then there’s Camp Verde. Its municipal TPT stood at 1% in 1988 and today stands at 3.65%—a 265% increase in the rate.

Apparently, pennies can reproduce when left unattended, even if they aren’t being minted anymore!

The Jail District?
The Yavapai County Jail District tax increased from 0.20% to 0.25% in 2003. Now Prop 497 asks voters to double it to 0.50% for 20 years.

Unlike Professor Harold Hill, the County does have something tangible to show voters: two detention facilities and more than 6,000 inmates passing through the jail system annually.

And taxpayers aren’t simply buying beds and bars. Jail expenses include security, food, transportation, medical and mental-health care, emergency hospitalization, substance-use services, Restoration to Competency and programs such as Reach Out.

The County projects annual Jail District expenses of roughly $41 million. Arizona law requires the County General Fund to contribute through a Maintenance of Effort payment, while existing revenues leave an additional projected funding gap. Federal grants and reimbursements help, but our research found that federal assistance represents only a small fraction of the overall expense.

And Then Come the Schools
Depending on where you live, the November ballot offers additional verses. Location matters.

Prescott Unified voters face Prop 405, a Maintenance and Operations (M&O) override, and Prop 406, a $20 million bond.

Humboldt Unified’s Prop 407 asks voters to authorize nearly $80 million in bonds for school facilities. HUSD says declining existing debt means the new bond is not expected to increase its overall current tax rate.

Cottonwood-Oak Creek voters face Prop 409, another school bond proposal.

A Prescott Valley voter within HUSD, for example, could vote on the county jail tax, Prescott Valley’s recreation tax and the school bond on the same ballot.

One proposition may sound like a piccolo. Put enough of them together and you’ve got 76 trombones.

Not every tax increase needs 76 trombones—or even 76 voters!
In 2024, the Yavapai College District Governing Board approved a 3.4% primary property-tax increase—about $1.87 million in additional revenue—without a countywide voter referendum. Arizona law allows community college boards to adjust their property-tax levies within statutory limits, using public notice, budget hearings and Truth in Taxation requirements rather than requiring voter approval for every increase.

Rate vs. Levy — Watch the Other Hand
Property taxes introduce another wrinkle. Politicians sometimes proudly announce that they held the property-tax rate flat or even lowered it. That doesn’t necessarily mean government collected the same amount of money.

Yavapai County’s primary property-tax rate has actually declined substantially over the long term—from roughly $2.60 per $100 of assessed value in the early 1990s to $1.6443 today. Meanwhile, property values grew. For FY2026, the County maintained the $1.6443 primary rate while its Truth in Taxation calculation projected approximately a 3.4% increase in the primary levy on existing property, excluding new construction.

No magic trick is required. The rate determines the size of the slice, but rising property values make the pie bigger. Government can therefore collect more property-tax revenue without technically “raising the tax rate.” When someone tells you the rate didn’t increase, ask another question: How much did the levy increase?

Phoenix and Washington Join the Band
Local government doesn’t perform solo. Arizona voters temporarily increased the state sales tax by a full percentage point in 2010. Importantly, that tax expired in 2013 as promised.

Federal taxpayers have absorbed increases too. The Affordable Care Act imposed an Additional Medicare Tax on higher-income taxpayers beginning in 2013, while more recent federal legislation imposed new taxes on certain large corporations and corporate stock repurchases.

Not every tax affects every Yavapai household equally. But your wallet doesn’t maintain separate accounts labeled Washington, Phoenix, Yavapai County, City Hall and School District. It just knows the money left.

Before You Vote, Do the Math
Professor Hill knew something about salesmanship: don’t let the audience spend too much time thinking about the transaction. Voters should do exactly the opposite.

Ask what each tax funds. Ask how much it will raise. Ask how long it lasts. Ask whether another tax is expiring. Ask whether the proposal replaces existing revenue or simply stacks another layer on top. And ask what government will cut—or fund differently—if voters say no.

Most importantly, don’t examine each proposition in isolation. A quarter-cent sounds tiny. Half a cent sounds tiny. A few dollars per month sounds tiny. Then add them together.

Because governments rarely raise your taxes all at once. They prefer installments—with a brass band playing in the background.

As always, this is not tax advice. Check the official prop text or a qualified tax professional for your specific situation.

text:
The H-1B program was sold as a temporary fix for scarce skills. For 36 years it has functioned as a settlement track: a job, a spouse who can work, public schools, a citizen child born here, and a later claim on family immigration. 

That package is life-altering for the household that receives it. It is also how a slice of the American middle class in technical work was steadily priced out of its own labor market; and out of the retirement those degrees were supposed to buy.

A visa that pays thousands below a comparable American is not a rounding error. Department of Labor files keep certifying large shares of these jobs at Level I and II wages; the bottom third of the scale, not the scarce-genius premium. 

Then the spouse, once an I-140 is approved, can take an open work permit in any occupation. That is not one guest worker. That is a two-earner household planted in the U.S. market while the original American is told to train the replacement or take the severance.

The Americans on the other side of that bargain did not arrive empty-handed. They borrowed for the degrees employers demanded. They are still carrying that debt when the layoff notice comes. Six to eight months between jobs is not a sabbatical. It is drained savings, paused 401(k) contributions, interest still compounding on student loans, and a résumé gap that makes the next offer weaker. Repeat that cycle across a career and “dignified retirement” stops being a plan and becomes a rumor.

The replacement ritual is not folklore. Disney, Southern California Edison, and other employers put U.S. IT staff through “knowledge transfer” as the price of a package. Off the visa, the same firms built a second workforce in India: more than two million people in global capability centers and more than $100 billion a year in software exports back to the United States. Remittances in the mid-thirties of billions are only the personal slice. The corporate slice is larger.

Children of temporary workers attend public school at local per-pupil cost. Children born here are citizens. At 21 they can sponsor parents. That is how a six-year specialty visa becomes a multi-generation foothold. Immediate family is real. Unlimited cousins are not. The front-loaded household—worker, working spouse, citizen kids, later parents, is enough to change the meaning of “temporary.”

Employment in technical occupations still grew. Firm profits grew. Indian households gained jobs, skills, and dollars. The American who financed a STEM credential, trained a cheaper replacement, and spent the next decade repairing a broken earnings path did not share those gains. 

Over 36 years the losses compound: missed peak-earning years, thinner retirement accounts, debt that outlives the job. Flat real STEM pay across long stretches after 2008 is what a surplus of substitutable labor looks like, not a shortage.

We should stop calling it a guest-worker program. It is a settlement track with a labor-cost discount attached. The winners get a new life. Too many of the displaced Americans stuck with massive student loan debt, working gig economy way past dignified retirement age.
