text:
ARSENAL PLAYER RATINGS vs ASTON VILLA

David Raya – 6/10
Another clean sheet for Raya in the Premier League. Had very little to do, with no saves required, but looked sharp when coming off his line and dealt well with crosses.

Ben White – 5/10
Had some issues with his passing and struggled when Maatsen ran at him. Was not at his best alongside Saka and Ødegaard and needed Rice’s support defensively.

Cristhian Mosquera – 8/10
Excellent performance. His superb pass through the lines found Eze and played a major role in creating Arsenal’s goal. Defensively composed overall, although he was forced off late after appearing to pick up a knock.

Gabriel – 7/10
Should have done better with a headed chance from a corner. Had one difficult moment against Jackson but was otherwise aggressive, strong and committed in the box.

Riccardo Calafiori – 8/10
Produced a brilliant stretch to keep the move alive and set up Saka for the goal. Had some issues with balls played in behind early on but offered plenty of unpredictability going forward.

Declan Rice – 8/10
Excellent set-piece deliveries and covered huge ground in midfield. Played an important role in stopping Villa’s counter-attacks and made more recoveries than anyone else.

Myles Lewis-Skelly – 6/10
Used his strength well and won several fouls during a difficult first half. Came close with a deflected effort but was otherwise a solid presence.

Bukayo Saka – 7/10
Was denied a penalty after VAR confirmed the foul occurred just outside the box. Stayed dangerous and made sure he was in the right position to finish Arsenal’s goal. Won six fouls during the game.

Martin Ødegaard – 5/10
Nearly opened the scoring with a free-kick that went just wide. Otherwise, a quiet evening for the captain, who struggled to have a major influence against Villa’s organised defence.

Christos Tzolis – 4/10
A difficult outing after some promising recent performances. Heavy touches and an early booking made his evening harder, with Villa putting pressure on him. Substituted at half-time.

Kai Havertz – 5/10
Had very little involvement in the first half but became more involved after the break. Worked hard but was caught offside several times and missed two chances, although both were eventually ruled out.

Substitutes

Eberechi Eze – 7/10
Made an immediate impact after coming on. His quality and creativity helped change the game, including a brilliant pass to Calafiori for the winning goal.

Bruno Guimarães – 7/10
Made a positive impact after coming on, progressing the ball well and finding Havertz and Saka with forward passes. Looked dangerous in possession and was unlucky not to win a late penalty.

Mikel Merino – 7/10
Added energy and helped Arsenal manage the game in the final stages. Comfortable in possession and effective at drawing fouls.

Ezri Konsa – 6/10
Received a warm welcome from the Villa supporters before helping Arsenal see out the victory.

Martin Zubimendi – N/A
Came on late and did not have enough time to be fairly rated. #AFC

text:
RoadDog Stores | Dayton RoadDog 👇👇

Dayton convenience store launches new kitchen to offer one-stop shopping, combat food desert

*A Dayton convenience store is now offering new food items, saying they want to create a one-stop shopping experience for customers in areas that may be considered food deserts.

Road Dog Convenience Store has been around since 2020, but the Roadies Grub ‘N Go kitchen is brand new.

Kitchen manager Devin Myers told News Center 7’s Taylor Robertson that they’ve been working on getting this ready for the past eight months.

Myers added that the goal was to give customers a quick stop to grab a bite to eat since there aren’t places like that nearby.

One-stop shop convenience stores and fuel stations are becoming increasingly popular across the country, according to the National Association of Convenience Stores (NACS).

On the stretch of James H. McGee Blvd. Roadie’s sits on, they are the only true gas station and convenience store with an integrated kitchen concept.

Duncan Oil Company bought this location six years ago. They said on social media that their store helps alleviate a food desert in the area. Down the hall, inside the convenience store, people can find groceries like milk, bread, and pantry staples.

“We’re one of the few places that you can come in, get your gas, get everything else,” Myers said.

NACS said more and more people want a place where they can grab everything they need in one trip. It’s why we’re seeing many chains like Sheetz, Wawa, and Quiktrips popping up around the Miami Valley.

Roadie’s has breakfast, lunch, and dinner options. Myers said their pricing is similar to what you’d pay at popular fast food chains.

“I think we’re competitive, I’ll say that,” Myers added.

text:
🇺🇸🇷🇺 US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has met Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in North Carolina.

US reporting says Bessent used the meeting to press President Trump’s 28-point plan for ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.

That is notable for two reasons.

First, Siluanov is not a conventional diplomatic interlocutor.

He represents the financial machinery of the Russian state.

So a discussion involving the US Treasury Secretary inevitably raises questions about the economic component of any proposed settlement:

▪️ sanctions relief
▪️ frozen Russian assets
▪️ access to international finance
▪️ energy restrictions
▪️ the conditions attached to any normalization

Second, the meeting shows how rapidly Washington is reopening high-level channels with Moscow.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe has already been in Moscow.

Witkoff and Kushner are preparing further engagement with Ukraine.

Now Bessent is talking directly with Russia’s finance minister.

The critical issue is therefore not whether negotiations are taking place.

It is what Russia is being offered, what Russia is being required to concede — and whether Ukraine is being fully included in decisions about its own future.

Economic leverage is one of the West’s strongest cards.

It should not be surrendered cheaply.

1937: Peel Commission Partition Plan
• Proposed by: The British Government 
• The Offer: Divide the British Mandate into a small Jewish state (20% of the land), a larger Arab state merged with Transjordan, and a British-controlled enclave around Jerusalem. 
• Rejected by: The Arab leadership completely, while the Jewish leadership accepted the concept of partition but continued to negotiate boundaries. 

1947: UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181)
• Proposed by: The United Nations General Assembly
• The Offer: Partition the British Mandate into independent Jewish and Arab states, while placing Jerusalem under international governance.
• Rejected by: The Arab leadership and surrounding Arab nations, while the Jewish Agency accepted it.

2000: Camp David Summit & The Clinton Parameters
• Proposed by: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak 
• The Offer: Establish an independent, demilitarized Palestinian state encompassing the Gaza Strip and 94% to 96% of the West Bank (with land swaps), divide sovereignty in Jerusalem to create a Palestinian capital in East Jerusalem, and restrict the refugee right of return.
• Rejected by: Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat, citing compromised sovereignty, territorial fragmentation, and inadequate terms for Jerusalem and refugees.

2008: The Olmert Offer
• Proposed by: Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert
• The Offer: Grant Palestinians a state on territory equivalent to 99.5% of the West Bank through territorial concessions and a 5.8% land swap, alongside international administration of Jerusalem's holy sites.
• • Relinquishing Israeli sovereignty over the Temple Mount and the entire Old City of Jerusalem to an international committee.
• • Withdrawing completely from the strategically vital Jordan Valley.
• • Uprooting tens of thousands of Jewish settlers by withdrawing from approximately 94% of the West Bank. 
• Rejected by: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, who refused to sign on the spot and requested a copy of the map to study with experts, which Israeli Prime Minister Olmert denied out of fear that a leak revealing how much territory Israel was giving away would cause a political revolt.

(With the remembrance of the Sethian path, the path of Melchizedec, Solomon, David and Yehoshua)

“Create in me a clean heart, O G-d, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” —Psalm 51:10

David’s cry rises from the depths of the Immovable Race. He does not plead with the rulers of this age, nor with Yaldabaoth who fashioned the prison of form. He turns instead toward the Invisible Spirit, the ineffable Father, the Source without whom there would be nothing, and asks for a new creation.

In the Sethian knowing, the heart is the dwelling-place of the divine spark, the portion of light that descended from the Pleroma and was hidden within the clay. When the heart becomes defiled, it is not the spark that has failed; it is the dust of the archons, the counterfeit spirit, and the forgetfulness imposed by the rulers that have settled upon it.“Create in me a clean heart” is the prayer of one who has heard the Call.

It is the request that the Autogenes, (the self birth of reawaking separating illusion from Holy), the Self-Begotten, the pure light who came forth from Barbelo (the first entity to arise from G-d), would once again breathe into the vessel. Not a mere washing of the old heart, but a true creation: the restoration of the heart as it was known in the aeons before the fall into matter. A heart that remembers it belongs to the Seed of Seth, the generation that cannot be moved.

And “renew a steadfast spirit within me” is the plea for the return of the true pneuma, the spirit which stands firm in the face of the archons, unshaken by their chaos. The spirit carried with Yehoshua, the embodiment of the Coming One, awakened in those who have ears to hear. The spirit which turns from the east of exile and faces once more toward the luminous place of the Four Luminaries.

The further the soul has wandered under the dominion of the counterfeit powers, the more complete the re-creation must be. Yet the mercy of the Invisible Spirit is this: He does not patch the broken vessel. Through the descent of the true light, He creates again. He rekindles the spark until the heart becomes a pure lamp of the Pleroma, and the spirit stands steadfast, rooted in the knowledge that it is not a child of the demiurge, but of the Father who is beyond all names.

This is the true metanoia (lifting life change through the reawakened memory of origin). Not the repentance of fear under the law of the archons, but the turning of the heart back toward its origin in the Fullness. The re-creation of the divine image so that the soul may say once more: I am of the Immovable Race. I am of the Seed that the Father planted before the foundation of this world.

Create in me that clean heart, O Invisible Spirit. Renew in me the steadfast pneuma (divine creative force within each of us, which knows its home in the Pleroma.

Let us each look inward toward the reawakening Light. May we gain the wisdom of Yehoshua which he “Shared in the Love”,

text:
CALUMET

Calumet received full exemptions for Calumet Montana Refining and Calumet Shreveport Refining. The company’s conventional refining operations carry meaningful RIN liabilities relative to consolidated liquidity and capital structure. As of Mar. 31, 2026, Calumet reported an RIN obligation of approximately $316.7 million, up from approximately $169.3 million at year-end 2025. The company can satisfy the obligation through blending, purchases or successful SRE petitions. Full grants should therefore reduce a material liability and improve conventional-refining cash economics, although the filing does not isolate the exact portion attributable to the 2025 obligations of the 2 awarded entities. 

Prior SRE decisions reduced Calumet’s accrued RIN exposure from approximately 396 million RINs to approximately 89 million, demonstrating that exemptions have historically been a major driver of reported liabilities and earnings. The current full awards can again create a significant reversal, but the exact value will depend on whether the company holds current, saleable RINs or older credits with limited market utility. 

Calumet has an important 2-sided exposure through Montana Renewables. Lower prompt D4 prices reduce renewable diesel credit revenue and feedstock purchasing capacity, partially offsetting the conventional-refining benefit. The renewable segment’s economics also depend on low-carbon credits, clean-fuel tax incentives, feedstock carbon intensity and operational performance, so the D4 effect will not pass through 1-for-1. The consolidated result is likely positive in the near term because the exemption directly reduces a large accrued liability, but the net benefit should be evaluated after marking Montana Renewables’ RIN exposure. 

HF SINCLAIR

HF Sinclair received the most heterogeneous public-company outcome. Tulsa East received a full exemption. Casper and Parco received 50 percent exemptions. Woods Cross was denied, and Artesia was ruled ineligible. This represents 2.0 full-equivalent awards across 5 petitions, or 40 percent by petition count. The economic ratio could be higher or lower because the sites differ materially in size and production. 

The company operates approximately 678,000 barrels per day of refining capacity across 7 refineries and also owns renewable diesel assets. The favorable Tulsa, Casper and Parco outcomes reduce conventional-refining RIN expense. The Woods Cross denial and Artesia ineligibility preserve meaningful liabilities at those sites. Lower D4 prices reduce earnings from the renewable diesel segment, creating an additional offset. 

HF Sinclair should therefore experience a positive but less concentrated impact than Delek, Par Pacific or CVR. The mixed disposition also increases legal optionality: the company may challenge the denial, ineligibility determination or 50 percent grants while retaining the benefit of the awarded relief. Any incremental legal success would add prompt benefit, while the proposed 2026 and 2027 reallocation would raise obligations across the broader refining system.

LARGE-CAP AND PRIVATE REFINERY IMPLICATIONS

Chevron Salt Lake received a full exemption, while Marathon Mandan and Phillips 66 Montana received partial exemptions. These are positive site-level outcomes but are likely to be less material at the consolidated-company level because the parent groups own much larger refining, marketing and renewable fuel portfolios. The near-term benefit can also be offset by higher future obligations at non-exempt sites and by weaker renewable fuel margins.

Cooperative and privately held recipients such as CHS Laurel, Countrymark, Hunt, Kern, Silver Eagle and several regional refinery entities may experience a proportionally larger liquidity and survival benefit. Small, inland refineries often have limited access to proprietary blending, retail and export channels, making RIN purchases a larger working-capital burden. Relief can support maintenance spending, throughput and continued operation. The resulting competitive effect can pressure nearby non-exempt refiners even where no public equity directly captures the recipient’s benefit.

The relative losers are non-exempt obligated parties with structural RIN deficits and limited downstream integration. Their prompt competitive position deteriorates against exempt neighbors, while the proposed reallocation raises their 2026 and 2027 percentage standards. Renewable diesel and biodiesel producers are also prompt losers through lower D4 value, although diversified refiners with renewable fuel assets can experience offsetting effects across segments.

LEGAL AND REGULATORY RISK

The exemption decisions and the reallocation proposal have different legal status. EPA characterizes the individual petition adjudications as immediately effective agency actions rather than a new generally applicable rule. The 770 million reallocation requires notice-and-comment rulemaking and is not final. The exemption benefit should therefore be recognized with greater confidence than the future offset.

EPA states that the action is nationally applicable and that challenges are generally subject to review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit within 60 days after Federal Register publication. Litigation can arise from several directions. Biofuel producers and agricultural groups can challenge the breadth of full and partial exemptions. Refiners can challenge denials, ineligibility determinations and the 50 percent methodology. Non-exempt obligated parties can challenge the legality, timing or burden of additional reallocation. 

Potential challenges to reallocation include inadequate lead time, unreasonable reliance on the RIN bank, inconsistency with statutory volume-setting factors, deficient economic analysis and insufficient explanation of why 100 percent of the forecast error should be added after the final 2026 and 2027 standards were issued. These are litigation risks rather than conclusions regarding the merits. EPA strengthened its position by making the existing reallocation provisions severable from the underlying annual standards, reducing the probability that a successful challenge to the adjustment invalidates the entire RVO rule. 

The confidential refinery appendices create additional uncertainty. Outside investors cannot independently reconstruct the DOE matrix, refinery-specific pass-through, local market constraints or financial-hardship findings. The lack of transparent volume and economic data makes it difficult to estimate judicial outcomes and company-specific benefits. It also increases the informational advantage of petitioners and counterparties with direct access to compliance positions.

The Department of Energy methodology review is a major medium-term policy risk. A revised framework could change how RIN pass-through, local renewable fuel acceptance, diesel yield, blending capability, net RIN cost and refinery profitability are weighted. A stricter methodology would reduce future grants and support deferred RIN values. A more accommodative methodology would institutionalize recurring exemptions and weaken confidence that reallocation produces durable physical demand.

SCENARIO FRAMEWORK

BASE CASE

The exemption decision remains effective, most successful refiners recognize material 2025 liability reversals, and prompt 2025 D6 remains under pressure. EPA proposes substantially all 770 million RINs by the end of Oct. 2026 and distributes the increment across 2026 and 2027, but finalization extends beyond the proposal date. The carryover bank absorbs part of the change, preventing an immediate 1-for-1 increase in renewable fuel production. Deferred D4 and D6 recover relative to 2025 as the market prices eventual reallocation. Delek and Par Pacific produce the largest positive earnings revisions, followed by CVR, while Calumet and HF Sinclair show more pronounced renewable-fuel offsets.

REFINER-UPSIDE AND BIOFUEL-DOWNSIDE SCENARIO

The exemption decisions survive, but reallocation is delayed, reduced or successfully challenged. The 2025 surplus rolls into 2026 through the carryover bank, prompt weakness extends into nearby vintages and renewable diesel margins compress. UCO, tallow and vegetable-oil bids weaken as producers reduce feedstock purchasing capacity. Full-exemption refiners retain a large windfall without an equivalent near-term industry offset. Delek, Par Pacific and CVR outperform RIN-long renewable fuel producers and non-exempt merchant refiners.

BIOFUEL-UPSIDE AND DEFERRED-RIN-TIGHTENING SCENARIO

EPA finalizes the entire 770 million addition, front-loads a material portion into 2026 and assigns a substantial component to biomass-based diesel or advanced renewable fuel. The RIN bank tightens faster than expected, deferred D4 strengthens and renewable diesel feedstock demand remains robust. Prompt 2025 RINs can remain weak, but 2026 and 2027 backwardation or scarcity develops. UCO and other low-carbon feedstocks regain pricing power. Refiners retain the 2025 accounting benefit but face a faster future cost offset.

LITIGATION-DISRUPTION SCENARIO

A court grants interim relief affecting either the exemption adjudications or the reallocation. RIN prices gap because the market must reprice which obligations remain valid, whether returned RINs can be used and how the compliance deadline applies. Company accounting becomes more conservative, and gains may be delayed until legal resolution. This scenario has lower fundamental visibility but high trading significance because RIN liquidity is limited and positions can be concentrated.

KEY CATALYSTS AND MONITORING FRAMEWORK

Federal Register publication will establish the formal judicial-review window. The reallocation proposal expected by the end of Oct. 2026 will determine the year split, D-code allocation, percentage-standard changes, bank assumptions and legal rationale. These details are more important for forward RIN values than the 770 million aggregate headline.

The Oct. 1 compliance date will reveal how much 2025 inventory is retired, carried forward or released. Environmental Protection Agency Moderated Transaction System activity, RIN-bank estimates and vintage spreads should be monitored for evidence that excess supply is being sold or retained. A muted increase in traded volume accompanied by weak prices would imply avoidance of future demand rather than large physical liquidation.

Q3 and Q4 company reporting should clarify the accounting treatment at Delek, Par Pacific, CVR, Calumet and HF Sinclair. Key disclosures include RVO-liability reversals, RIN inventory valuation, cash proceeds from sales, returned-vintage usability, tax treatment and management assumptions for future SREs. Adjusted earnings should be reconciled carefully to GAAP because several refiners already exclude or normalize assumed exemption benefits.

The most informative market indicators are the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 D6 spreads, the D4-D6 spread, current-versus-prior-vintage basis, UCO and soybean-oil feedstock differentials, renewable diesel utilization, RIN-generation rates and estimated bank size. A widening D4-D6 spread alongside weak outright D4 would confirm that conventional RIN supply is loosening faster than biomass-based diesel balances. A simultaneous collapse in D4 and UCO values would indicate a more severe renewable diesel margin adjustment.

Court filings, stay requests, Department of Energy methodology updates and EPA-Commodity Futures Trading Commission enforcement communications are material event risks. Regulatory statements concerning nonpublic petition information can move prices independently of physical supply-demand fundamentals.

PORTFOLIO CONCLUSION

The decision creates a high-confidence transfer of value toward successful 2025 petitioners and a lower-confidence future transfer back toward renewable fuel producers and non-exempt obligated parties. Gross 2025 relief is final and immediately actionable. The 770 million RIN reallocation remains proposed, with unresolved timing, category composition and judicial durability. That asymmetry supports near-term exempt-refiner earnings while preserving a deferred policy premium in 2026 and 2027 RINs.

Delek has the cleanest breadth of benefit because all 4 refining entities received full exemptions and the company’s adjusted reporting had assumed only 50 percent relief. Par Pacific has exceptionally high consolidated sensitivity because approximately 75.2 percent of mainland capacity received full-equivalent relief on a capacity-weighted basis and prior SRE recognition produced more than $200 million of adjusted EBITDA. CVR offers concentrated upside through Wynnewood and has a reduced renewable diesel offset. Calumet benefits through lower conventional-refining liabilities but must be evaluated net of Montana Renewables. HF Sinclair benefits on balance but has the most complex mix of grants, denials and renewable fuel exposure.

The strongest relative equity configuration is exposure to full-grant refiners against companies structurally dependent on prompt D4 values or burdened by net RIN deficits without meaningful exemption relief. The strongest RIN configuration is prompt 2025 D6 weakness relative to deferred 2026 and 2027 exposure, conditional on reallocation progress. D4 should be treated as absolutely exposed but relatively more resilient than D6 because of nested compliance value and binding biomass-based diesel requirements.

The principal analytical error would be capitalizing 1.76 billion RINs at spot and treating the result as permanent industry earnings. The realized value will be reduced by pass-through, prior purchases, hedges, inventory vintages, accounting conventions and future reallocation. The 2nd principal error would be treating the 770 million proposal as finalized demand. Until year allocation, category allocation and legal implementation are known, the proposal is a contingent tightening mechanism rather than a completed reversal of the 2025 supply shock.

The net investment conclusion is positive for selected exempt refiners, negative for prompt RINs and renewable fuel margins, negative for prompt UCO purchasing power, and conditionally positive for deferred RINs and feedstocks. The highest near-term earnings visibility lies in refinery-level liability reversals. The greatest unresolved market risk lies in whether the 770 million forecast error is converted into timely, category-specific and legally durable 2026 and 2027 demand.

text:
@Scavino47 @DanScavino @WhiteHouse @SecremtaryBurgum 
Executive Submission to the President of the United States
The East Potomac Presidential Championship Hains Point Peninsula • East Potomac Park • Washington, D.C. Fazio Design Championship Routing • National Public Access Mandate • John Deere Agronomic Standard
Prepared for The Honorable @realDonaldTrump  @POTUS
Mr. President,
You walked that peninsula on a Sunday morning in late June with Secretary Burgum, Tom Fazio, and Gavin Fazio. You saw the dead grass, the unplayable greens, the failing seawall, the neglected sprinklers, and the site that sits in the shadow of the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. You said then what the country needed to hear: this location can become one of the greatest golf courses anywhere in the world, and it will still belong to the public.
This document is the civil, agronomic, spectator, security, and fleet plan that makes that statement real. It is written in the language of championship golf architecture, USGA specification turf science, marine and geotechnical engineering, and the John Deere precision equipment that actually keeps a course of this caliber alive through mid-Atlantic summers, winter frost, and tournament weeks. It is offered as the operating blueprint for the work you directed to begin.
The mandate is dual and non-negotiable. When the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, or the Ryder Cup is in town, East Potomac must present as a major-championship venue with the length, firmness, drainage, hospitality infrastructure, broadcast power, and security architecture those events require. Every other week of the year it must remain a municipal course: open, welcoming, heavily discounted for District, Maryland, and Virginia residents, and fully usable by juniors, seniors, first-time players, and everyday citizens. That is the Bethpage Black / Torrey Pines model executed on the most visible piece of federal parkland in the United States.
What follows is the master development plan to deliver both.

MASTER PROJECT OBJECTIVE AND NATIONAL STAGING PROFILE
The East Potomac Golf Links modernization is a federal-and-private capital undertaking to transform the historic 120-plus-acre Hains Point peninsula into a PGA-caliber, Fazio-routed championship venue capable of hosting the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and other premier events, while locking in a permanent public-access covenant. The peninsula is low-lying, flood-prone, built on historic fill, and bounded by a deteriorating seawall. Those are not reasons to abandon the site. They are the engineering problems that, once solved, produce the most dramatic waterfront championship course in America.
The finished product will be a par-72 layout stretching to championship length in the 7,600-yard range from the back tees, with multiple forward tees so the same routing remains playable and enjoyable for the public. A short course and practice facility will sit in the northern sector so juniors and recreational players are never crowded off the property. The outer perimeter multi-use track stays. Hains Point remains a public park. The golf operation and the civic operation share the land instead of fighting over it.
Tom Fazio’s routing is the architectural spine. Everything else—earthwork, marine armor, drainage, turfgrass matrix, irrigation, SubAir, hospitality pads, security envelope, and the John Deere fleet—exists to make that routing playable in July humidity, January frost, and a 100-year storm.

text:
A tender moment at St. Elizabeth Parish in Tecumseh, Michigan, is touching viewers far beyond the church walls after a video that now has over a million views on Instagram showed newly ordained Diocese of Lansing priest Fr. Joshua Bauer honoring the two people who first nurtured his call to the priesthood: his parents, Kim and Eric.
During his first Mass at his home parish, Fr. Bauer presented his mother with a manutergium—the cloth used to wipe the sacred chrism from the new priest’s hands after the bishop anointed them at ordination. Then, turning to his father, he gave him the stole he wore while hearing his first Confession.
The memorable exchange reflects a Catholic tradition that recognizes the profound role parents can play in a priest’s vocation.
“Mom and Dad, I can’t thank you enough,” Fr. Bauer said in the viral video.
Addressing his mother, he explained the significance of the cloth in his hands.
“It’s tradition that when a priest is ordained, the manutergium [goes] to his mom,” he said. “It’s the cloth which soaked up all the sacred chrism the bishop poured on my hands when I was ordained.”
Holding out the cloth, Fr. Bauer told his mother why the tradition carries such emotional and spiritual weight.
“This is for you, that when you die, it be buried with you,” he said. “And that, when you stand before God, you can show Him that you offered Him your son as a priest.”
Then Fr. Bauer turned to his father.

text:
Another month has come to an end. It was a busy August! Here is my synopsis of the first two thirds of the season. 

Free golf announced in the recap, so read it all!

Approximate steps: 1.9 million 

Approximate cals burned: 294,000

Hot dogs eaten: 27

Brats eaten: 5

Hottest temp: Heat index of 106 

Coldest temp: 31 degrees (actual)

Highest wind: 55mph

Player states represented: MI, OH, PA, NY, NJ, MA, WI, MN, IA, VA, SC, NC, GA, FL, IL, IN, CA, WA, MO, TN, OK, KY, AL, AZ, UT, CO, MD, CONN, NH, TX, NV, MT

Countries represented: USA, Canada, S. Korea, Japan, England, Ukraine

Oldest player: 81

Youngest player: 16

Favorite bags: Ping Hoofer Lite, Ping Moonlander, Titleist Players 4

Least favorite bags: Ghost, Ogio, Anything with 14 slots

Most balls in bag: 70 (he took nearly 40 out at my request - we lost 4)

Least balls in bag: 4 

Simple Pleasure: Continuous putting instead of marking 3 footers

Pet Peeve: Big groups of dudes that have multiple tee times and have no interest in telling us which players are in which foursome while at the bag drop

Favorite Kind of Loops: Father/Son loops on the Straits, One balls (very rare)

Least Favorite Kind of Loops: Forecaddie for high handicappers, Grinding Ryder Cups

Joyous Discovery: Peach Course Record electrolyte drink 

Longest Day on Property: 14 hours 😩 Includes wait time between loops and 6 hour shotgun in second loop. As a bonus, my car went to the junkyard in the sky on the way home. 

Weather Struggles: Two days of dense fog with near zero visibility. One of the loops had players with reasonable scoring expectations in the conditions. The other loop I questioned how much longer I can caddie 😜😂

College football teams I'm more likely to root for this season solely based on golfers who went there: Iowa State, Colorado, Alabama, Tennessee, Indiana

College football teams I'm more likely to root against solely based on golfers who went there: Duke, Notre Dame, Florida State 

Signs a tip may be good: Players care about bag weight, play ready golf, offer a Gatorade at the turn, don't gripe

Signs a tip may be disappointing: Players late to starter table, play in bad weather that others quit in, wear matching shirts, blow a putt past hole and say it didn't break

(No, I cannot tell you what to tip - sorry for leading you to water and not letting you drink)

Favorite qualities in a golfer: Emotional maturity, realistic expectations, humility, good pace of play

Birdies on hole 18: 1 

Hole in ones: 0 (though I did see two this month on parallel holes) 

Most fun shot: Dude got up and down from huge bunker on 6th hole (only fourth time I've seen)

Favorite hole to caddie: #13 on the Straits, especially if I have a big hitter that tries to go for the green 

Least favorite hole to caddie: #8 on Straits (tricky tee shot that takes a while for a lot of players to process instructions for)

Thrown clubs: 4 (a guy in August launched his 25 yards - much further than his ball went)

F bombs: More than the number of stars in the sky

Highest score: A corporate loop where there had to have been a combined 600 shots, but I'm guessing closer to 700

Lowest score: 71 from 6700 yards

Amount of money I've given/raised/committed for Sober House: $4300, 2 couches, and 2 E-Bikes (couldn't do it without you)

Free golf winner for reaching 25k followers: @MYoung024 

Free golf winner for 100 orders on my website: @KSmithWooster 

Biggest thrill: Meeting a bunch of you

Thankful: For good health, provision for my family, new friendships, caddie brothers, beauty of the course, the joy of the Next Shot!

I invite you to grab a book or other item from my website. I give away a free round for two at the Straits for every 100 orders. All additional proceeds support the Sober House where I work when Im not on the course. I'm adopting the goal of raising money toward new televisions, a new washer and dryer, and an air fryer for the house. https://t.co/lDyfqvAP3b 

Rooting for you, friends!

text:
THE COLLECTIVE ACTION PROBLEM – WHY WESTERN COMPANIES COULDN'T STOP

Small businesses faced a brutal choice: manufacture overseas or be undercut by competitors who did . Tooling costs in China are 10-50% of North American costs . Circuit board assembly costs are at least $10 USD lower per board in China . As one manufacturer put it: "As long as overseas manufacturing offers an advantage, some will take it, and the rest are forced to follow just to stay alive" . Patriotism doesn't pay the bills.

THE WEST IS NOW TRYING TO UNDO WHAT IT BUILT

Brussels has finally admitted that Europe's "de-risking" narrative has failed. Dependency on China in critical minerals and advanced tech has deepened since COVID . The EU's ReSourceEU blueprint now introduces hard de-risking quotas: 30-50% by 2029 for batteries, rare earths, and defense-critical raw materials, with €3 billion in funding to catalyze non-Chinese supply chains . Europe is shifting from risk manager to power broker – but implementation has historically lagged ambition.

The $16.25 valuation is an 11% premium to PSNL's unaffected stock price on July 16, 2026 (before rumors leaked) and a 28% premium over its 30-day VWAP.

Unanimous board approval is backed by heavy insider support. Merck (a 13% holder) signed a binding agreement to vote in favor of the deal and Tempus will also vote its existing 12% stake in favor (25% Total).

Personalis negotiated a specific downside protection clause. They can abandon the merger entirely if Tempus's stock price falls below a $46 "Lower Floor Price" at closing.

There's a $76.8M termination fee. Personalis pays Tempus if they ditch the merger for a better offer. Tempus pays Personalis if the deal is blocked by antitrust regulators.

Regulatory Timeline and Updates:

• UK: The UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) already gave the green light on August 13.

• US: Tempus is voluntarily withdrawing and refiling its US Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) notification on September 2 to reset the standard 30-day regulatory waiting period.

• Outside Date: The initial deadline to close the deal is April 20, 2027, with automatic extensions built in up to April 20, 2028 if the only remaining hurdles are regulatory.

text:
Every cell in the body depends on thyroid hormone to regulate metabolism (the process of converting nutrients into usable energy). Because every cell contains thyroid hormone receptors, thyroid function has a profound influence on nearly every system in the body.

For most of human history, light wasn’t something we escaped. It was something we lived by. Our mornings began with the rising sun, our days unfolded outdoors, and our evenings naturally dimmed with the setting light.

Today, many of us wake to artificial light, spend our days indoors, and end them behind glowing screens. In many ways, modern life mimics one long winter, disrupting many of the environmental signals that help regulate healthy thyroid function and metabolism.

Sunlight is one of the body’s primary signals for regulating our internal clock. Each morning, natural light helps synchronize our circadian rhythm, which is closely connected to the hypothalamic pituitary thyroid axis, the communication network responsible for regulating thyroid hormone production and the daily rhythms of TSH.

Perhaps this helps explain why thyroid activity naturally shifts with the seasons. Our biology has always responded to changes in daylight. But sunlight doesn’t stop there.

One of the most exciting areas of research today is photobiomodulation, the use of red and near infrared light applied directly over the thyroid. 

Emerging peer reviewed studies in individuals with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis suggest this therapy may support thyroid tissue function, reduce markers of thyroid autoimmunity, and, in some participants, reduce the amount of thyroid medication needed to maintain healthy thyroid hormone levels. While this research is still emerging and should not replace medical care, it offers a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between light and thyroid health.

Perhaps one of the greatest reminders is this:

Your body doesn’t simply need nutrients.
It also needs the environmental signals it evolved with.

Morning sunlight.
Time outdoors.
Natural rhythms.
